#5680. Opinion: I research MAHA and Black Americans. The relationship is complicated — and fascinating

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Ezell is an epidemiologist and assistant professor at the University of Chicago Medical Center.

When one thinks about the key supporters of MAHA, they likely don’t envision Black people, and rightfully so. A 2025 poll from KFF and The Washington Post found that only 30% of Black Americans support the MAHA movement, compared with 43% of white Americans.

But the data belie a stark reality: On an issue-to-issue basis, Black people are strikingly aligned with MAHA, at least in terms of their concerns around the movement’s tentpole issues. I’ve been studying why, or rather how, this came to be.

According to a May poll from Global Strategy Group, 47% of Black people, compared with 35% of white people, strongly agree with the statements “I am concerned about environmental toxins and pesticides” and “I am concerned about ultra-processed foods and artificial ingredients in our food” — key MAHA flashpoints.

The same poll found that 51% of Black people, a staunch Democratic voting bloc, either strongly or somewhat agreed with the statement “I am skeptical of vaccines,” compared to 58% of Republicans and 28% of Democrats. Moreover, the poll found that 26% of Black people strongly or somewhat support eliminating fluoride from public drinking water, a not-so-secret desire of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This figure nearly mirrors the 28% of Republicans who also want the additive nixed from our water supply, while

This crossover makes some sense. MAHA is perhaps the sole part of the Trump administration’s sprawling attempt to remake American society that can be said to be, at least on the surface, apolitical. Its broad agenda amplifies everyday public health issues like food quality and safety while elevating thorny but universally relevant topics like Big Pharma’s role in the overmedicalization of Americans.

This explains why a number of people on the left who would seem to be politically opposed to MAHA sometimes begrudgingly, and sometimes warmly, endorse it. In recent months, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who appears to have 2028 ambitions, has glowingly discussed her conversations with MAHA activists and characterizes the MAHA cause as nonpartisan. Uber-progressive physician and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed actively campaigned on some of MAHA’s hallmark principles.

Many in clinical medicine have also come out in support of MAHA, or at least components of it. In The Atlantic, emergency physician Craig Spencer encouraged public health practitioners to swallow their pride in service of the lightning-in-a-bottle moment for reform that MAHA was serving up, aligning with a number of respected public health influencers who’ve encouraged the same kind of acquiescence.

To some, including me, this sudden embrace of MAHA and pandering to the movement’s voters looks like acute Stockholm syndrome. And that’s largely because its intentions are often assumed a priori to be politically neutral, and its origins are rarely questioned.

A January tweet from California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s press office noted that “MAHA started in California,” highlighting the likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender’s statewide ban on ultra-processed foods in 2025. In early October, Democrat Rep. Chellie Pingree (Maine), who made MAHA a centerpiece of her successful reelection campaign, tweeted that she’d “been fighting for a food system that puts people and farmers first long before the ‘MAHA movement.’”

But Black scholars and activists played the biggest role in bringing to light the systemic fissures in our health care and food systems that MAHA — and some left-leaning opportunists — now assume a gatekeeper role over.

Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Black activists around the country began to lead coordinated efforts to address the harms caused by industrial pollution in the U.S. and tackle the industrialization of the food system.

In 1969, Fannie Lou Hamer, a Black organizer, pioneered land cooperatives in Mississippi to usher in food sovereignty, aiming to curb her Black contemporaries’ increasing reliance on large, sprawling food production systems. Hamer foresaw what would become a reality in the 21st century: a loss of community control over food production and the proliferation of ultra-processed, unhealthy foodstuffs, a talking point deeply embedded in Kennedy Jr.’s Eat Real Food initiative.

In 1978, Black residents in Warren County, N.C., began organizing to protest a landfill that was poised to store some 60,000 tons of cancer-causing PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) in their rural, low-income community. Over the next several years, as legal motions to stop the state government-endorsed plan were quashed, hundreds of Black demonstrators would be arrested in nonviolent protests against the site. It wasn’t until two decades later that the protesters’ persistence would pay off: An $18 million site detoxification process was initiated in 2002 and completed in 2004.

It’s evident Kennedy, a trained environmental lawyer, learned a great deal from cases like these. When running as a presidential candidate in 2024, Kennedy made several direct appeals for addressing environmental injustice, the racially inequitable distribution of environmental harms in minority communities. For instance, during a visit to Loyola Marymount College while on the campaign trail, Kennedy discussed the legacy of polluting facilities and noted, “We’ll have a cleaner environment if rich people and white people have to bear the equal burdens for people who are poor among the minorities.”

This was a racial justice battle cry, virtually right out of “Dumping in Dixie,” a seminal environmental justice text authored by the godfather of the movement, Robert Bullard.

This past “woke” iteration of Kennedy is deeply at odds with the present version, considering the term “environmental justice” is now essentially forbidden in research grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health, and that the NIH has substantially curbed funding for studies focused on racial disparities.

Ultimately, MAHA’s template is a retread, warmed over and confusedly repackaged for the anti-science and contrarian crowd keen on bringing the culture wars as deep as possible into public health.

To this end, Kennedy’s subtle homages to Black activism have been undercut by his public commentary and policy, which in addition to distorting and cherry-picking aspects of evidence-based science, is imbued with MAGA’s distinctive brand of political grievance and racial myopia.

Even as Kennedy and his MAHA consorts have cribbed from the Black activist playbook, they’ve actively undermined and misrepresented Black identity and culture. Part of this has been accomplished by playing into the fears that many Black people harbor against doctors and the medical establishment, including by using disinformation to gin up concerns about vaccines in Black communities, a population already highly skeptical of immunizations. Going back to the Tuskegee experiments, where Black men’s treatment for their syphilis was withheld, Black populations have held significant distrust for clinicians and medical research.

In a Kennedy-produced documentary, “Medical Racism: The New Apartheid,” a piece of unabashed agitprop released in 2021, the current health secretary recruited Nation of Islam Minister Tony Muhammad to help peddle the fantastical claim that vaccine-makers are nefariously targeting Black kids as a means of widening racial disparities.

And this tactic isn’t new. Republicans and anti-abortion activists have long sought to curry the support of Black people by claiming abortion is a subversive tool being used by white liberals and medical elites to facilitate Black genocide.

On a podcast before the 2024 election, Kennedy argued that Black people have a stronger immune response to certain antigens than other races, thereby warranting a change in their vaccine scheduling, a scientifically debunked notion that he nevertheless doubled down on during his Senate confirmation hearing.

He has also been a vocal cheerleader for a controversial study to assess the effects of hepatitis B vaccine dose timing on a cohort of infants in the small West African country of Guinea-Bissau, where local officials recently raided the offices of an RFK-Jr.-allied research group supporting the study.

The most positive reflections on MAHA have largely centered around the trope of the genteel “MAHA mom,” a racially coded term painting white mothers as singularly focused, doting caregivers who just want their kids to be healthy. Contrast this with Kennedy’s thoughts on Black parents. In a 2024 podcast, he advocated “reparenting” Black kids with ADHD, a population he said was “just standard put on Adderall, SSRIs, benzos, which are known to induce violence.”

It’s no surprise that prominent Black politicians haven’t accepted the Faustian bargain that MAHA represents and rallied around MAHA as their white peers have. Kennedy’s vision of and prescription for Black America is antiquated and dangerous. The spoils MAHA may otherwise offer — if we’re willing to whitewash its ethos — are no consolation.

With the midterms serving up a colossal defeat for MAGA, it stands to reason that MAHA’s day of reckoning may not be too far off. Calls for RFK. Jr’s impeachment are already bubbling among Democratic party leaders, a group that no longer needs to actively curry favor with MAHA proponents.

Only time will tell if the movement and its baggage can thrive without a titanic political force like MAGA behind it. Public health will be better off if it doesn’t.

Jerel Ezell is an epidemiologist and assistant professor at the University of Chicago Medical Center.

#5679. Opinion: 3 things new governors must do to lead on health

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Cohen is former secretary of health and human services for North Carolina and former director of the CDC. Montz is former chief deputy at the Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services and former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS.

As former state health leaders, we know the challenges and opportunities facing the 21 new governors stepping into their roles on Jan. 1. Health is what lets people go to work, raise their kids, and enjoy the years they’ve earned. Health is also the largest line item in most state budgets and a primary driver of the affordability crisis for American families.

To succeed in harnessing the power of state government to improve health and well-being and tackle affordability, new governors need to do three things: hire operators, see the trouble that’s already here, and set a focused agenda.

A governor’s three most consequential health appointments are the state’s health and human services secretary, Medicaid director, and public health officer. The attributes that matter most in these leaders include, foremost, a track record in getting things done in and with government. Look for leaders who have managed large government teams, legislative processes, and stakeholder associations.

Expertise matters, especially in this moment. The Medicaid director should understand evolving federal financing rules, eligibility systems and operations, and the state’s Medicaid delivery system, which is often managed care. The public health officer should have run an outbreak response.

Relationship and communication skills are paramount in managing a large government agency through change. The governor’s health leaders need to have the trust of legislators of both parties, hospitals, health centers and other health care providers, local leaders, consumer groups, and community partners. This team will be the state’s public face and primary communicators in a crisis.

Issues that are already hitting states hard will become even more challenging in the coming year. Governors-elect should be briefed on them now.

Medicaid eligibility requirements: In expansion states, work requirements and more frequent redeterminations of Medicaid eligibility are set to go live on Jan. 1, 2027. These new road rules require expansion adults ages 19 to 64 to document 80 hours a month of work, school, or service and to prove eligibility for Medicaid every six months. Experience shows that coverage losses will be high and come from paperwork, not because residents aren’t eligible for Medicaid anymore. These federal mandates will have major local impact. Governors should know:

Measles: The U.S. has already recorded more cases of measles in 2026 than in any year since 1991, nearly all among unvaccinated people. An international review this week will assess whether the country has lost its elimination status. On day one, governors should know kindergarten vaccination rates by county, confirm outbreak plans and surge staffing, and have a crisis communication plan at the ready for when an outbreak hits.

Medicaid program integrity: Medicaid program integrity is a concern for every state, and governors should expect CMS scrutiny to continue. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has required all 50 states to submit Medicaid provider revalidation plans and has withheld federal payments from at least one state. New executive health teams should assume a review is coming and give the state’s fraud and inspector general units the resources they need and make program integrity the state’s own priority.

Aligning priorities across program and funding silos is a core job of the governor and their health team. With sustained leadership and clear focus, a state can unlock enormous untapped potential across Medicaid, public health, social services, insurance regulation, the state employee health plan, and rural health funds. This should include clarity of which levers states control and which require federal partnership (such as Medicaid or ACA waivers and financing changes). Governors should prioritize action in those areas that the state can drive.

Governors should elevate key priorities to name in the first State of the State, fund in the first governor’s budget, and show results within two years. Strong candidates for priorities are:

Coverage: Ten states still have not expanded Medicaid access. For these states, four of which have new governors coming in January, expansion should be a priority. It’s still the biggest lever for coverage, rural hospital sustainability, and funding. In any state, governors can create a public option to make premiums more affordable and give struggling small employers relief.

Affordability: The first affordability priority for new governors — indeed, for all governors —  should be relief that families feel soon. Options to consider include capping out-of-pocket costs for high-use medications, making primary care available before the deductible kicks in, and reining in pharmacy costs through pharmacy benefit manager reform and drug price transparency.

States can also protect patients from surprise and excessive bills by limiting facility fees, strengthening hospital financial assistance standards, and adding medical debt protections.

Lasting affordability also requires bringing down the overall cost of care — something that is a shared responsibility across hospitals, insurers, and drug manufacturers. Governors can set cost growth targets and compel public reporting. They can use combined state purchasing power to drive value-based payment and cut administrative waste. They can also pay for care models that improve access and chronic disease management, such as value-based primary care and technology-enabled models aligned with Medicare’s ACCESS model.

Rural health: Every state received a Rural Health Transformation Program award, averaging about $200 million a year through 2030, and later funding depends on meeting the commitments in each state’s application. It’s critical to avoid the “peanut butter” approach — spreading the dollars over so many priorities that the money is thin for all. Set a few measurable goals, such as keeping obstetric and emergency services open, building regional referral networks, and building and maintaining primary care and behavioral health access. Plan for how to sustain the work after federal funding ends.

States should approach artificial intelligence thoughtfully as they invest rural health and other state funds. Used well, AI holds promise to improve access, health, and the work of state government. Used poorly, it can drive up costs and deny care.

To guide AI investment, governors should set clear, simple rules that protect consumers through disclosure, consent, and clinician review, aligned with other states. Use Medicaid managed care contracts and state purchasing to require disclosure of AI use and reporting of outcomes, steering vendors toward tools that improve access and affordability rather than AI automation billing wars. Start small with initiatives inside state government where AI can support your workforce including by piloting AI in chatbots, call centers, and eligibility processing, with human review of any decision that denies or ends coverage.

A divided government in Washington likely means few federal solutions are coming soon. States have always been laboratories of innovation, and that power has never been more critical to harness than at this moment.

Mandy Cohen, M.D., M.P.H., is former secretary of health and human services for North Carolina and former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She is a national adviser at Manatt, a legal and consulting firm. Ellen Montz, Ph.D., is former chief deputy at the Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services (Virginia Medicaid) and former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. She is a managing director at Manatt.

#5678. CareSource launches $1M grant program to support AI-powered solutions

CareSource launches $1M grant program to support AI-powered solutions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nonprofit insurer CareSource is launching a $1 million program that aims to back responsible AI solutions in healthcare.

The initiative, launched through the CareSource Foundation, is seeking proposals for ways to advance and identify deployments for AI that can drive better outcomes and address barriers for individuals enrolled in Medicaid or who otherwise struggle to access care.

The program will provide up to $1 million over the course of two years to ensure that the tool can deliver on meaningful and scalable benefits for the communities it serves.

Erhardt Preitauer, CEO of CareSource, said in an email to Fierce Healthcare that AI offers the potential to improve not just patient care but the experience for providers too as they navigate complex conditions.

"I'm a big believer that when technology, healthcare and the people in our communities rally around a shared purpose, magic can happen," said Preitauer. "Leaving no stone unturned is the only way we can make healthcare work better for people, and AI gives us the power to explore every possibility."

The program will include two phases. First, interested applicants can submit shorter proposals, with the goal of generating interest. Applications that are selected to move on will be tasked with submitting a more fleshed-out proposal, including details on implementation, AI governance and sustainability.

CareSource is aiming to identify solutions that are ready for implementation and has the potential for scale. Potential focus areas include care coordination, member engagement, behavioral health and rural healthcare. Solutions should use AI to support care delivery, but it should not replace human judgement or oversight, the insurer said.

To be eligible, a qualified nonprofit organization must be leading the effort, according to the announcement. Technology companies, academic researchers, healthcare organizations and community-based groups can also play a role as partners.

#5677. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5675. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

#5674. The 10 Affordable Cities Where Homeowners Are the Least Locked In by Housing Costs

Many homeowners who began the year hoping to move may now be locked in by soaring mortgage rates that threaten to nearly double their monthly payments—but a handful of budget-friendly markets still offer relief.

These rare pockets of affordability are clustered primarily across the Midwest and South, including Pittsburgh; Baltimore; Buffalo, NY; New Orleans; Detroit; Birmingham, AL; San Antonio, TX; Akron, OH; McAllen, TX; and Philadelphia.

Nationally, the typical U.S. mortgage holder pays roughly $1,300 in principal and interest per month. If they were to purchase a home today, that payment would surge by more than 85%, or $1,100, according to a new report on America's "locked-in" homeowners from Realtor.com®.

The market's current predicament can be traced to the COVID-19 pandemic years, when historically low mortgage rates whipped up a buying and refinancing frenzy. As of July 2026, more than a quarter (27%) of all fixed-rate mortgages on record for single-family homes and condominiums were originated in 2020 and 2021 alone.

Once mortgage rates began climbing again in 2022, homebuying and refinancing both hit a wall. Over the subsequent four years, only about 1 in 4 mortgages on record was originated, highlighting the sharp pullback in activity as a result of higher borrowing costs.

"For those who purchased before mortgage rates shot sharply higher, the sentiment of 'I couldn’t afford to buy my home today' continues to ring true in most cases, contributing to historically low mobility and some of the leanest for-sale inventory on record," notes Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

In other words, homeowners who were fortunate enough to secure a sub-4% mortgage rate at the height of the pandemic are reluctant to list. Trading up or downsizing today means taking out a mortgage with a steeply higher rate, gobbling up a much bigger share of their income.

Just how much bigger? Purchasing a median-priced home at the Oct. 22 rate of 7.32%, assuming a 14.3% down payment, would translate into a monthly principal and interest payment of nearly $2,500, almost double the $1,300 typical owners currently pay.

However, in parts of the U.S. where home prices remain accessible, the "lock-in" effect is felt less acutely, keeping inventory—and people—moving and creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

"The affordability of these markets enables mobility, which means the typical outstanding mortgage rate is higher, which helps reduce the payment jump associated with moving, which reinforces affordability," explains Jones.

In the South and Midwest, approximately three-quarters of mortgages carry a rate below 6%, compared to 78% nationally.

Additionally, nearly a quarter of all outstanding mortgages in these two regions were originated within the past four years at 6% or higher, compared with 21.6% in the Northeast and 17.7% in the West.

"That mix means fewer homeowners in these regions are clinging to 3%–4% rates, which lessens the lock-in effect," says Jones.

Across the 100 largest metros, Pittsburgh stands out as the nation's least "locked in" housing market, where a seller purchasing a new home in town would see a 43% increase in their monthly mortgage payment—a modest penalty compared to the 165% in San Jose, CA.

Baltimore is a close second, with a 45% payment gap, followed by Buffalo, at 46.1%.

"A 3% mortgage is a great reason to stay in a house, but it's not always a great reason to stay in a house that no longer fits your life," Colleen Collier, associate broker at Re/Max Plus in Buffalo, tells Realtor.com.

The latest housing data reflects the market's mobility and affordability. In October, Buffalo posted the largest year-over-year increase in active listings (+34.4%) among the 50 largest metros, paired with the largest growth in new listings (+13.1%).

At the same time, the median listing price in the metro registered at $259,999, down 2.8% from a year ago and sitting more than $155,000 below the national median.

Collier notes that while more local homeowners are willing to make a move, it does not necessarily mean they are comfortable giving up their low rates. They are being compelled by life changes.

"They're retiring, downsizing, or relocating to be closer to family," says the broker. "Many are looking to reduce maintenance and their overall living expenses. Others are relocating to a warmer climate. ... They're taking the equity they've built and putting it toward their next purchase."

Collier recently represented clients who sold their home of 30 years to downsize into an apartment. They were able to get a final sale price well above asking, which was enough to cover at least 10 years of apartment living, and fund future travel plans and a new car.

"What made this experience so rewarding was that the homeowner had more equity than they realized," says Collier. "After more than three decades in their home, selling wasn't simply about moving into a smaller space. It was about creating financial freedom and enjoying the next chapter of life."

In Akron, a typical homeowner currently paying just $868 per month should expect to see that figure rise nearly 62% under present-day market conditions—well above Buffalo’s level but still a far cry from the most locked-in coastal markets.

"The financial difference between staying in a home with a low mortgage rate and purchasing another home may be less dramatic here than in higher-priced markets," Mike Valerino, CEO of Akron Cleveland Association of Realtors, tells Realtor.com. "However, that doesn't mean the mortgage rate lock-in effect has disappeared."

According to Valerino, in Summit County, where Akron is located, new listings and closed sales were down in September while the average sales price increased, suggesting that despite the market's relative affordability, homeowners are still weighing the financial implications of moving.

"Life circumstances remain important drivers of housing decisions," he says, echoing Collier's argument. "Growing families need more space, empty nesters may want to downsize, and job changes, retirement, and family considerations can create reasons to move that outweigh the financial benefits of staying put."

At the same time, Valerino says that Akron's relative affordability does not insulate buyers and sellers from the challenges affecting housing markets nationally.

"The mortgage lock-in effect may be less severe here, but the cost of the next home still plays a major role in whether someone decides to move," he says.

In roughly a third of the 100 largest U.S. metros, a move to a median-priced home would more than double the monthly payment. Ballooning borrowing costs disproportionately penalize expensive coastal and fast-growing markets, leaving local homeowners feeling virtually trapped by their lower mortgages.

According to the latest data, the most "locked-in" markets in the U.S. include Portland, ME, San Jose, and Los Angeles, where anticipated monthly mortgage payments surged by more than 140%, grinding mobility to a halt. That friction has severely squeezed inventory and put upward pressure on home prices, sidelining first-time and budget buyers.

"Because homes in these markets are already expensive, buyers typically rely on larger mortgage balances, which amplifies the impact of rising rates," says Jones.

In Portland, for instance, a current owner holding on to a 4% mortgage rate makes a median payment of $1,270 per month. If they were to purchase a home comparable to theirs with a 26.2% down payment and took out a 7.32% mortgage, their payment would jump a staggering 167% to $3,392.

Mortgage rates would have to drop a long way from their current 7.18% level to close the gap between what current owners pay and what a buyer would pay today.

Rates would need to reach 6% before half of U.S. households could afford the median-priced home, and even then a move would still mean a payment about 62% higher than what the typical mortgage holder spends now.

Crucially, however, Jones stresses that falling mortgage rates alone are not enough. Because home values have appreciated significantly over the past few years, buying a median-priced home with a 4% mortgage would still cost about 29% more per month than what existing homeowners pay on their original COVID-19-era loans.

Valerino agrees, maintaining that there is no one "magic number" that will unlock the market.

"Rates in the 5% range could make moving more attractive to some homeowners, but affordability involves more than the interest rate," he says. "Home prices, property taxes, insurance, and accumulated equity all factor into that decision."

The market is poised to loosen gradually rather than all at once as more households buy in to higher rates, softening price growth narrows the gap, and rising incomes boost buying power.

"The lower-priced Midwest and South markets, where the gap is smallest and more loans carry higher rates, are likely to see the most activity first," predicts Jones. "Large coastal markets will need both lower rates and lower prices or significantly higher incomes before sellers feel free to move."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

Carelon agrees to pay $10M to settle ghost network, coverage denial allegations in New York" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Carelon will pay more than $10 million across two settlements in New York over mental health networks and coverage denials.

The company, a division of Elevance Health, will pay $2.35 million in penalties, fees and costs as well as up to $8 million in restitution for members who paid out-of-pocket for out-of-network mental healthcare, to reimburse those whose claims were improperly denied or to overhaul its networks.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said in an announcement that the settlements resolve two investigations from her office that determined the company misled members by directing them to seek care from providers that were out-of-network—through so-called "ghost networks"—and improperly denied coverage for treatment for substance abuse disorder.

James noted that Carelon administers behavioral health benefits for multiple plans, including Anthem Blue Cross, EmblemHealth, Independent Health and the Empire Plan, which covers state and local government workers.

Across these insurers, Carelon manages behavioral health benefits for more than 4 million people in the state, James said.

The alleged behavior also goes against a 2015 agreement with the AG's office, where the company agreed that it would maintain accurate provider networks and "use approved criteria" when denying substance abuse treatments.

"When someone is ready to seek help for a mental health condition or addiction, every day matters," said James. “Carelon left New Yorkers calling provider after provider who could not see them and made it harder for people to get the treatment to which they were entitled."

"These settlements will help people get the care they need and put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets," she said.

Elevance Health said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare that it is committed to ensuring patients have access to the most up-to-date provider information.

"Carelon Behavioral Health is committed to helping people find and access high-quality mental health and substance use disorder care. Accurate, up-to-date provider information is an important part of that effort," the company said. "We continue to invest in tools and processes that support accurate provider information and work closely with providers and other partners to help connect consumers with the care they need."

Carelon was hit with a lawsuit in April over the alleged ghost networks and their impact on the Empire Plan in particular. In the case, plaintiff's attorneys conducted secret shopper calls to analyze Carelon's network, calling 300 providers. Just 17% of those contacted took insurance and were open to new patients.

These "ghost networks" have also drawn concern in other markets, such as for maternal care services in Medicaid and in Medicare Advantage. A study released last month found that commercial plans also routinely have inaccurate provider directories.

#5671. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5669. American Cancer Society revises guidelines, urges routine PSA screening for prostate cancer

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

In a major change to screening guidelines, the American Cancer Society recommended on Thursday that American men between ages 50 and 69 at an average risk of prostate cancer should test their prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood levels every two years.

The prior guidelines, released in 2010, left testing for average-risk men to their discretion, after assessing cancer risk with a physician.

Similarly, PSA testing recommendations were strengthened for high risk groups — Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer. They are now encouraged to get PSA-based screening yearly starting at 45. Black men in particular disproportionately die from prostate cancer, and the guideline authors said they hope that increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with cancers at advanced stages.

Then, starting at 70, the decision on whether to continue screening becomes individualized as the balance of benefit and harm is not as clear after that age. Screening should be interrupted after 80, or in men who are not expected to live another 10 years.

The changes reflect recent findings that screening through PSA levels reduced disease specific mortality for certain men, bringing the indicator back into specialists’ good graces. Once a preferred biomarker to identify risk of prostate cancer, routine PSA screening had fallen out of favor — and was dropped from the guidelines in 2010 — for its lack of specificity, which resulted in many men undergoing follow-up procedures when they had no cancer, or very slow-growing tumors.

The U.S. Preventive Service Task Force, a federally appointed panel of outside experts, has not changed its guidelines since the new evidence became available in 2025, and continues to recommend against routine, population-wide PSA screening, suggesting instead individualized decision-making. But the panel, whose recommendations determine the preventive services that insurers must cover, has announced an upcoming update.

The cutoff for PSA levels to be considered high is established as 3.0 nanograms/milliliter or higher for men aged 45 to 69 years old. This is an important clarification, said James Eastham, chief of urology at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Most PSA blood tests in the United States, when they’re reported, say under 4.0 [ng/ml] is normal, but it really should be under 3,” he said. “I think [the update] will hopefully help primary care physicians refer folks a little bit earlier.”

To limit the risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, the guidelines also now recommend two elevated PSA readings, followed by an MRI scan and/or testing for other biomarkers of prostate cancer, with the aim of reducing the number of patients undergoing biopsies. “We just wanted to give a little bit of flexibility for folks who cannot easily obtain an MRI,” said William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the ACS and a contributing author of the guidelines, about including both biomarkers and MRIs as a possible step following elevated PSA levels. However, he noted that an MRI would still be recommended prior to biopsy, should a biomarker test come back abnormal.

Though there are a variety of biomarkers, the guidelines don’t recommend one over the other. Dahut said ACS researchers  intend to look more closely at biomarkers to establish which may be more effective in predicting a more aggressive cancer.

“I think the new guidelines are certainly a balanced approach for early detection of prostate cancer,” said Eastham. “There have been many men undergoing unnecessary biopsies, and many low risk cancers that were subsequently overtreated,” he said. By recommending some steps between an elevated PSA and a biopsy, he said, the new recommendations reflect the evidence that while being a good biomarker, PSA alone would identify too many men as biopsy candidates.

Finally, the guidelines emphasize the importance of active surveillance in men with slow growing cancer: “If you screen more men, you’re going to find more men with early-stage disease, and we need to be strong in our position that that does not mean that you need to rush for therapies or that you need to have therapies at all.”

For Eddie Baynes, a 56-year-old prostate cancer survivor and advocate, the new guidelines “hit the nail on the head” when it comes to recommending routine PSA screening. As a Black man, he knew he was at higher risk of developing prostate cancer, yet it wasn’t until the fraternity he belonged to organized a screening event that he, at 52, started getting regular PSA tests with his bloodwork. Though routine screening wasn’t part of the ACS recommendation at the time, it led to a cancer diagnosis and a prostatectomy.

That’s why he’s been advocating for men to get PSA levels tested, and relatively frequently. With the new guidelines, men like him will start routine screening earlier than he did. “Part of my advocacy is getting tested more frequently. So now, just to have that announcement coming from the American Cancer Society, it just makes what I’ve been urging individuals to do for a while stronger,” he said.

#5667. ‘Wake-Up Call’: Trump’s Former Housing Commissioner Says New Congress Must ‘Get Serious’ About Housing Affordability

Democrats and Republicans both understand Americans are broadly worried about the cost of living, and a former Trump administration official says it's time for both parties to take action.

In a bitterly divided Washington, DC, it remains to be seen whether lawmakers will heed that call when the 120th Congress convenes in January, with Democrats back in control of both the House and Senate.

After campaigning hard on affordability concerns, Democratic leaders say they'll use their new majorities to focus on the cost of living. Republican leaders admit they didn't heed voter concerns about the economy. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has threatened to use his veto power freely.

The summer's 21st Century Road to Housing Act, with its dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape, was a rare example of bipartisan consensus. What follows that landmark legislation remains an open question.

Republicans want more deregulation while Democrats aim for more support for housing. And each side must now contend with an upswell of hard-liners pushing policies that could radically change the market.

Many of the prominent names in both parties who built the housing bill are returning, including Rep. French Hill (R-AR), Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC). They're likely to return to the House and Senate committees on housing and banking.

"Now is a wake-up call," Trump's former Federal Housing Commissioner Frank Cassidy tells Realtor.com®. "Senate, House, White House. Everyone needs to get serious about tackling and addressing housing affordability. It can't be ignored anymore."

Congress had some bipartisan momentum to provide tax incentives that encourage the buying and selling of homes.

Colin Allen, executive director of the American Property Owners Alliance and a former housing issues adviser to Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), said that could mean some ideas pitched in this Congress could come back as part of larger bills.

"They have good working relationships and have already done some bipartisan work," Allen said.

Take, for instance, the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act, which would create a new tax credit to buy and renovate homes in economically distressed areas. The bill drew 70 sponsors from both parties.

Real estate groups put in significant groundwork this year to update the capital gains tax scheme for the first time in more than 30 years. The More Homes on the Market Act came close to 200 sponsors in Congress. It would double the exclusion for many filers. It's been floating around Congress for several years and has been a target of the National Association of Realtors® and other groups.

Trump expressed some support for changing the capital gains tax scheme, though a specific plan hasn't yet materialized from the White House.

"We've done a lot of legwork to get folks behind it," Allen said. "If we're looking at a larger bipartisan bill, you can see a scenario where a few of those ideas get together. The debt limit is coming up, and there are a few other opportunities to package together."

Hill and Republicans have lobbied for more changes to the financing system. They were able to get several banking reform provisions into the Road to Housing bill. They've also floated new financial reforms to change and rescind banking rules codified in the Dodd-Frank Act and the Basel III accords after the subprime mortgage crisis. Republicans say they've chased smaller banks out of the housing market.

This summer, Hill called Dodd-Frank a "massive overreaction."

"For our smaller banks, the new regulations were a poor fit, burying them in compliance work and bureaucratic red tape," Hill said. "Instead of helping customers, their attention was diverted to filling out forms and satisfying examiners."

Mortgage reform is also a lever Congress can pull. A bipartisan group of six members of Congress pitched the First-Time Homebuyer Affordability Act this summer. It would expand access to low-interest mortgages for first-time homebuyers.

"By expanding access to financing, we can help more hardworking families achieve homeownership, strengthen our communities, and build long-term financial security," said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-IL) said.

Then there's the matter of new construction. Democrats and Republicans found some bipartisan ground in cutting some of the federal red tape that blocks construction of new homes.

Republicans also said they favor rolling back Build America Buy America provisions. Builders, they say, have complained that the sourcing requirements are time-consuming and expensive. But they've also targeted some environmental regulations that Democrats passed.

Dennis Shea, chair of the J. Ronald Terwilliger Center for Housing Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells Realtor.com that some public housing authorities saw costs climb by double digits. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's waiver process is every bit as time-consuming for builders.

"A sentiment exists in both parties to change the rules, but ultimately it takes an act of Congress to exempt housing," Shea said.

Hill and other lawmakers such as Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) have said that Congress' action should shift some burden onto states to implement reforms at the local and state level. The American Enterprise Institute said this year that state and local policy changes could boost annual homebuilding by six figures. But many of those new homes are accessory dwelling units.

Congress and the White Hose also found common ground on manufactured housing reform. All sides recognize they need to keep eyeing supply-side reforms, says Cassidy.

"Ultimately, the problem in this country is supply," Cassidy adds. "You could lower rates to 2% tomorrow, and all that will do is increase home values. It's not going to solve the underlying issue."

The other big question will be funding of the many provisions created under the Road to Housing Act. While the provisions in the bill were bipartisan, Congress must still approve funding for some of those programs. Some of those discussions are coming in the 2028 fiscal budget and beyond.

Over the months of negotiations on the Road to Housing bill, some Republicans took issue with unfunded mandates in it. Concerns about funding programs, and at what level, could spill over into congressional proceedings in coming years.

Tony Marquez, director of American University's real estate program, who has a long career in real estate and banking, tells Realtor.com that the industry is still amenable to a few different ideas for how to solve housing. It doesn't rely on one side's control of the government.

"My un-professional assessment is we'll have a certain amount of gridlock over a number of years where Democrats may come up with some suggestions," Marquez says. "But the answer to affordable housing is not just one silver bullet. It can have many elements."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Happy Thursday. We’ve got a great lineup for you today, including an inside look at shuffles within the Senate’s health committee, and what it might mean for “Medicare for All.”

The American Cancer Society released a major update to its guidelines today, recommending testing for prostate-specific antigen blood levels every two years starting at age 50 for men with an average risk of prostate cancer. Men in high-risk groups, like Black men and men with a significant history of prostate cancer in the family, are urged to get tested annually starting at 45. The guideline’s authors hope that increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with cancers at advanced stages, as this demographic is disproportionately represented in prostate cancer mortality.

The changes reflect recent findings that screening through PSA levels reduced disease-specific mortality for certain men. It had fallen out of favor for its lack of specificity before recent findings returned it to specialists’ good graces. Read more from STAT’s Annalisa Merelli.

The Senate health committee is in the spotlight once again.

Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee members announced they will vote next week on whether to nominate Heidi Overton as commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. Republicans are still in power in this lame duck session, but Overton’s approval is not a given, STAT’s Margaret Manto explains, since a key Republican hasn’t said whether he backs her.

And colleague John Wilkerson noted Tuesday that Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) plans to move the party towards supporting “Medicare for All” once he becomes chair of the committee in January. But he’ll have a new Republican colleague to spar with.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) announced yesterday that he will forgo his leadership of the Senate homeland security committee to join HELP as the top Republican next year. Why is this bureaucratic shuffling noteworthy? The senator used the homeland security committee’s unusually powerful subpoena authority to accuse Anthony Fauci, without evidence, of conspiring to cover up the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic. Committee members voted along party lines to hold the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director in contempt of Congress.

Moving to the health committee will allow Rand to fight with Sanders over Medicare for All and all manner of other health issues.

(Most of the information about Paul came from John Wilkerson and our D.C. Diagnosis newsletter. If you want puns and great updates about which senators STAT reporters are chasing down in the bowels of Congress, you can sign up here.)

Body mass index is a flawed measure for obesity, but it remains deeply entrenched in global medical systems. If the world replaced it, obesity rates would increase and millions of people’s obesity diagnoses could flip, according to a new study.

Experts took a framework developed last year that offers a new understanding of how weight can impact a person’s health outcomes and applied it to obesity rates in the United States, the United Kingdom, China, and Spain. After analyzing 844,000 participants, the researchers calculated that BMI-based obesity missed 6.2% of adults compared to the new metric.

The measure ditches BMI’s focus on a person’s height and weight to include where fat is stored in a person’s body, most notably abdominal fat. It could have major implications for accurately assessing the mortality risk from obesity. Read more about the study from STAT’s Andrew Joseph.

Two new First Opinion pieces explore how the movement’s history informs its present. In one, professor Jerel Ezell argues that MAHA has coopted strategies from Black environmentalists fighting systemic health and food system fissures for decades. “Even as Kennedy and MAHA have cribbed from the Black activist playbook, they’ve actively undermined” Black Americans, he writes.

In another, professor Gavin Yamey argues that it’s not surprising key leaders are standing by convicted rapist Russell Brand, given the movement’s history of cozying up to violent men. “There is a rot of toxic masculinity and violence at MAHA’s core,” Yamey writes. Read more.

If you’ve ever spent months cycling through different doses of the same drug to find one that works, it could be your pharmacogenes at work. This set of genes affect how your body responds to prescription drugs, impacting what dose works for you and potential side effects.

Scientists have just identified thousands of new variants in these genes, thanks to a study using data from nearly 100,000 Americans through the National Institute of Health’s All of Us program. The advances are partly due to the program’s collection of genetic data from diverse backgrounds.

The study found that every participant carried at least one variant in the 16 pharmacogenes they studied, and that one in four participants had taken a medication that could be affected by these variants — everything from selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors to chemotherapy. Anil Oza has the write up.

#5665. Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027

Duet nabs $15M series A, plans to launch first NP-led ACO in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Nurse practitioner-owned primary care practice network Duet secured $15 million in series A funding to expand its clinic network and grow its partnerships and team.

Kairos led the funding round, with participation from Lerer Hippeau.

Kairos co-founder and co-CEO Alex Fiance said in a statement the company is “one of those rare businesses where everybody wins.”

“It reaches patients in need, helps clinicians become business owners, and brings costs down for the payers and the U.S. government by catching problems early,” Fiance said. “We believe Duet has the potential to reshape care across the country in a highly scalable way and are excited to help fuel their growth.”

Duet is the largest network of independent NP-owned primary care practices in the U.S., the company says. It helps practices earn compensation through its various partnerships with insurers, including Anthem, Cigna and Centene.

Duet Founder and CEO Jonathan Goldberg told Fierce Healthcare the company’s platform “combines practice advisors with AI-powered tools” to offload administrative work and give NPs more time for patient care.

“Our technology identifies people who are drifting out of care and gets them scheduled. It threads together patient data ahead of every visit, so an NP knows who is at risk and what to focus on,” Goldberg said. “And we help extend care into the home for those who need extra attention with remote technology and wraparound support.”

Goldberg continued, “There’s a lot stacked against small practices. Our mission is to help NPs show up for people that the system has overlooked.”

Patients visiting Duet clinics had an overall NPS of 92 across approximately 400,000 visits a year, Goldberg said.

“Patients often comment that this is the first time they felt heard, had someone take the time to read through their chart, or had a condition diagnosed that other clinicians had dismissed,” Goldberg said. “The clinical results follow from that. Practices that join Duet see preventive screenings for conditions like breast cancer and colon cancer rise 30%, and ER visits fall 20%. We also bring back 25% of the patients who are unengaged, and those are the patients who tend to end up worse off.”

The company has raised $22.5 million to date and works with more than 130 clinics across 21 states, executives say.

Goldberg said the company plans to use the fresh capital in three main ways: serve more clinics, deepen its value-based care partnerships with insurers and add engineers to its team. He added that Duet is launching an accelerator program in 2027 to help clinics “start strong.

Alongside the funding round, Duet announced it plans to launch the first-ever NP-led Medicare Accountable Care Organization (ACO) in 2027.

NPs will design and govern the company’s new model, which Goldberg says will allow practice owners to maintain “their autonomy while getting the technology and resources to strengthen their care.”

“NPs already practice prevention first, and this gives them a way to be recognized for it,” he said.
