#5609. Spec Versus Built-to-Order: Builders Navigate a Changing Market

For builders, the push and pull between speculative homes and built-to-order (BTO) homes is a classic struggle, reflecting the desire to balance operational efficiency against market demand. A favorable mix directly dictates a company’s profit margins, inventory risk, and customer satisfaction.

Spec homes allow builders to more directly compete with resale inventory, offering faster move-ins that can capture demand from buyers looking to move quickly. In strong markets, heavier spec exposure can increase sales velocity. In slower markets, builders with large levels of spec inventory are exposed to carrying costs and pricing risk.

A built-to-order approach reduces that inventory risk and offers buyers greater personalization in their final purchase. Built-to-order homes typically carry higher sales prices and translate into healthier margins while requiring buyers to wait longer to move in.

While several companies are steadfast in their approaches, such as the 100% spec commitments of Meritage Homes and CBH Homes and the 70% BTO target set by KB Home, the spec-BTO balance often shifts over time.

In the immediate post-pandemic period, many builders leaned more heavily into spec production. Unprecedented levels of demand and rapidly rising home prices set a backdrop for many large builders to offer more spec and quick move-in (QMI) homes because homes were absorbed at record levels. Similarly, the standardized production and simplified SKU packages helped builders guard against pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and labor shortages.

When mortgage rates began to spike in late 2023, a go-to-market approach with spec production remained prevalent to help buyers with certainty of price and move-in timing. Public builders at the time noted buyers were less willing to commit many months ahead given rate uncertainty and favored move-in ready homes. Builders favoring a heavier spec production mix were able to lean into financing incentives in the form of price cuts and rate buydowns to capture demand as economic uncertainty began to mount.

At the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026, one of the more notable themes to emerge is a more concentrated shift toward a higher built-to-order mix. KB Home began sharing its goal of a 70% BTO mix in the second quarter of 2025, noting the approach is customer-centric and that a design-forward, personalized approach is a differentiator in a market where incentives were prevalent.

“Our buyers choose their lot, floor plan, and personalized finishes. The result is a home that has a real specific value to the people who will live in it,” president and CEO Rob McGibney said during an earnings call with investors. “Homes built to customer specifications do not require heavy incentives to sell.”

Similarly, in the past couple quarters PulteGroup has highlighted its efforts to skew production more toward BTO homes, targeting a 60-40 mix.

“Our decision to build more spec homes once supply chains collapsed and build cycles effectively doubled was the right one at the time, but we much prefer having a growing backlog of sold homes,” PulteGroup president CEO Ryan Marshall shared during a recent earnings call.

The shift is not just occurring among large public builders, with Texas-based Stylecraft Builders reporting a shift toward the BTO model. After carrying essentially no to-be-built volume as recently as 12 to 18 months ago, the company is targeting a goal of 20% to 25% of sales from BTO orders.

Spec-heavy, BTO-heavy, and hybrid operators are all succeeding in the current challenging market. Rather than converging toward a single model, many builders increasingly view spec and BTO homes as complementary tools that can be adjusted based on market conditions, buyer behavior, and community characteristics.

For many builders, spec homes and BTO homes are not an either-or strategy, and a flexible approach that puts buyers front of mind yields the most successful results.

“They serve different customer needs and we want to execute both approaches well,” David Weekley Homes chief operating officer Ladd Fargo tells BUILDER. “The approximate mix depends on the market, buyer behavior, product type, and price point.”

The by-market approach is one that resonates strongly with Trumark Homes. As a private builder that serves as the western hub for Daiwa House, Trumark Homes leans into the local expertise of its division operators to meet the market with the best approach across its operating platforms in California, Colorado, and Washington.

“We know that we have strong operators in all our markets, and we trust our division teams to understand their buyer profiles, have a pulse on the competition, and utilize the data and tools available to plan accordingly,” Trumark Homes chief operating officer Steve Kalmbach says. “We will continue to be nimble and make the best strategic decisions for each community along the way.”

Fred McConnell, vice president of brand and performance marketing at Risewell Homes, tells BUILDER the company has become more intentional about creating built-to-order opportunities while maintaining a strong offering of quick move-in, spec homes. The mixed approach allows Risewell to be both consumer-led and market-responsive while aligning the company’s core brand platform, Built Well to Live Well.

“Our goal is to maintain the flexibility to respond to both the consumer and the dynamics of each individual market and community,” McConnell says.

Huntsville, Alabama-based Davidson Homes has seen a shift toward more BTO homes, but the company’s core strategy has not changed. CEO Brandon Jones says the company continues to meet buyers where they are, offering a solution for those who need to move in 45 days or those who want to choose every detail from homesite to interior finishes. He says the market has not picked a winner between spec or BTO and has instead rewarded builders who are disciplined about using both approaches.

“We start with the buyer, not the model. A lot of our industry has moved to one way of building,” Jones continues. “We’ve kept real personalization on the menu because buyers still want it, and we keep inventory on the ground because some buyers can’t wait. If we get the buyer right, the mix takes care of itself.”

CBH Homes has been a 100% spec builder since 2019, placing high value on the efficiencies gained in the building process and the simplification it provides to the buyer experience. The efficiencies gained early, from purchasing to scheduling trade partners, provide consistency and synergy that allows real value to be passed on to the buyers.

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable,” CBH Homes president and owner Corey Barton explains. “Our buyers can walk through a home, see the finishes, know the price, and know when they can move in. There are fewer unknowns.”

In the current market, where some builders are shifting approaches back toward a heavier BTO mix, Barton says CBH Homes still sees value in its 100% spec approach.

“When rates move or the right opportunity presents itself, our buyers don’t have to wait months for their home to be built,” Barton says. “On top of that, we know if a buyer has the option, they will want to make changes. Not allowing change orders allows us to keep costs down and construction efficiency high. Our goal isn’t to give the buyer a thousand decisions to make. It’s to do the work up front and create a beautiful, professionally designed home they can walk into and say, ‘This is it.’”

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable.”

Meritage Homes made a similar transition to an all-spec approach in 2016, focusing on the entry-level segment and leaning into competition with resale inventory. The builder’s shorter cycle times allow it to start homes later while also maintaining its 60-day closing guarantee. CEO Phillippe Lord says that its trade relationships and limited SKU counts set it apart from other builders and provide greater certainty to its vendor partners. While the builder has been market responsive and has increased its portfolio of move-up product given market conditions, Meritage Homes remains committed to its 100% spec approach.

Houston-based David Weekley Homes has leaned more heavily into move-in-ready spec homes to respond to a buyer that is placing more value on speed and certainty. Fargo says the shift has been driven by changes in buyer preferences rather than operational considerations.

“In a more uncertain market, many buyers are less willing to commit far in advance. They want to know what they’re buying, what it will cost, and when they can move in,” Fargo explains. “With quick move-in homes, the goal is not simply to build more inventory. It’s to be thoughtful about which homes we start, where we build them, the price points we target, and when the homes will be available.”

Similarly, Kalmbach notes Trumark Homes is seeing more contingent buyers in the current market. For these buyers, knowing what homes are available within a given time frame can be an important factor when they are looking to move but still must sell their previous home. Spec homes represent a solution for this buyer.

For builders that have leaned more heavily into a BTO approach, most cite personalization, design, and customer centricity as core factors. By allowing buyers to choose lots, floor plans, and personalized finishes, says KB Home’s McGibney, the company is best able to serve its customers.

“Buyers are already invested in and feel a connection to the homes they created,” McGibney said. “This is in contrast to a speculative business model where incentives are used to create value. In that model, the builder increases the incentives to the point at which the buyers believe they have been adequately compensated for features and finishes they did not choose.”

Erlanger, Kentucky-based Fischer Homes has seen an increase in interest in BTO homes in 2026, with the builder noting many buyers are placing an emphasis on personalization. BTO homes utilize Fischer Homes’ Design Studio, giving buyers the opportunity to select finishes and details that bring a unique vision to life and allowing the builder to deliver a home that reflects the specific needs and preferences of a particular buyer.

“The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

Beyond design, KB Home’s McGibney said a BTO-forward approach provides visibility, predictability, and limits risk. When a buyer commits and the company locks in a price, the direct costs can be established before a shovel hits the ground and KB Home knows the margin it will achieve at delivery before a home is started.

“We view this as a fundamentally lower risk profile than a speculative model, where a builder starts a home with an assumption for the future sales price and then finds later, at the time of sale, that market conditions may require price reductions or heavy incentives,” McGibney said. “The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

PulteGroup’s shift toward increasing built-to-order homes reflects the preferences of move-up and active-adult buyers. The builder’s lower cycle time allows it to selectively use rate buydowns to facilitate BTO sales while still achieving higher margins than on spec sales.

“[Move-up and active-adult buyers] are individuals who expect choice, and our operating model allows them to choose their preferred lot and select the options and upgrades they desire,” Marshall said.

For luxury builder Toll Brothers, the company can provide a design-forward experience even to spec buyers given its timing and approach to sales. The builder is focused on selling specs as early as possible in the construction cycle to allow personalization through its design studios, providing an experience that is like the BTO experience in all but name.

Several builders say the spec-versus-BTO decision is often less about philosophy and more about the product being sold and the customer buying it.

Decisions are closely tied to what different buyer segments prioritize in the purchase process. For entry-level buyers, value is often concentrated in price, payment certainty, and speed, characteristics that favor a spec approach. Move-up buyers, by contrast, are often purchasing for the home itself and have greater flexibility to prioritize personalization and design choices over speed.

“A first-time buyer is usually solving for payment and timing. A move-up buyer is solving for the home itself,” Jones of Davidson Homes explains. “Spec answers the first. Built-to-order answers the second.”

Kalmbach of Trumark Homes adds that buyers who are seeking customization in the home buying process are more likely to have the resources and time to engage earlier in the purchasing process, beginning with lot selection and continuing through the full design process. Fargo of David Weekley Homes echoes this distinction: standardized, higher-density, and entry-level products generally lend themselves more naturally to move-in-ready construction while higher-priced, customizable homes are better positioned for BTO.

“In general, building from the ground up allows customers the opportunity to personalize their home and participate more fully in the home building process,” says Fargo. “The longer timeline also gives our team members more time to understand the customer, build a relationship with them, and help create a home that is right for them. That relationship and the experience we provide the home building process are things we value.”

Vincent Salandro is an editor for Builder. He earned a B.A. in journalism and a B.S. in economics from American University.

#5608. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5607. As Kubernetes inference faces launch-day deadlines, CoreWeave deepens its open-source involvement

Cloud providers are scaling Kubernetes inference to serve frontier AI models, and the problems they encounter in production are helping shape the open-source projects they rely on.

CoreWeave Inc. sits near the center of that shift as AI agents reshape enterprise infrastructure. The company describes itself as a cloud built from the ground up for AI rather than retrofitted for it. Much of its growth traces back to the open nature of the container orchestration platform and the ecosystem around it, according to Yoshi Tamura (pictured, left), principal product manager at CoreWeave. CoreWeave has now upgraded to Platinum, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s highest corporate membership tier, to help shape how Kubernetes handles the large AI workloads its customers run.

“Without [Kubernetes], I don’t think we would’ve been able to get this kind of explosive growth,” Tamura said. “With this upgrade to Platinum, we indicate that we really mean it. We want to give back to the community. We want to be more involved.”

Tamura and Rita Zhang (right), principal software engineer at CoreWeave, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why CoreWeave upgraded to CNCF Platinum membership and what it takes to run Kubernetes inference in production. (* Disclosure below.)

Open source can get a model into a cluster, but that doesn’t guarantee it will perform at scale. CoreWeave’s inference team brings together infrastructure specialists and machine learning engineers, working with model labs and open-source inference engines to patch engines and runtimes for newly released models, according to Zhang.

“Running in production is hard,” Zhang said. “We work a lot with the open-source community, not just on the inference stack, but also with the model providers. Just because it’s on Hugging Face and you download the weights doesn’t mean it will work per your requirement. This is where we work very closely with the labs and the open-source community — like vLLM, SGLang — to make sure that for day-zero models we actually are able to patch the engines and provide our own kernels and patch the runtime.”

Kubernetes special interest groups rely on users to bring them production problems, such as finding nodes with the right devices and accounting for cluster topology when scheduling large training and inference jobs, Zhang explained. CoreWeave remains smaller than incumbent cloud providers and relies on open source more than many realize, Tamura added. Its work with leading AI model builders now gives it an early look at where frontier workloads are headed.

“We’re in a very unique position,” Tamura said. “Maybe we can actually find a way to kind of bring it back to the community and sort of lead which direction Kubernetes, a larger community, could go.”

#5606. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5605. North Korea Hackers Launches Elon Musk Memecoins to Launder $6.4B Binance Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

North Korea backed hackers have created Elon Musk themed memecoins to launder stolen crypto in the $6.4 billion Binance hack. The hackers are using fake trading activity to disguise the movement of stolen funds.

One of the tokens featured Musk beneath an “Elon 2028 President” banner. Five others carried cartoon animals, crude jokes and familiar dog-coin branding. All six were created within three days and quickly abandoned.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic identified 117,000 NEAR tokens, worth $430,000, passing through the homemade coins between November 5 and November 7. The operation offers another look at how North Korea’s crypto laundering networks are adapting their techniques to move stolen assets.

Elliptic identified six newly created tokens on the NEAR blockchain: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI and SINU. Each token was paired with NEAR in its own decentralized exchange liquidity pool. The hackers then used one group of wallets to purchase the tokens with stolen NEAR before another group sold them back.

North Korea’s launderers are creating their own meme coins to move funds stolen from Binance.Between November 5 and 7, they launched at least six tokens on NEAR, dressed up with meme-coin logos such as a monkey in a pink bow and a duck in front of a US flag. Stolen NEAR went…

This separated the buying and selling wallets, preventing the stolen funds from moving directly between them. The transactions consequently resembled ordinary crypto trading, with the receiving wallets appearing to collect proceeds from successful memecoin trades.

Blockchain investigators could still follow the money. Elliptic found that almost all trading activity came from wallets connected to the laundering operation. Outside buyers accounted for less than 1% of one token’s trading volume.

The operation was also remarkably inexpensive. Creating each token cost just as low as 25 NEAR, or worth around $90. Five of the six token creators received funding from wallets that had already participated in earlier token sales.

The tokens were effectively disposable. All six stopped trading by November 8, with the creators of four withdrawing remaining liquidity.

The technique does not erase the transaction trail. Instead, it introduces additional steps that slow investigators trying to connect stolen funds with their eventual destinations. The firm previously identified a similar approach following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. North Korean launderers moved at least $24 million through homemade tokens using the same basic mechanism.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The memecoin operation represents only a small fraction of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance. The approximately $6.43 billion was taken from the exchange on October 29, making it the largest crypto theft ever recorded. Binance estimated its losses at $6.3 billion.

The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Investigators have identified multiple laundering techniques since the breach, including cryptocurrency swaps, cross-chain transfers, and movements through decentralized finance platforms.

Approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen, representing around 44% of the stolen assets. This leaves billions requiring further tracing as investigators race to identify wallets and freeze assets wherever possible.

The use of North Korean hackers and memecoins adds another disposable layer to this operation. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional exchanges or direct wallet transfers, hackers can manufacture trading activity around virtually worthless tokens.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s expanding Layer 2 ecosystem is attracting developers looking to introduce faster transactions and programmable financial applications to the network.

Bitcoin Hyper is among the projects pursuing this approach, combining a Solana Virtual Machine-based execution environment with Bitcoin settlement. Its proposed infrastructure targets near-instant transaction finality alongside decentralized applications and DeFi functionality.

#5604. EXCLUSIVE: Inside a Record-Breaking $4.9 Million Riverside Townhouse in the Affluent Mountain Town of Basalt, CO

A record-breaking townhouse on the banks of the Roaring Fork River in Basalt, CO, has sold for $4,895,000.

At $1,973 per square foot, the transaction marks the highest price per foot ever paid for a townhouse in the midvalley Basalt area, according to Plus Real Estate, the group that handled the sale.

It’s also the fourth-highest residence to be sold in the mountain town, beating out a number of single-family homes.

The per square foot price of this sale is nearly 45% higher than the median for Basalt, which, according to Realtor.com® data from October 2026, was $1,361.

As one of only a few properties available on the water in Basalt River Park, it’s no surprise that the home was highly desired.

"It really comes down to scarcity," Walker Moriarty of Plus Real Estate tells Realtor.com.

"This is one of only five new townhomes on the river in Basalt, and new riverfront construction almost never comes up for sale in this area," the listing agent, who handled the sale, continues. "Add the views, proximity to downtown restaurants, the private elevator, and a true lock-and-leave setup. The buyers recognized it as a one-of-a-kind opportunity."

"Buyers who once only looked in Aspen are discovering what the midvalley offers," adds Tatiana Moriarty, also of Plus Real Estate. "The same mountain lifestyle, world-class fly fishing and trails, and a downtown that's having its own revival.

"This sale shows that buyers will pay a premium for quality and location here and that Basalt has become a destination in its own right," she says.

The townhouse spans three levels and includes three bedrooms, four bedrooms, and a flexible space that can be used as an office or gym—a priceless feature for residents who are balancing a remote or hybrid work schedule.

It certainly offers a luxurious atmosphere, with a private elevator and floor-to-ceiling windows boasting breathtaking views of the river and mountains.

“The residence features an open-concept living space with elevated, contemporary finishes and a seamless flow for both everyday living and entertaining,” the listing explained.

The light-flooded living room is neatly situated in the corner of the unit and has a sleek fireplace to keep residents cozy during the coldest winter months. The space also includes built-in shelving with recessed lighting.

A generously sized kitchen offers plenty of cabinet space, as well as some open shelving by a window that keeps the vibes airy. A kitchen island anchors the room and offers a casual space to dine, while a formal dining space is accompanied by a bar and a wine refrigerator just steps away.

The main living floor also has a powder room and a utility space, with a stacked washer and dryer, storage, and a sink.

Upstairs, the sprawling primary suite has an en suite bathroom with a double vanity, and a soaking tub positioned in the corner between two windows offers striking views of the outdoors. The sizable walk-in closet has plenty of storage solutions, as well as a window that makes it feel like a room of its own. A private terrace with a hot tub solidifies the suite as a full-fledged escape from reality.

The top level also has an additional en suite bedroom, with its own walk-in closet and full bathroom.

The ground level contains the main entrance of the home, which is accompanied by a thoughtfully designed mud room space. There’s also the flexible office or gym room, an additional en suite bedroom, and access to the garage.

Outside, a dining deck overlooks the park, which has a weekly summer concert series. The free event has hosted a series of local bands across genres, and encourages attendees to bring their own picnics for a night of fun.

A two-car garage is another perk for those interested in mountain living and value indoor parking and ski storage.

#5602. Red Hat and Nvidia’s OpenShell puts AI agents on a deny-by-default leash

Prompt injection attacks and silent data exfiltration have turned AI agent security from a theoretical worry into an urgent enterprise concern.

As agents move from developer laptops into data centers, companies need guardrails that don’t strip away what makes agents useful. Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have expanded their partnership to tackle that problem through OpenShell, an open-source project that sets limits on what agents can do. The threat model for agents differs sharply from that of traditional software, so the industry has to build a shared standard to secure them, according to Derek Carr (pictured, left), senior distinguished engineer at Red Hat.

“Agents can’t get access to your secrets. They need deny-by-default networking, and you need a rich policy framework for what happened and when for this class of apps,” Carr said. “Nvidia had reached out to us and noted that they were seeing the same problem domain. No one wants to work on this alone. It’s better to work together.”

Carr and Mrunal Patel (right), distinguished engineer at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShell helps enterprises run AI agents in production with safeguards against prompt injection and data leaks. (* Disclosure below.)

Viral projects such as OpenClaw showed the industry that agents could take real actions on their own. Of course, that power also bred anxiety about agents leaking secrets or spending company money, with concrete warning signs appearing early, Patel noted.

“As soon as we started hearing about the prompt injection attacks and how like folks were seeing the data getting exfiltrated outside, that was scary,” Patel said. “We realized we needed a solution.”

To that end, OpenShell lets operators give agents access to specific endpoints while keeping credentials hidden from the agents and scoped to those endpoints, according to Carr. A policy advisor asks agents to justify blocked actions in plain language, while operators can update policies as workloads change. With OpenShell now under open governance at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation following Nvidia’s contribution, Red Hat aims to make deploying agents on OpenShift as routine as running traditional apps, with prompt injection defenses built into the platform.

“Many companies are struggling to get to one agent in production, let alone thousands or millions,” Carr said. “By having a project like OpenShell in the ecosystem, it provides a blueprint for companies to follow — to get from their first idea of ‘I want to do something with agents’ to a point where they’re safely doing one, 10 or 20 in production.”

#5601. Douglas Elliman Goes All-In for AI After Q3’s Flat Earnings

After a middling third quarter, Douglas Elliman CEO Michael Liebowitz told investors that recent changes and efforts to the company are to “modernize” and build a “more efficient platform” by early 2027.

The luxury brokerage’s revenue fell short in the third quarter at $252.1 million for 2026, a $10 million drop compared to 2025’s revenue of $262.8 million.

For the first nine months of the year, revenue also dropped and was reported at $749.9 million. In 2025, that revenue was reported at $787.6 million.

During the Q3 earnings call for Douglas Elliman, Liebowitz claimed that the last quarter was about “technological upgrades” and emphasized the company’s movement toward execution.

“Technology is central to our strategy, and the transformation we introduced last quarter has continued to advance as part of our broader efforts to modernize the business and reduce costs,” he stated.

The company has faced struggles both in the market and internally over the past two years, with C-suite turnover and competition in its home market of New York City.

After the earnings report, the company’s stock jumped 12%, though it is still down 30% this year.

Liebowitz also mentioned multiple additions to Douglas Elliman this past quarter, including Sharon Milz as head of AI technology transformation, Nick Patino as director of AI enablement and Jamie Gagliano as chief operations officer.

“Sharon is overseeing our enterprise AI strategy and deployment as well as the broader technology transformation across the company,” he added. “Nick focuses on making sure these capabilities become part of how we get things done across the company, translating new technology into adoption, productivity and measuring business value. Jamie brings significant experience working with agents and building businesses. She’s already looking across our national operations at how we simplify processes, strengthen support and build a more scalable organization.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Aside from a drop in revenue, Douglas Elliman also reported a drop in operating income (loss) annually. For Q3 2026, the company reported an operating income of $6.3 million, while last year’s operating loss clocked in at $10.7 million.

Bryant Kirkland—Douglas Elliman’s CFO—stated on the Q3 earnings call, however, that the year-over-year comparisons lean negatively because of 2025’s data.

“The year-over-year comparisons for the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026 are impacted by a difficult comparable, due to an unusually strong first quarter of 2025,” he noted.

Adjusted EBITDA—or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization—may signal positive growth for the brokerage, as Q3’s EBITDA was $5.3 million compared to last year’s $1 million.

While the adjusted EBITDA grew for Q3, the company’s adjusted net loss greatly overshadows many gains, as it reported the adjusted net loss at nearly $8 million, compared to last year’s $1.4 million.

Existing-home sales, Kirkland mentioned, were up 1.9% from October 2026, compared to October 2025. But, this result was weighed down. October 2026 had one fewer sales day than last year, Kirkland said. In reality, the receipts from existing-home sales were down 2.7% in October 2026 compared to October 2025.

Liebowitz attributed many of the Q3 losses to changes, and called it a “growth stage.”

Kirkland claimed the company would see returns on its current investments—such as the development marketing pipeline of $26 billion and the additional $11.8 billion scheduled to come to market Dec. 31, 2027—between 2026 and 2032. In particular, Kirkland mentioned Florida’s real estate market and its marketing value.

“We see positive indicators within our development marketing business in Florida, with approximately $19.5 billion gross transaction value, of the $26 billion of gross transaction value that is being actively marketed,” he added. “For most projects in Florida, we receive progress payments during the marketing process and defer the related revenue and commission it spent until the earnings process is complete, which is when the underlying sale closes.”

After investing in an “AI transformation” last quarter, the Q3 earnings release noted that the initiative is expected to gradually drive significant savings in non-commission operating expenses over the next three years.

“Modernizing those systems should make the company more efficient while giving our agents and employees better tools and more time to focus on clients, relationships and growing their businesses,” Liebowitz claimed. “That work is underway, and we remain focused on gradually realizing meaningful efficiencies in our non-commission operating expenses beginning in 2027.”

#5600. Kylie Jenner Faces Fourth Household Staff Lawsuit—Former Housekeeper Alleges Dog Bite, Being Trapped in Closet

Kylie Jenner's former housekeeper is suing the beauty mogul, claiming that she was trapped inside Jenner's closet, bitten by her dog, and pepper-sprayed in the face.

The lawsuit, which is the fourth filed by a member of Jenner's household staff since April, was brought by Dinora Cabria Amaya, who began working for the reality TV star in March 2025.

In the 20-page filing, which was obtained by The Rolling Stone, Amaya claimed that she was denied overtime and experienced a hostile work environment.

She also claimed that she suffered workplace injuries, including being hit with pepper spray, which allegedly caused “severe burning and vision problems.”

According to the lawsuit, she messaged her manager, “Sorry to interrupt you, I had an accident at work, someone left pepper spray and took off safety." The manager then allegedly replied, "Thanks for letting us know."

They then requested that the housekeeper fill out a report and provide it to Jenner's security before seeing a healthcare professional.

She then claimed she experienced “significant eye pain, blurred vision, headaches, burning, irritation, and sensitivity," but received no accommodations due to pain.

“The more plaintiff complained that she was hurt, the harder defendants made her job,” the lawsuit claimed.

Amaya then claimed that she was often "confined in a room because defendant Jenner did not want to see her” and that her “repeated reports of ongoing pain” were not regarded with importance.

In one alleged incident, she described using a passcode to enter the TV personality's closet, only to became locked inside and suffer a panic attack.

“No one is at the house that can let you out, and I cannot give the password to anyone else; you just have to wait,” the housekeeper's manager allegedly replied when Amaya told her she was locked inside.

Amaya claimed that her manager "mocked her" during their call.

The housekeeper then recalled the alleged incident that saw Jenner's dog biting her while she was cleaning the doghouse.

“Again, no meaningful assistance was provided. Plaintiff purchased over-the-counter medication and treated the injury herself. She continued reporting that her eyes hurt, her arm and wrist hurt from the dog bite, and her back hurt from the increasingly physical work," the filing states.

Amaya was fired on Feb. 6, 2026, after requesting mileage reimbursement for her trips to Jenner's homes.

Jenner owns multiple homes in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and a property outside of Palm Springs.

The housekeeper is now claiming that she was fired because she spoke up about her treatment.

The filing names the beauty mogul, her company Kylie Jenner Inc., staff supervisors Laura Dooley and Itzel Sibrian, Tri Star Services, and La Maison Family Services.

The lawsuit claims wrongful termination, false imprisonment, disability discrimination, failure to provide reasonable accommodations, whistleblower retaliation, failure to prevent discrimination and retaliation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Amaya is seeking unpaid wages, past and future monetary earnings, and damages. The housekeeper is being represented by lawyer Della Shaker.

Amaya earned $40 an hour working for Jenner—$23 more than the state's minimum wage. Amaya worked six days a week.

Jenner’s lawyer, Michael Rhodes, noted that Shaker is the same lawyer representing the other members of Jenner's staff who sued earlier this year.

“It’s clear that this lawyer wants to use publicity to try to extract an unwarranted payday. We’re not going to be intimidated into doing that. As such, we’ll defend these meritless cases vigorously and look forward to telling our side of the story," Rhodes told The Rolling Stone.

In response, Shaker told the outlet, “For employees working in high-profile households, the fear of losing future employment opportunities can be overwhelming. When your livelihood depends on discretion, references, and powerful professional relationships, speaking out can feel impossible. But no employer has the right to retaliate against workers for protected complaints. The truth should never be buried behind wealth, fear, or silence.”

Amaya's lawsuit comes after former housekeepers Angelica Hernandez Vasquez and Juana Delgado Soto also filed suits against Jenner, also alleging mistreatment and whistleblower retaliation.

#5599. British inference chip developer Fractile raises $720M in funding

Fractile Ltd., a British startup that develops artificial intelligence inference chips, has raised $720 million in funding.

Reuters reported today that the Series C round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. They were joined by about a dozen others including the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, the British Business Bank and Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG investment arm. Fractile is now worth $7 billion.

Fractile was founded in 2022 by AI researcher Walter Goodwin (pictured), who serves as its chief executive. The company reportedly expects its chips to provide up to 100 times better performance than current silicon. Furthermore, Fractile is promising a 90% reduction in energy use. The chips deliver those improvements by removing the need for AI models to move data to off-chip HBM memory.

Large language models generate prompt responses through a workflow that involves numerous steps. When an LLM completes a processing step, it sends the results to an off-chip HBM memory chip. It then retrieves those results to lay the groundwork for the next step. Those repeated data round-trips take a significant amount of time, which slows down inference.

Fractile is not the only AI chip supplier tackling that bottleneck. Cerebras Systems Inc., which went public in May, offers wafer-size accelerators that reduce data movement by keeping information in a large onboard cache. That cache is faster than off-chip HBM modules. The company’s newest processor, the WSE-3T, can hold 44 gigabytes of data.

Cerebras’ on-chip cache is based on SRAM, a type of memory that was historically added to processors in only small quantities. SRAM cells, the technology’s basic building blocks, have six transistors apiece. Those transistors read and write data faster than the single transistor found in HBM cells. At the same time, SRAM’s speed comes with certain trade-offs: it’s expensive and has limited capacity.

Fractile is taking a different approach to reducing data movement. Instead of integrating SRAM into its inference chips, the company is stacking standard DRAM memory on top of them. Placing a memory module immediately above a processor’s logic circuits minimizes the distance that data has to cover. That speeds up traffic while lowering the amount of electricity needed to shuffle it back and forth.

Samsung Electronics Co. is developing a similar technology. In August, the company debuted an HBM variant called zHBM that can be stacked atop AI accelerators. It uses tiny copper wires to move data to and from the host chip. Samsung says the technology will be eight times faster than HBM5, a future iteration of HBM more performant than the versions in use today.

Fractile, for its part, estimates that its chips will enable LLM to process several thousand tokens per second. It plans to ship the processors as part of rack-scale systems that will also include custom software. Many AI chipmakers offer custom compilers, software tools that automatically turn customers’ LLMs into a format compatible with their silicon.

Fractile expects to start shipping its chips next year.

#5598. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5597. Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC Connect Florida and Indiana Property Data Through RPR View

Business professional using laptop with connected digital document icons, representing document management, data sharing, cloud workflow, file organization, and business automation.

Realtors Property Resource (RPR) has announced that Realtors serving clients with real estate interests in both Florida and Indiana will have access to additional property information through a new data-sharing collaboration between Stellar MLS and MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative (BLC).

According to a release, using RPR View, the MLS data-sharing capability from RPR, eligible customers in both markets will be able to access approved off-market listings, including historical listing data, across MLS boundaries.

RPR says the collaboration reflects a natural connection between Indiana and Florida, where seasonal residents, relocating homeowners and buyers often have real estate interests in both markets. Expanded access to listing history gives Realtors additional context to research properties, understand past market activity and help clients make informed decisions.

“Buyers and sellers deserve informed guidance wherever their real estate goals take them,” said Shayne Fairley, CEO of Stellar MLS. “Often, they don’t stop at market boundaries, and neither should access to trusted listing information for the real estate professionals who serve them. With strong ties between Florida and Indiana, especially among seasonal residents, our collaboration with MIBOR BLC and RPR will provide greater access to property information across both markets, so the professionals who guide their clients can do so with greater confidence.”

He added: “We’re pleased to bring this expanded access to our collective customers, and we look forward to creating similar opportunities with other MLSs and associations.”

A practical approach to cross-market data sharing

Beyond the benefits to Realtors, the release says the collaboration demonstrates how MLS organizations can expand property data access using technology already available through RPR.

With RPR View, participating MLSs determine which listing information to share and which markets can access it. This gives organizations flexibility to expand access while maintaining control over their data-sharing permissions.

For Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC, the arrangement enables reciprocal access to approved off-market listing information, including historical listing data, through an established platform, without developing a separate data-sharing system.

“MLS organizations create the greatest value when we look beyond traditional market boundaries and focus on how real estate professionals actually do business. Our partnership with Stellar MLS reflects that philosophy,” said Shelley Specchio, CEO and President of the MIBOR Broker Listing Cooperative in Indiana. “By connecting the Indiana and Florida marketplaces through RPR, we are reducing friction for professionals working in both states and demonstrating what is possible when MLSs collaborate around the needs of brokers, agents and consumers.”

Building connections through existing infrastructure

The release notes that as of October 31, 341 of the nation’s 487 MLSs (70%) participate in RPR View data sharing, representing more than 1 million Realtors. The Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC collaboration demonstrates how this existing infrastructure can support cross-market access while allowing each organization to maintain control over its shared data, RPR says.

“One of the advantages of RPR View is that MLSs can expand data access without having to build a new solution,” said Liz Gunski, vice president of Industry Relations at RPR. “Stellar MLS and MIBOR BLC are showing how existing infrastructure can support collaboration while keeping participating organizations in control of their data.”

The expanded data access is scheduled to become available to eligible customers in both markets beginning Nov. 4.

#5596. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.
