#5578. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5577. How Bravo Star Joey Zauzig Turned an 1,100-Square-Foot WeHo Rental Into His Postdivorce ‘Sanctuary in the Sky’

Food influencer Joey Zauzig has worked closely with famed interior designer Jeff Lewis in broadcasting for years, yet the luxury West Hollywood apartment where he often delivers his signature saucy meal reviews and motivational speeches is one he decorated without help.

Zauzig, 34, is a fan favorite on Lewis’ SiriusXM show, “Jeff Lewis Live,” and a recurring cast member on “Still Flipping Out,” Bravo’s new spinoff of Lewis’ original “Flipping Out” series.

On both programs, Zauzig and Lewis have had their differences, but Zauzig reveals to Realtor.com® in Celebrity Sanctuary that when it comes to the style of his L.A.-area home, he believes they’re totally aligned.

“We have a similar sense of taste when it comes to homes and when it comes to renovations,” states Zauzig, while clarifying that Lewis hasn’t been by his place but is always welcome to visit. "I’ll let him see it whenever he wants to come over. I think he'll like it."

The former “The Real Friends of WeHo” star moved into the 1,100-square-foot, two-bedroom, two-bathroom rental unit located inside a high-rise residential tower in West Hollywood in October 2024. At the time, the Virginia native was seeking a safe place to start over following the breakup of his marriage and an unsettling break-in at a previous WeHo residence.

Today, Zauzig’s “small, but perfect” dwelling is his preferred space to comfortably work on his personal brand—and work on himself. It’s where he filmed one of his most popular social media posts “in a tux, shooting the sh*t, eating a shrimp cocktail in the kitchen,” and where he intentionally watched his Bravo debut alone so he could learn and grow through some serious self-reflection.

“To just be in my own home, watch it by myself, and be able to go through those emotions by myself—I was under the covers with a heating pad, face mask on,” recounts Zauzig.

“The best therapy you can ever get is to be able to watch yourself back on TV,” he continues. “I’m by no means perfect. We all make mistakes. We all have things we want to tweak about ourselves when it comes to the journey of becoming your best self. Mine got accelerated from the show, and that's a great thing. Joey 2.0 is going great.”

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Zauzig details how he’s gotten to “a good place” as he and his carefully curated West Hollywood home continue to be “works in progress.”

I really got this place because of the views. I was going through a divorce. I needed a little sanctuary in the sky, and that's what I got, and it just makes me happy because it's mine and it's beautiful.

I always had my eye on this building. A lot of cool people from my industry live here. It’s [got a] full-time security doorman, marble, light oak wood in all of the hallways. I was like, “If I move into a building in L.A., it has to be this building specifically.” I really was dead-set on that and also safety. I wanted somewhere that I felt, [as] someone that travels so much, could just pick up and leave without any worry.

I definitely made a lot of changes to the place. Farrow & Ball did all of the painting. They sent a paint specialist over. I went really dark. I did a sexy, dark-brown chocolate bedroom, and then my closet is all dark-brown lacquer. The roof is also lacquer, so it reflects [and] it looks bigger. The rest is this taupe-beige. It's a muted white. I didn’t want stark white walls, because it gives rental.

I changed a lot of light fixtures because that was important to me. There was this bubble light fixture in the kitchen, these glass bulbs. It was awful, and it was stark white light. I changed that to this Lulu and Georgia overhead, and I changed the placement of the lighting so it's over my island now, which is really nice. Then there [were] these alien-looking lights! They're not cute, so I changed those into CB2 canister lights. They're a dark black, which goes really nice with the tan [paint]. It feels more warm, cozy.

Other than that, I just made it my own. I made some custom cushions for the balcony outside.

[With] a rental, you never know if you could make changes, but there’s still some tweaks I want to do. Definitely some changes in the kitchen. I hate the green subway tiles. If I felt like putting money into this place, that's what I would change because I am in the kitchen so much. They've got to go. I’m not a subway-tile kind of guy. I would do a marble.

My family room is definitely my sanctuary because I have this white boucle chair where I sit. That's where I edit all my content.

You know when you can't wait to get home and go into that one spot that you're going to relax in, chill in, scroll for hours, watch TV? That's my family room and my specific chair. I love a swivel chair. They help my anxiety a little bit. I just can't wait to get home, get into that boucle chair. I work, I eat, I watch TV. It really is my sanctuary.

The swivel chair is vintage from Mid-Century Modern in Burbank, CA. It was my first vintage piece, and it's special to me. He re-covered it in white boucle. It's so comfortable.

I should probably separate [work and home life] better, but I like to feel comfortable when I'm doing my work, especially when I'm editing. When I need to focus, I like to be in a comfortable chair. I am a really tall guy, so I need to be chillin’ and cozy.

Once I put my phone and my work stuff away, I can actually make the sanctuary a relaxing space.

It's a mix of vintage and Design Within Reach. I have one of those Design Within Reach consoles, this really beautiful silver and glass coffee table, and a CB2 silver lamp. It goes well together with the white boucle and the Design Within Reach dark wood. Then I have a huge Lulu and Georgia Jake Arnold rug, and it's so fluffy and comfortable. It's a smaller family room, so you can have people on the floor and sitting down around the coffee table. It's a really fun little gathering area, and it's comfortable.

Then I have a huge 80-inch TV because I do watch a lot of TV, so I need it to be big. I know a lot of people say you shouldn't have the TV in the family room because it's trashy—I’ll have a TV in my family room all day long, no matter where I live. I think it's chic. I want people to know I'm a TV watcher. I think it adds a little something.

I have this [Pierre] Jeanneret chair to the right of my other chair, and that was a piece that I got as a gift to myself when I was filming my first reality show. It's an original Jeanneret chair. It has one of the red inscriptions in the back, which is one of the most rare Jeanneret chairs. The wicker part had to get redone because someone sat in the chair, broke it, and fell through, so that [part] is not original, but it's fine.

I’m going to change some things for sure soon. I need a new couch.

Just as I'm a work in progress, so is my sanctuary. It's getting there, it’s just not there. It actually makes perfect sense for where I'm at right now. We're all works in progress, and I'm becoming Joey 2.0, so I'm excited.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. #5575. Nvidia’s board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after reports of a second affair

Nvidia Corp.’s board of directors is reportedly preparing to oust its founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang after reports emerged that he had a second extramarital relationship with an executive at the company, just days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Earlier today, the New York Times said Huang (pictured) was suspected by five people at the company of having an affair with Nvidia Healthcare Vice President Kimberly Powell. Hours later, the Wall Street Journal said Nvidia’s board is preparing to meet on Thursday to discuss Huang’s future at the company, and that all options are on the table, including his possible dismissal.

The Times said Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera together being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California, in March.

The latest reports come just days after Huang admitted in an email to company employees that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese woman called Alice Huang, who was formerly the CEO of the Singaporean data center supplier Megaspeed. Alice Huang, of no relation to Nvidia’s CEO, is suspected of working for China’s Ministry of State Security, but it’s not clear if she has passed on any of the company’s secrets.

In response to that report, Nvidia’s board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead an investigation into the affair and try to determine what secrets, if any, were leaked.

Huang reportedly first became involved with the Chinese woman last year, but rumors of an affair between him and Powell have circulated for years. One reason for that is that Powell does not have any background in health or science, despite her high-level role at Nvidia’s Healthcare business.

On Nvidia’s website, Powell’s bio explains that she’s responsible for the company’s healthcare business, “including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery and healthcare analytics.”

The Healthcare business is much smaller than Nvidia’s main data center unit, which accounts for the lion’s share of its multibillion-dollar revenue. It makes chips for medical devices such as MRI machines. The company does not break out sales figures for the unit, instead reporting its revenue within the broader data center business.

Powell appeared at Nvidia’s annual GTC conference in San Jose in March, where she delivered a keynote talking about how the company’s AI technology can help to accelerate drug discovery and enhance clinical efficiency. She has been running the business since 2017.

If Nvidia were to oust Huang, the company that sits at the heart of the artificial intelligence revolution would face an uncertain future. Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, controlling around 90% of the global market for computer chips used in AI, becoming a major driving force behind the global economy.

Its brand has become synonymous with Huang, who is involved in all aspects of its business and has appointed family members to key roles in its executive team. Huang is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, holding a 3.56% stake in the company. Should he be ousted, there is no clear successor.

Nvidia’s rise amid the AI boom has made Huang one of the wealthiest and most influential people in the world. He has become a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, who was previously told about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy but decided to take no action. Trump has come out in defense of Huang, saying that he’s an “honorable man” and that he did not know of the woman’s connections to Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia’s stock fell more than 9% in late trading on Wednesday and is likely to extend its downward trend for a sixth straight week.

#5574. ‘It’s Like Facebook Again’: How AI IPOs Could Further Upend the Real Estate Market

A robotic hand presents a house icon with a percentage symbol, symbolizing growth and investment in a modern office space, merging technology with real estate. Synapse

(TNS)– The deluge of wealth the artificial intelligence boom has brought into San Francisco has already pushed luxury home prices to record heights. Now, with Anthropic’s initial public offering poised to bring even more money into the city, could things get even worse?

Real estate professionals say yes—but that a lot of the growth is already baked in.

Let’s take stock of what’s already happened. San Francisco’s home prices have risen most sharply in neighborhoods that were already exclusive, such as Pacific Heights or the Marina. The median home price for luxury homes in the San Francisco metropolitan area—properties sold in San Francisco and San Mateo counties at or above the 95th percentile price—was nearly $7.5 million from July to September 2026, Redfin data shows. That was up a whopping 23% from the same period in 2025, and up more than 60% from 2019.

Now, some experts suggest that AI IPOs could cause demand to spill even further, raising prices for the few home types—or communities—in the Bay Area where middle-income families might still afford a property.

Already, some data indicates that even non-luxury homes in the city have seen strong appreciation over the past year.

“Typical” San Francisco area homes—those in the 35th-to-65th percentile sale price range — saw a record median sale price of $1.6 million in September 2026, an increase of 6.5% from 2025. While that’s a much lower jump compared to the San Francisco area’s luxury market, it still diverges sharply from that of the rest of the United States, where high mortgage rates and economic woes have caused prices to dip.

Redfin economist Daryl Fairweather believes the heat in San Francisco will spread to other parts of the region. In some ways, it already has; the city’s surging rents have caused many tenants to seek refuge in relatively more affordable cities like Oakland, pushing up prices there.

“This has been the story for at least … 15 years: San Francisco prices and rents going up and people being displaced,” Fairweather said.

Demand for fancy homes will likely keep surging

Some real estate agents say that the AI workers and investors fighting bidding wars in San Francisco often don’t want to give up on their dream house, even as prices rise. That’s part of the reason demand has flowed into other expensive cities in Marin County or the Peninsula, where there are more fancy homes for the buying. Phil Chen, a real estate broker at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said that demand for Hillsborough has soared, with buyers citing a desire for strong schools — and security.

“It’s my first time hearing, ‘Is the glass bulletproof and are there panic rooms?’” Chen said.

Zillow data indicates that home values in Hillsborough, Menlo Park and Piedmont have risen faster over the past year than any other Bay Area city with at least 10,000 people except San Francisco, suggesting that some wealthy buyers are expanding their search radius. In some cities, such as in Piedmont, starter home values—those in the 5th to 35th percentile—have actually climbed more than top-tier values. Still, a “starter home” in Piedmont still costs more than a mid-tier property in San Francisco.

It’s unclear how much demand could rise for homes that aren’t luxury properties or in expensive neighborhoods. One 2019 study found that IPOs increase demand for high-priced homes near the company’s headquarters, but not for low-priced properties. The study’s results also indicated IPOs increased the probability low-income residents moved to lower-income neighborhoods.

But Fairweather said that junior tech workers with smaller windfalls than their senior peers could start to make offers in parts of the Bay Area where their money will go further. Vanessa Hatvany Kitchen, a real estate agent with Compass’ Team Hatvany Kitchen, said her team has seen more people buying condos and smaller single-family homes in San Francisco, fearing they won’t be able to get a foothold after companies like Anthropic go public.

But much of the demand increase is baked in

If there’s any silver lining for buyers, though, it’s that a lot of those companies’ impact on the Bay Area real estate market is already here. Arrian Binnings, a San Francisco real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate Sereno, said many AI workers have been able to get cash by borrowing against their stocks or selling their shares via company-approved tender offers, while investors have benefitted from the strength of the public equity market. That’s consistent with some research showing that merely filing for IPOs can raise home prices near a company’s headquarters.

“I don’t see the IPO as the starting gun of a new race. I see it as … we’re probably already at the 50-yard line,” Binnings said. “But I do still see plenty of room to run.”

IPOs don’t always result in an explosion of wealth. In the months after Uber went public in 2019, the company’s stock price plummeted, erasing billions of dollars in value. A similar fate for a public Anthropic or OpenAI would send a chill through the real estate market, some real estate agents say.

But many buyers are optimistic. Chen said some of his clients plan to sell their newly purchased homes in five years, expecting to increase their budgets from $10 million to $25 million. after the IPO. Those buyers, he added, are relatively junior-level employees.

“It’s like Facebook again, but 10x,” Chen said.

#5573. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5572. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5571. NYC’s First Pied-à-Terre Tax Bills Are Coming—and Buyers Are Recalculating

New York City's new tax on high-value second homes was designed to raise revenue. But changes to the tax code can also influence how people buy and sell property.

"There's always the risk of avoidance," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Tax bases are famously mobile—especially across municipal boundaries—and that's doubly true for wealthier individuals."

With the first surcharge bills expected to be mailed in the coming days, Realtor.com analyzed the nearly 1 million property and residential-unit records in the city's supplemental tax roll, identifying 24,218 potentially exposed homes that met the relevant valuation thresholds.

Of those, 2,536 (10.5%) sat within just 5% above the minimum valuation required for taxation, while 560 (2.3%) fell within 5% on either side of a higher tax-rate threshold.

Which side of that divide a home falls on can come with huge financial stakes for owners—and agents say buyers are already taking notice.

"The biggest change since July is that buying a second home in New York has become a much more calculated decision," says Donald Brennan, a real estate broker with Engel & Völkers.

In at least one building, two apartments with government-assigned market values just $6,009 apart could face a $37,813 difference in annual surcharges simply because they fall on opposite sides of a tax-rate threshold—assuming neither qualifies for an exemption.

New York City has long attracted wealthy buyers looking for a second residence, whether for work, leisure, or the opportunity to spend part of the year in the city.

"I might be biased, but it's a fantastic place to live, especially if you can afford it," says Krimmel.

His caveat is telling: if you can afford it. With an estimated 52% of New York City renters already burdened by housing costs, wealthy second-home owners present a tempting target for Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s tax-the-rich agenda.

But the new tax will add considerable expense even for those who can afford multiple homes.

For condos and co-ops, the surcharge starts at 4% of their Department of Finance market value at $1 million. One- to three-family homes face an initial rate of 0.8% beginning at $5 million.

The city values houses using comparable sales but condos and co-ops based on their potential rental income, so their tax thresholds aren't directly comparable. At either entry point, however, the annual surcharge starts at approximately $40,000.

Brooklyn accounts for 560 of the 713 Class 1 properties just above the minimum threshold, while Manhattan accounts for 1,700 of the 1,823 condo and co-op units in the equivalent position.

But local brokers point out that many of these properties may never face the surcharge at all.

"In Brooklyn, I think this creates a slightly different conversation because so many of our luxury buyers are purchasing homes they actually intend to live in," says Jessica Peters, a Brooklyn-based broker with Douglas Elliman.

Already, thousands of owners have secured exemptions from the new tax. Of approximately 17,000 notices mailed to owners, close to 11,000 exemption applications had been submitted and more than 8,800 approved as of Oct. 29, Gothamist reports.

That leaves a great deal of uncertainty around how much revenue the city will actually be able to bring in.

While the city budgeted $500 million in annual revenue from the new tax, an April report from City Comptroller Mark Levine warned that exemptions and other behavioral changes could reduce collections to between $340 million and $380 million.

But exemptions aren't the only factor affecting what owners could owe. There's also the matter of the threshold values.

Condo and co-op rates rise to 5.25% above $3 million and 6.5% above $5 million. Rates for one- to three-family homes, meanwhile, increase to 1.05% above $15 million and 1.3% above $25 million.

And because the higher rate applies to the property's entire value, even a small difference in valuation can trigger a monumental increase. The owner of a $3 million condo or co-op subject to the 5.25% rate, for example, would owe just over $157,000.

These higher-rate thresholds have a much narrower geographic footprint, too. Of the 270 records sitting within 5% above a higher-rate threshold, 264 are in Manhattan, including 33 in ZIP code 10022 and 29 in 10021.

Krimmel says owners could respond by reconsidering where they buy or how they use their properties.

"The question is whether there are other places which act as a close substitute for the newly taxed properties," he says.

Brennan sees that calculation emerging among buyers who may spend only a few months a year in New York.

"When you're looking at a multimillion-dollar apartment that you might only use a few months out of the year, that additional tax becomes part of the conversation very quickly," he says.

Some may decide to rent rather than purchase, he adds.

Those decisions could ultimately help free up housing for other buyers or tenants, as Krimmel notes. At the same time, those sales could also reduce the number of properties generating surcharge revenue.

Owners are also challenging the tax in court. Three lawsuits have been filed, two of which remain pending.

A Nov. 4 appeals court ruling dismissed a lawsuit challenging the city's rollout on standing grounds, while the remaining cases challenge its constitutionality.

But homeowners don't need to overturn the law to challenge what they might owe. They can also dispute the city's valuation of their properties—and for those sitting just above a tax threshold, even a small adjustment could eliminate the surcharge entirely.

Narrowing the analysis to properties within just 1% of a tax threshold identified 602 records, including 496 just above the minimum valuation required for taxation.

An additional 106 records fell within 1% of a higher-rate cutoff, including 61 just below and 45 above. All were in Manhattan, and of those, 66 were condos or co-ops near the $3 million threshold, where the annual surcharge increases from 4% to 5.25%.

From a bird's-eye view of the city, those differences might seem negligible. But when looking at a specific building, they are more dramatic.

At 111 West 57th St., a luxury condominium tower near Central Park, unit 57 has a DOF market value of $2,999,794—just $206 below the higher threshold. Unit 38, meanwhile, is valued at $3,005,803.

That $6,009 difference in valuation translates to a $37,813 difference in potential annual surcharges, with the higher-valued apartment facing a charge of approximately $157,805.

A similar disparity appears at 768 Fifth Ave., where two units separated by $19,337 in DOF market value face a $38,317 difference in potential annual charges.

That’s no small sum, even for a wealthy homeowner.

"If they're already paying substantial carrying costs, they're going to look for ways to offset that expense, whether through the purchase price or other concessions," says Ben Jacobs, a Douglas Elliman broker specializing in Manhattan and Brooklyn.

A lower asking price wouldn't automatically reduce the government's valuation or the tax owed, but it could help buyers offset the cost of carrying the property.

Krimmel sees another potential consequence: The surcharge could change what economists call a property's option value—the value of being able to use it differently in the future. Condominiums, for instance, typically offer more flexibility to rent out than co-ops, making that potential rental income part of what a buyer is purchasing.

The same principle could apply to homes that buyers might eventually want to use as second residences.

Even if a property is exempt today, the possibility of a future surcharge could become another consideration in negotiations. Jacobs adds that uncertainty can create its own complications.

"Buyers want to know exactly what their exposure will be before they commit," he says. "When those answers aren't immediately clear, it can slow down a transaction."

To his point, there are early signs of a sharper slowdown in New York City's luxury condo and co-op market since the city began notifying potentially affected property owners in July.

New condo and co-op listings initially priced between $1 million and $3 million fell 11% year over year from July through Nov. 7, compared with a 1% increase between April and June, according to an analysis of Realtor.com listing data.

The decline was even steeper among properties priced between $3 million and $5 million, where new listings fell 16% year over year after July, following a 5% decline in the preceding three months.

By comparison, new listings priced below $1 million fell just 1% year over year since July, after rising 7% between April and June.

Of course, the pied-à-terre tax can’t shoulder all the blame for the slowdown. The luxury market was already showing signs of weakness before the city began sending tax notices, and rising mortgage rates have added another headwind.

Brokers, meanwhile, say some second-home buyers are approaching purchases with greater caution.

"I don't think this means wealthy buyers are suddenly abandoning New York. They still want to be here," Brennan says. "But they're looking much more closely at the numbers."

Peters expects some prospective second-home buyers to delay their decisions or consider renting until they have a better understanding of their potential tax bills.

"What concerns me more is how the additional cost could influence decisions before buyers even start looking," she says.

The first surcharge payments are due on Jan. 1, 2027, and the larger market response—if there is one—will likely take even longer to untangle from the myriad other factors affecting buyer and seller behavior.

But for now, two things are clear: Thousands of potentially affected properties sit close to tax thresholds with huge financial consequences, and new luxury condo and co-op listings have slowed considerably since the city began notifying owners.

Whether those developments are connected—and whether the tax ultimately changes the number of second homes in New York City—remains to be seen.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5570. Op-Ed: Open Real Estate Shouldn’t Need an Announcement

The announcement of Open Real Estate was welcome news. It also raised an uncomfortable question: How did we reach the point where keeping the housing market open required an announcement?

Buyers should be able to find available homes. Sellers should understand who can see their property and what they may sacrifice by limiting its exposure. Brokerages should compete on the quality of their advice, service and results.

These principles should be ordinary expectations of our profession. The fact that they now need a name, a coalition and a public defense is a troubling sign of how far the conversation has veered off course.

Brown Harris Stevens, where I serve as executive director, is an initial participating member of Open Real Estate. I support the initiative’s stated commitment to broader access, informed seller decisions and fair competition. But the larger issue extends beyond any platform or participating company. Openness should be how we conduct business every day.

The appeal of exclusive inventory to a brokerage is easy to understand. If buyers believe they need a relationship with a particular company to see certain homes, that company gains an advantage. Exclusive inventory can help attract buyers, recruit and retain agents and strengthen the firm’s position.

The benefit to the seller is less easy to understand and requires a separate explanation. A brokerage’s ability to use a listing to grow its business does not establish that limiting the property’s exposure is the best strategy for the homeowner. Those interests may align in a particular transaction, but that does not make them interchangeable.

Compass has made private exclusives and phased marketing central to its offering, promoting the opportunity to test pricing and generate interest before a broader public launch. Those claims deserve scrutiny because they concern decisions sellers are trusting their advisors to help them make.

What does the seller gain during that period? Which potential buyers cannot see the property? How representative is pricing feedback from a limited audience? What opportunities might the seller lose while broader exposure is delayed?

The recruiting appeal of the strategy is clear: Access to inventory agents and their buyers might otherwise miss. But sellers deserve to hear the other side of that pitch. The inventory attracting people into the network is their home, and restricting access may exclude buyers who could compete for it.

A large brokerage network can provide meaningful exposure, but it still represents only part of the market. The strength of that network does not, by itself, establish that a seller benefits from postponing access to everyone else.

For sellers seeking the strongest price within a practical time frame, I believe broad exposure should be the starting point. Making a home available to more potential buyers creates more opportunity for competing offers and gives the seller a fuller picture of demand. A recommendation to delay that exposure should explain what the seller stands to gain and what they may give up.

The pricing argument also deserves scrutiny. Sellers hire brokers in part for their ability to analyze comparable sales, assess competing inventory and recommend a pricing strategy. If an agent recommends testing a price privately, the seller should ask: Why is feedback from a limited audience more useful than feedback from the broader market? What uncertainty does this approach resolve, and why does resolving it require restricted exposure?

A broker should be prepared to answer those questions with evidence specific to the property and the seller’s circumstances. And the answer shouldn’t be just about obfuscating days on market. When we evaluate how quickly the strategy produces a sale, we should count any private marketing period. The absence of public days on the market does not mean the seller’s clock has stopped.

Some sellers have legitimate reasons to limit exposure. Security, personal circumstances, timing and discretion can all matter. A thoughtful advisor should understand those priorities and recommend a strategy that reflects them.

Those needs existed long before private exclusives became the manufactured proposition they are today. They deserve individual solutions. Their existence does not justify making restricted access the default starting point for sellers.

Seller choice matters. So does how an advisor presents that choice. Which option is introduced first? Which benefits are emphasized? Are the limitations explained with the same conviction? Did the conversation start by asking what the seller’s goals are in the selling process, or did the broker prescribe a strategy without first understanding the specific circumstances and goals?

A signed disclosure is needed, sure, but the quality of the conversation that leads to that signature matters even more.

An individual brokerage may argue that its private network is large enough to serve its sellers well. But imagine that argument becoming the operating model across the industry. Buyers would need to navigate multiple networks to understand what is available.

Their selection could depend on which brokerage they contacted. Sellers could reach substantial audiences while still missing qualified buyers connected to other firms. Each company might describe its own network as an advantage. Together, those networks could create a more fragmented and less useful marketplace.

Consider Southwest Airlines. For years, travelers searching online travel agencies would not see its fares. They had to search Southwest separately. In 2025, Southwest expanded distribution to Expedia, Priceline and the other aggregators, making its flights available where more travelers were already shopping.

The parallel has limits, but the visibility question matters: How many potential customers never consider an offering because it doesn’t appear where they are looking?

In real estate, that question carries an additional responsibility. An airline decides how to distribute its own inventory. A brokerage advises a homeowner on how to market theirs. If a brokerage recommends limiting exposure, it should explain why that serves the seller better than reaching the broader market.

Brokerage leaders have a responsibility to consider the marketplace our decisions create. Our clients, buyers and sellers alike, depend on it, and the practices we normalize shape its usefulness.

Open Real Estate’s promise deserves support. Its implementation will deserve scrutiny. Its governance, participation rules and distribution practices must deliver the openness it advocates. Every participating company, including my own, should be held to that standard. The initiative must demonstrate that it expands access in practice.

The underlying principle should already guide our decisions: a homeowner’s marketing strategy should serve the homeowner’s goals. Any benefit to the brokerage must be evaluated alongside that responsibility, and any conflict should be explained candidly.

Our advantage should come from understanding a property, interpreting the evidence, negotiating effectively and helping a client make a sound decision. Those are the capabilities clients hire us for. They should also be the basis on which we compete.

I welcome an initiative that helps protect those conditions. But its announcement should prompt industry-wide reflection. When keeping the housing market open becomes a position companies must organize to defend, we’ve let the conversation drift too far from the people we serve.

Open Real Estate should not be a novel idea. It should describe how we do business.

Jared Antin is the executive director of Brown Harris Stevens.

#5569. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5568. Google’s GKE Labs turns reinforcement learning into a Kubernetes workload

Model fine-tuning through reinforcement learning is fast becoming one of the most demanding jobs in AI infrastructure. It mixes training, inference and sandboxed agent work in a single loop, often with research code tangled into the systems beneath it.

Google LLC has been tackling that problem from inside its Kubernetes engineering group, and recently donated the result, OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The GKE Labs team got there by building an AI agent for Kubernetes tasks, then a benchmark to grade models on that work, according to Sunil Arora (pictured, left), senior software engineer at Google Cloud.

“If you look at reinforcement learning, I think of it as a kind of a super app of AI because it involves training. It involves sampling. It involves agents actually doing things in a sandbox and sometimes kind of evaluating the work,” Arora said. “It’s kind of a very diverse workload and it is, I think, pushing the boundaries of our infrastructure.”

Arora and Justin Santa Barbara (right), developer at Google, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed model fine-tuning and their work in GKE Labs, which puts experimental projects in users’ hands early. (* Disclosure below.)

OpenRL debuted as a research preview in June 2026, offering a self-hosted training API for a company’s own Kubernetes cluster. It splits the reinforcement learning loop from the compute plumbing, so infrastructure engineers handle scaling while researchers keep control of experiments, Arora explained.

“With OpenRL, one of the things that we are trying to do is kind of abstracting away the infrastructure as kind of core primitives so that researchers and AI engineers can just focus on their RL loop,” Arora said.

Sandboxes are where that loop meets agent infrastructure, since calculating rewards can mean running millions of isolated commands. Google’s Agent Substrate packs more of those sandboxes onto limited compute, according to Arora. For Santa Barbara, the need surfaced one step at a time.

“We built kubectl-ai, and in theory, kubectl-ai could have formatted my hard disk,” Santa Barbara said. “I would quite like a sandbox for this so that if it formats a hard disk, it formats that sandbox and no damage.”

#5567. Brooklyn Building Collapse Leaves 8 Dead as Crews Race to Search for Survivors

A three-story building in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood collapsed Wednesday afternoon, killing at least eight and leaving 17 people injured.

At a press conference Wednesday night, FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said that seven of the casualties were children, but did not specify whether those children were among the dead or injured.

More than 250 firefighters along with a canine unit and search drones were on the scene at 1321 Flatbush Avenue combing through debris to search for survivors on Thursday morning. Roads around the collapsed building have been closed to traffic.

Part of the wall of 1323 Flatbush also came down in the collapse, leaving apartments in that building exposed to the elements. Neighbors were evacuated from the property and brought to the nearby Flatbush YMCA as a precaution.

The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush, in Brooklyn's Little Haiti neighborhood, was built in 1930 and had four apartment units on the second and third floors while the first floor was a commercial storefront.

At the time of the collapse workers were excavating a lot adjacent to the property at 2625 Bedford Avenue. Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said that the Bedford lot had been approved for a three story, 64-unit building but another permit application had been put in for a nine-story building on the site. A stop work order was issued for that project.

1321 Flatbush Avenue has 98 recorded violations according to the city's department of Housing, Preservation, and Development dating back to 1972. Eleven of those violations are from this year alone, and include "unsafe electrical wiring" and a notice to "provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe."

The Brooklyn District Attorney’s office, alongside the Department of Buildings and local law enforcement, has launched an active joint inquiry to determine whether any criminal negligence or building code violations contributed to the disaster.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement: “There are no words for a loss of this magnitude. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.“

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

Skyline of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA in early spring as the sun sets.

AI-tech firm SERHANT. has announced the launch of SERHANT. Utah, bringing its proprietary AI platform, S.MPLE, and the largest media reach in real estate to Salt Lake City and Park City.

According to a release, SERHANT. Utah opens with more than 40 agents from firms including Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices, Engel & Völkers, Real, Sotheby’s International Realty, and Windermere Real Estate, who together have closed $700 million in sales over the past 12 months. Utah marks the firm’s sixth new market across the U.S. in 2026, following launches in Massachusetts, California, Texas, Colorado and Illinois earlier this year, and brings SERHANT.’s national footprint to 21 states.

Founded by Ryan Serhant, star and executive producer of Netflix’s hit series Owning Manhattan, SERHANT. has more than 11 million followers across social channels, making it the most followed real estate brand in the world. Every SERHANT. agent has access to S.MPLE, the firm’s proprietary platform, which puts AI-powered tools for lead generation, marketing and transaction management in agents’ hands.

“Buyers in markets like Park City can live anywhere in the world, and they expect the agents representing them to operate at the highest level. We’re launching with the best in the market, and our AI platform, S.MPLE plus our media engine will give them the reach to put every listing in front of the right buyer, wherever that buyer is,” said Ryan Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT.

Utah is led by Bridgette Osguthorpe, as managing director and principal broker, bringing more than 20 years of real estate experience and extensive executive leadership in Utah’s luxury market. Julie Snyder joins SERHANT. as a founding member from Summit Sotheby’s International Realty, bringing her Park City-based team, Inhabit Park City, and more than $350 million in career sales to the firm, the release stated. Named one of the Top 100 Sotheby’s International Realty advisors worldwide in 2025, Snyder closed more than $105 million in volume last year. That total includes representing the buyer of a legacy property in Park City’s Old Ranch Road area, listed at $25 million and purchased for an undisclosed record-breaking price. Snyder has worked in real estate for a decade and represents buyers and sellers across Park City, Deer Valley, and the Wasatch Back, on everything from fractional ownership to luxury estates, land, and investment properties. #5564. A decade in, KubeVirt pushes virtual machines into the AI agent era

Confidential computing is drawing fresh interest as enterprises weigh where their most sensitive AI workloads can safely run. That shift is giving virtual machines a new role alongside containers on Kubernetes, rather than a slow retirement.

The timing lines up with a milestone for KubeVirt, the open-source project that runs VMs inside Kubernetes clusters, which graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation this week. Its maintainers are now steering the project toward AI isolation, agent sandboxes and confidential computing, a long-standing technology that is regaining momentum, according to Itamar Holder (pictured, left), principal software engineer and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat Inc.

“I think it’s one of the blockers for a lot of companies to join public cloud in general, like companies that really care about super sensitive data,” Holder said. “I think it unblocks them to join.”

Holder and Vladik Romanovsky (right), technical lead and KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how KubeVirt is evolving from a virtualization tool into an operating layer for AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

KubeVirt’s core idea is running VMs and containers on the same Kubernetes cluster without maintaining two separate stacks. That pairing matters more in the AI era, with Nvidia Corp. developers helping the project integrate dynamic resource allocation for GPU hardware, Holder noted. Romanovsky sees the two forms of compute as partners rather than rivals.

“VMs will do kind of the heavy lifting and larger isolation, and the pods that are running around them would provide a better scaling for cache applications,” Romanovsky said. “In general, it belongs together. VMs and containers can run as one application as well.”

The project is also eyeing a role in AI agent sandboxing, an area where Red Hat is building out infrastructure. The maintainers want KubeVirt to become another isolation backend for the Kubernetes agent sandbox repository, Holder explained.

“I think that we can offer a lot of benefits that other isolation backends don’t have,” Holder said. “We can use live migration and complex hardware configurations with DRA and a lot of other sweet stuff.”
