#5547. If you own the asset, you should own the project data

Owners often inherit thousands of closeout files but lose decision context stored in contractor systems. A persistent owner-controlled record improves operations, diligence, portfolio learning and future AI analysis.   AI Summary

Real estate owners spend years making decisions before a shovel hits the ground, then decades living with the consequences of those decisions after construction is complete. Yet during construction, something unusual often happens: The most complete version of the project can end up living inside systems controlled by a project team whose role is temporary.

That is not an argument against general contractors or the technology they use. Contractors need their own systems to execute the work — to manage RFIs, submittals, drawings, schedules, changes, commitments, field activity and the hundreds of other workflows required to deliver a project. The issue is what happens to all of that information when the project ends.

For the owner, construction is only one chapter in a much longer relationship with the asset, and the information created during that chapter should remain just as durable as the building itself.

By the time a general contractor mobilizes, an owner may already have spent months or years developing the project. There has been an investment thesis, underwriting, capital planning, site diligence, entitlements, early budgeting, design development, consultant coordination, procurement decisions, lender requirements and investor approvals.

Each of these steps creates information and, more importantly, context: why one design option was selected over another, why the budget moved, which assumptions drove the underwriting, which risks were identified early and which decisions were deferred into construction.

Then the project moves into delivery, and the volume of information accelerates. Drawings are revised, RFIs are answered, submittals are reviewed, contracts are executed, schedules change, pay applications are processed and change orders are negotiated. Decisions are documented across meetings, email, project-management software and individual files.

When construction ends, the asset’s operating life continues. The asset moves into operations, warranties begin to matter, capital projects follow, systems get replaced, spaces are renovated and new teams inherit the property. The asset may later be refinanced, sold or redeveloped. The asset’s history needs to remain accessible through changes in project teams, operating staff and ownership. The way that history is maintained should reflect that reality.

During construction, it is completely reasonable for the general contractor to operate its own project-management environment; in many cases, that is where the day-to-day execution record is most complete. The problem begins when that environment also becomes the owner’s only durable record of what happened.

At turnover, owners can receive thousands of files — drawings, warranties, manuals, RFIs, submittals, schedules, photos, meeting records and closeout documents. Technically, the information was transferred, but information and usable history are not always the same thing.

A folder can tell you what the final drawing was; it may not tell you why the design changed. A change-order file can tell you what was approved; it may not clearly preserve the sequence of decisions that created the change. A final budget can tell you where the project landed; it may not preserve how the forecast evolved along the way.

The distinction matters because the value of project information is not simply in possessing the files. It is in maintaining enough structure and context to understand what happened and why. When that continuity breaks at turnover, the next team has to reconstruct the story.

The answer is not for owners to dictate every piece of software used by every project participant — that would create a different problem. General contractors, architects, engineers, consultants and trade partners all have tools and workflows that support their roles, and those systems are important to project execution and should continue to be.

What the owner needs instead is a persistent layer of information that remains under its control throughout the asset lifecycle. That record should begin before construction, remain active while the project is being delivered and continue after turnover. During construction, information can move between the owner’s environment and the systems used by the project team through workflows, integrations, APIs, exports or agreed reporting processes.

In practice, that means being able to access, export and reuse the agreed project record without depending on a former project participant’s account. Owners should define the required records, their format and responsibility for maintaining them before delivery begins.

The goal is not to duplicate every click made inside a contractor’s software. It is to make sure the information that matters to the long-term owner does not disappear when the temporary project organization dissolves.

Not everything created during construction has equal long-term value. The enduring record should focus on the information required to understand how the asset became what it is.

That starts with the financial history: approved budgets, commitments, forecast changes, contingency usage, major cost movements and the financial impact of significant project decisions. It also includes the decision history — major approvals, design changes, scope decisions, responsible parties and the supporting information behind those decisions.

Then there is the technical project record: drawings, specifications, RFIs, submittals, schedule information and other documentation that explains what was designed and ultimately built. Finally, there is the turnover record — as-builts, warranties, manuals, punch and closeout documentation and the information future teams will need to operate, maintain or modify the asset.

The important point is not the specific software used to store each item. It is continuity. Five years after completion, someone working on the property should be able to understand the decisions made five years earlier without starting an archaeological dig through old inboxes, shared drives and archived contractor accounts.

Construction information is often treated as though its usefulness peaks at closeout. For owners, the opposite may be true. A complete development and construction history can become increasingly useful as the asset ages: operations teams can use it to understand equipment, warranties and design intent and asset managers can use it when evaluating future capital work.

The same history also supports investment and portfolio decisions. Development teams can compare budgets, scopes and outcomes against previous projects, and executives can benchmark performance across a portfolio. Future project teams can understand why earlier decisions were made instead of repeating the same analysis, and the information can also support underwriting, refinancing and disposition diligence by making the history of the asset easier to understand.

This becomes even more valuable for owners with multiple properties. One project record is useful; a consistent record across 20, 50 or 100 assets begins to create institutional knowledge. Patterns become visible, assumptions can be tested, budget performance can be compared and recurring problems can be identified — lessons learned on one project can actually influence the next one. The organization’s experience stops resetting every time a project team changes.

Artificial intelligence makes this conversation more important, but not because every owner needs an AI strategy for every construction workflow today. The larger issue is much simpler: AI becomes more useful when it has access to complete, structured and trustworthy information.

An owner might want to understand why similar scopes repeatedly generated changes, how contingency usage varied across developments or which underwriting assumptions proved wrong. Answering those questions requires more than a collection of final documents; it requires a traceable history of decisions and outcomes.

If each project’s information is fragmented across contractor platforms, consultant systems, shared drives, inboxes and archived files, an AI model faces the same problem a human does: the information may technically exist, but reconstructing the story becomes difficult. The owners that preserve a consistent project history today are not simply improving document retention — they are building the information base from which future analysis becomes possible.

There is an important distinction between controlling a project and controlling the enduring record of a project. Owners do not need every contractor to abandon the systems that help them build effectively, and they do not need to centralize every workflow or capture every administrative action performed during construction. What they do need is continuity over the information that explains the asset they ultimately own.

The owner owns the building. It carries the financial consequences of the decisions made during development, operates the asset after the project team leaves, funds the next capital program, and answers the questions of the next lender, investor, buyer or development team. The information describing how that asset was conceived, financed, designed, built and changed should be treated accordingly.

Construction teams move on, and ownership can change. The project record should remain with the asset, available to the people responsible for its future.

Adam Stark is a Special Forces veteran and construction technology executive with experience spanning development, project delivery, construction management and operational systems in the built world.  This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5546. Pfizer is tapping Blackstone for up to $1.5 billion to fund its weight-loss drug

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Blackstone would be eligible for milestone payments tied to U.S. approval of monthly berobenatide, while Pfizer keeps full control

Pfizer $PFE and Blackstone Life Sciences announced a co-funding agreement on Wednesday in which Blackstone-managed funds will shoulder as much as $1.5 billion of berobenatide's R&D expenses between now and 2028. The drug is an investigational monthly injection being studied for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.

In return, Blackstone could receive payments tied to the achievement of certain milestones, the companies said. The payments depend on U.S. regulatory approval of monthly dosing of injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management, and on certain commercial sales milestones. Any payments earned will be made over a multi-year period.

Blackstone does not acquire any rights or ownership in berobenatide, and Pfizer retains full operational control and decision-making over the program, the companies said. Funds managed by Blackstone's perpetual private equity strategy, BXPE, will invest alongside the Blackstone Life Sciences funds.

"Our aim is to bring important new medicines to patients while taking a disciplined approach that pairs internal research investments with targeted investment from capital partners," Pfizer Chief Financial Officer Cecile Guegan said in a statement. "Today's announcement helps us advance our comprehensive obesity program and maintain the financial capacity and flexibility to invest in our broader pipeline across all therapeutic areas."

Nicholas Galakatos, global head of Blackstone Life Sciences, said in a statement: "We are pleased to further expand our relationship with Pfizer and support the broad and rigorous development of berobenatide as the anchor of Pfizer's cardiometabolic pipeline."

Pfizer intends to move forward with over 20 studies covering obesity and related conditions during 2026, the company said. Those include 10 ongoing and planned Phase 3 trials for berobenatide, which is being studied for conditions such as knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea. The company is developing the drug as a monotherapy and in combination with other peptides, including amylin analogs.

Pfizer is pushing into a weight-loss field currently dominated by Eli Lilly $LLY and Novo Nordisk, according to Bloomberg. The company acquired Metsera in 2025 in a deal worth up to $10 billion.

#5544. Winning in a buyer’s market

With inventory rising and pending sales hitting historic lows, today's buyers have leverage they haven't seen in years. Jennifer Beeston breaks down three common client hesitations—high rates, high prices and closing costs—and outlines how agents and lenders can use seller concessions and buydowns to get deals across the finish line.   AI Summary

As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America.

Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable. It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales!

Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates?  Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies.

Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate.  I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there.

Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay.  It is up to the seller to say yes or no.

Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that’s a missed opportunity.  The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer.  Write the offer.

Did you know many buyers don’t realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller’s market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer’s market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays.

As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes?  No, but that is the beauty of the buyer’s market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it.

Jennifer Beeston is the EVP of National Sales at Chairman’s Circle (NMLS ID: 247743). This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5543. Michael Burry warned Jensen Huang affair could invite antitrust crackdown on Nvidia

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The investor said the affair could revive U.S. scrutiny of Nvidia's China chip trade and the Justice Department's antitrust probe

Michael Burry attends the "The Big Short" New York premiere at Ziegfeld Theater on November 23, 2015 in New York City. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

Michael Burry warned that the scandal involving Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang could reopen examination of how Nvidia sells its top-end chips into China, as well as the Justice Department's antitrust probe, according to Benzinga. The investor made the argument in a Substack post.

Nvidia’s board has ordered an independent review of Jensen Huang’s ties to a businesswoman suspected by intelligence agencies of spying for China, according to Benzinga. Huang is said to have had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. Investors sent Nvidia stock lower after the news.

Burry thinks the affair is unlikely to hurt the underlying profitability of Nvidia's operations, according to Benzinga. He wrote that he had not seen the news coming and described himself as "a bit shocked" by the rush of shareholders to exit the shares.

Burry said Nvidia's dealmaking is the real exposure. Nvidia's "mafia-like behavior investing in and making requirements of many players in the AI space has, to me, long seemed ripe for anti-trust prosecution," he wrote, according to Benzinga.

"There is a lot there if Justice and Commerce and various enforcement agencies stop ignoring and start investigating," Burry said, according to Benzinga. Until recently, he had no idea what would trigger that change, and the Huang news altered his view. "The mighty are only mighty until they have fallen. The fallen attract all manner of opportunists, both righteous and repugnant," he wrote.

The Justice Department has been examining whether Nvidia attempted to sidestep antitrust review of its licensing agreement with the AI chip startup Groq, The New York Times reported in September.

Burry said he has no interest in holding the stock over the long haul. "I believe Nvidia's competitive advantage will shrink over the next five years," he wrote, adding that the scandal makes it more likely the decline will arrive sooner. He holds puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, the Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 index, Oracle $ORCL and Palantir $PLTR Technologies, among other names, according to Benzinga.

Burry has maintained a short position in Nvidia this year. In August, he said all of his short positions were profitable except his bet against Nvidia. Earlier this year, he added to that bet by buying January 2027 puts on Nvidia with a $115 strike price at $3.30 per contract.

#5541. Horizon3 launches Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab built on NodeZero attack data

Autonomous penetration testing company Horizon3 AI Inc. today launched its new Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab.

The lab will draw on data from NodeZero, Horizon3’s penetration testing service, which is used by more than 7,000 organizations including banks, federal agencies and hospitals.

Purdue University’s Z. Berkay Celik has been named the lab’s inaugural director. Celik is an associate professor of computer science at Purdue and co-director of the Purdue Security Laboratory. Much of his work deals with finding software vulnerabilities and building defenses for autonomous systems, and he has run joint projects with industry and government.

According to Horizon3, NodeZero tests now produce about 30 billion tokens of anonymized data a day. Gathered on customers’ live production networks, the data also shows how their defensive tools reacted to each NodeZero command.

Snehal Antani, Horizon3’s co-founder and chief executive and a former chief technology officer of Splunk Inc., said the company has “spent years collecting” the data. Putting it to use in research like this is the next step, he said.

The lab’s first projects include research on coordinated groups of AI agents used in attacks. Deception is another, building on a Horizon3 paper titled “Honeyquest for LLMs.” Also on the list, according to Horizon3, are “interruption and rollback mechanisms” for autonomous security agents.

Horizon3 published a paper on keeping such agents under control in May. Using Anthropic PBC’s Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Haiku 4.5 models, it tested a design that limited the AI to a fixed list of approved tools, and Horizon3 said the system never proposed an action outside that list across more than 420 deployments.

Trained separately for each customer, Horizon3’s cyber world models give its red and blue agents a shared memory, and the lab is expected to speed up their development. Horizon3’s Cyber Resilience Centers of Excellence, which focus on critical infrastructure, will also report to the lab.

Horizon3 said in October that it had passed $100 million in annual recurring revenue, with growth of 120% year over year. NodeZero has run more than 350,000 production-safe tests to date. Horizon3 said about 80% of its customers have moved from annual to monthly penetration testing.

Founded in 2019, Horizon3 raised $250 million in August at a valuation of more than $2 billion.

#5540. Homebuilders and their partners team up to salute our veterans

Builders recognized Veterans Day through nonprofit partnerships, including mortgage-free home giveaways and support for transitioning service members. Regional builders also promoted limited-time military savings, typically $1,000 to $3,000, and some offered up to $2,500 toward closing costs in select communities.  AI Summary

Each Veterans Day, millions of Americans take a moment to honor the sacrifices that our military veterans have made for generations.

On a personal note, today I’m remembering both of my late grandfathers. One served in the Navy, while the other received a Purple Heart and numerous other medals for his bravery and service during the Vietnam War.

Across the country, homebuilders are marking Veterans Day with a range of initiatives, including special promotions and discounts for military families, mortgage-free home donations and workforce development programs designed to support veterans transitioning into civilian careers.

The following are some of the ways homebuilders are recognizing and supporting veterans this year.

PulteGroup, in partnership with Operation Homefront, announced that it gifted multiple newly constructed homes to military service members in cities like Anna, Texas, Wixom, Michigan and Richmond Hills, Georgia.

Meritage Homes, also in partnership with national military nonprofit Operation Homefront, will donate a brand-new, mortgage-free home to a military family in Gulfport, Mississippi.

The lucky recipient of Meritage Homes’ giveaway was Navy Personnel Specialist 2nd Class Maggie Coleman, who served 13 years in the Navy. Coleman will receive a 2,000-square-foot home with four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have. I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories,” Coleman said in a press release.

Lennar partnered with national nonprofit Operation Finally Home and country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan to surprise two military families with brand-new, mortgage-free homes in celebration of Veterans Day. The surprises unfolded Monday evening in Austin, Texas, during a reception in which the veterans believed they were simply attending as honored guests of the foundation.

And earlier this week, Invitation Homes announced that it has teamed up with Home Builders Institute to fund hands-on training, industry credentials and job placement for transitioning service members and veterans.

Many smaller, regional homebuilders, which don’t have the resources to give away homes for free, are honoring Veterans Day by offering temporary promotions for Veterans and military service members.

Taylor Homes, which builds in Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio, announced that it doubled its “We Salute You” bonus to $2,000 throughout November, giving military members a price reduction on a new home.

Tennessee-based Pratt Home Builders, meanwhile, is offering veterans, active-duty military and reservists $3,000 in savings toward a new home during November and December. Buyers can apply the savings toward the purchase price, design upgrades or appliances.

Other builders are offering similar incentives in select markets, either temporarily or on an ongoing basis. D.R. Horton, for example, is offering up to $2,500 toward closing costs through its Home of the Brave program in select San Antonio-area communities.

Landmark Homes offers active-duty military members and veterans a $1,000 incentive that can be combined with other promotions in Northern Colorado.

In Idaho, Hubble Homes offers a $2,500 Homes for Heroes discount, as does Drees Homes in markets like Jacksonville and San Antonio.

David Weekley Homes, meanwhile, provides military personnel with $1,000 in Flex Dollars in the Charleston, South Carolina market.

Many of these programs extend beyond veterans and military personnel to include teachers, police officers, firefighters and other first responders, grouping them under broader Hometown Heroes or similar initiatives.

#5539. Bitcoin slips to about $73,000 as Nvidia CEO turmoil rattles risk appetite

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 10% in late trading Wednesday, and U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have seen roughly $2.5 billion in net outflows since Oct. 30

Bitcoin fell as much as 2.2% on Thursday as reports of a possible leadership change at Nvidia $NVDA weighed on technology stocks and risk appetite. The cryptocurrency traded between about $72,900 and $73,400 in the early morning, and Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures were down 0.6%.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 10% in late trading Wednesday and was down about 7% in premarket trading Thursday. Nvidia is working with an outside firm to find possible successors to CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he had two extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman believed to have been spying on behalf of China, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia has yet to make any decision public, according to CoinDesk.

Withdrawals from U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds added to the pressure. Flows into the funds turned negative on Oct. 30, and net outflows since then total roughly $2.5 billion, according to Bloomberg. The funds shed $299.9 million Wednesday, extending their run of withdrawals to a fifth consecutive day, according to CoinDesk.

Bitcoin dropped to its weakest level in three months on Tuesday, when a stronger-than-forecast U.S. inflation reading strengthened bets on additional rate increases, according to Bloomberg. The Federal Reserve holds its next meeting Dec. 8-9, and CME $CME FedWatch pricing puts the odds of a rate increase near 90%, according to CoinDesk.

"Bitcoin is showing signs of a changing market structure, with selling pressure concentrated in derivatives while spot market activity remains comparatively resilient," wrote Dean Chen, who works as an analyst for the crypto exchange Bitunix, in a Thursday note, according to Bloomberg. Chen said traders are pulling back on leverage, though investors' positioning does not point clearly in one direction.

Open interest in bitcoin futures fell 2.9% over 24 hours, and bitcoin led all coins in liquidations with $62.9 million, according to CoinDesk. Render, a token tied to a decentralized network of graphics processors, fell 3.1% as Nvidia stock slid.

Nvidia's board was set to meet Wednesday evening to weigh removing Huang over two extramarital affairs, and no clear successor exists. Huang apologized to employees Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife. The board announced an independent investigation that day and said it had confidence in him.

Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

#5536. A Veterans Day reflection for building leaders and the work ahead

A Veterans Day editorial urging the housing and homebuilding community to pair gratitude with action. It spotlights two mortgage-free home commitments in Texas and outlines leadership traits tied to durable affordability progress.  AI Summary

Today, amid the quickened pulse of our nation’s political and cultural divisions, Veterans Day gives Americans a chance to take stock of something that transcends the moment’s disputes and divides.

We have inherited something incalculably, extraordinarily valuable.

Generations of men and women who served in the United States Armed Forces have helped preserve and protect a nation where we can live, work, worship, disagree, build businesses, raise families and decide what kind of future we want for ourselves and for those who come after us.

Those freedoms don’t exist in a vacuum. They’re neither inevitable nor self-sustaining, though we may act as if we take them for granted. They exist only because people before us accepted duties, endured pain, and made sacrifices for beneficiaries they didn’t know and ultimately never would.

Our children. Our children’s children. Their children. And on and on.

That generational commitment deserves more than our gratitude, though gratitude is where we begin today. And where we need to begin each day. A salute and a deeply felt debt of gratitude are an open invitation. It asks each of us to examine what we do with our hard-won inheritance. It asks us all what we are willing to do to preserve and improve it for generations beyond our own.

For those of us whose livelihoods center on making homes and neighborhoods for people to live in, that searching examination resonates. We work in a business community whose homes, neighborhoods, infrastructure and institutions endure. They’re a bedrock for generations. They profoundly nurture and shape the possibilities, the very dreams, available to American families and households.

Military service and homebuilding are not equivalent sacrifices. Still, much to learn from the commitment to mission, dependence on others, the discipline of preparation, and the willingness to serve a purpose larger than oneself that distinguishes the best traditions of military service.

This Veterans Day, we have a moving example of what happens when gratitude becomes a commitment to act. In Austin, Texas, this week, Lennar and nonprofit Operation Finally Home, joined by country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan, surprised two military veterans and their families with the promise of new, mortgage-free homes.

Marine Corps Sgt. Kevin Gallmeier served a decade in uniform, including combat deployments to Iraq, before retiring medically after sustaining service-related injuries. Army Spc. Jordan Taylor served in Baghdad and later continued serving his community as a firefighter and EMT until a serious injury forced him to retire.

For Taylor, his wife Aylynn, and their four children, financial hardship meant selling their family home and moving in with relatives. The promise of a new home offers a chance to regain stability and independence.

For Gallmeier and his family, a groundbreaking this week at Lennar’s Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas, marked the start of a new chapter.

Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath describes the organization’s mission as fighting with hammers, nails, and humility to restore dignity and peace of mind.

Nothing magical makes these homes a reality. Land must be secured, capital committed, plans developed, materials and products donated and skilled people coordinated through hundreds of decisions and handoffs before families receive their keys.

What makes the effort extraordinary is that people across organizations commit their capabilities and resources to a shared purpose, with the needs of two families at its core.

That is gratitude expressed through action.

And as HousingWire TBD reporter Tyler Williams chronicles in his Veterans Day reporting, this spirit of service spans the nation’s homebuilding community, from West to East and from South to North. From PulteGroup and Meritage Homes donating mortgage-free homes to regional builders offering military families financial assistance, and industry partners helping veterans transition into civilian careers, the commitment takes many forms.

Behind these named initiatives are countless unheralded builders, tradespeople, suppliers, employees, and volunteers who contribute their skills, resources, and time in communities across America. Their efforts reflect a deeply rooted conviction that building homes and communities also means honoring those whose sacrifices have made our freedom to do so possible.

Human beings have an extraordinary capacity to imagine a better future. That capacity is among our greatest strengths, enabling us to conceive of possibilities that do not yet exist and to organize our efforts to make them real.

We also tend toward magical thinking: believing that our wishes, convictions, or the triumph of our preferred outcomes will somehow deliver the future we envision without the difficult work required to bring it about.

Housing affordability offers a case in point.

For years, builders, developers, investors, policymakers, and families have wrestled with the interrelated constraints of lots, labor, lending, local approvals, and lumber — shorthand for the broader building-products supply chain. These five L’s often pull against one another. Improvement in one area does not necessarily lead to meaningful progress overall. In reality, getting one right often comes at the expense of one or more of the others.

And then there’s the sixth L: leadership. No single technological breakthrough, policy initiative, favorable interest-rate cycle, or election result will solve the interconnected problems of producing homes more Americans can afford.

There is no abracadabra. Only the sustained work of learning, adapting, cooperating, and improving remains.

The traditions of military service provide a useful standard for leaders in our industry to examine their own responsibilities. Five interdependent qualities stand out: character, capability, collaborative culture, customer centricity, and competitive fire.

Character means doing what is right even when it is difficult or costly. Capability is the accumulated knowledge, judgment, training, and practiced skill that enables people to perform under uncertain conditions. A collaborative culture recognizes that complex missions depend on people with different strengths coordinating their efforts toward shared objectives.

Customer centricity keeps the needs of those being served at the center of decisions. Competitive fire is the determination to keep improving, refusing complacency while adapting intelligently to adversity.

These qualities reinforce one another. Competitive fire without character becomes recklessness. Capability without collaboration becomes isolated expertise. Customer commitment without operating discipline leads to promises you can’t keep.

They also take time to develop. The strongest organizations invest in people, relationships, processes, and productive capacity, whose value can endure long beyond any individual leader’s tenure.

That is especially important now, as housing’s affordability, capital, and demand challenges strain the industry’s capacity to withstand adversity while preparing for the opportunities ahead.

Our country’s political divisions can make it mightily tempting to believe that progress requires defeating those whose beliefs differ from our own rather than finding ways to work with them. But the nation’s hardest problems will not yield simply because one side has won an election or one set of leaders has replaced another.

Nor can we assume that the good will inevitably prevail if we simply wait long enough.

Housing’s challenges remind us why cooperation matters. No single builder, developer, lender, investor, trade partner, or government agency can solve the affordability problem alone. People and institutions with different interests must find enough common ground to accomplish what none can achieve alone.

We may first need to slow the deterioration of some problems, then stabilize conditions, and only then make sustained progress toward better outcomes. That may not satisfy our appetite for quick solutions, but it is how durable improvements are achieved.

Generations of Americans have taken oaths of service without knowing whether they would live to see the fruits of their sacrifices. Their service has helped secure and preserve a nation in which we are free, individually and together, to decide what kind of future we want to pursue.

That freedom is a gift. What we do with it is our responsibility.

For those of us who build homes, develop communities, and invest in America’s future, that responsibility includes creating places where families put down roots, neighbors form communities, and children grow up with opportunities that may surpass those available to their parents.

We will not achieve those objectives through good intentions alone or by waiting for a more favorable economic cycle or a less divided political environment.

We must refuse to do nothing. We must not tolerate inaction. And we must recognize that a bigger tent, built on mutual respect and shared purpose, can accomplish more than one defined by animosity and division.

To the veterans of our United States Armed Forces, and to their families: Thank you for the freedoms you have helped protect, the sacrifices you have made, and the example of commitment to people you may never meet.

May we honor that inheritance through what we choose to build together – for our children, our children’s children, and all the generations to come.

#5535. CoreWeave is planning to raise at least $4 billion in a new high-grade loan

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Morgan Stanley and MUFG are leading the potential financing, which could reach the market as soon as next week

CoreWeave is seeking an investment-grade loan of at least $4 billion, and Morgan Stanley $MS and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group are heading up the possible deal, according to Bloomberg.

The loan could come to market as soon as next week and would be sold to investors in phases, though the plans are not final and could change, according to Bloomberg. Spokespeople for CoreWeave and Morgan Stanley would not comment, and MUFG did not reply to an inquiry.

The financing is expected to use chips and related contracts as backing, a structure CoreWeave has used to secure cheaper borrowing costs than it gets in the high-yield market, according to Bloomberg. CoreWeave is rated below investment grade.

Early discussions point to a yield of 7% to 7.5% on the new loan, according to Bloomberg, which cited CoreWeave's earnings call on Tuesday. That works out to roughly half of what CoreWeave's junk bonds currently pay.

CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, with revenue of $3.661 billion, up from $1.365 billion a year earlier. The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion. Wall Street had predicted an average of $12.9 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company posted a net loss of $709 million for the quarter and net interest expense of $846 million. It expects interest expense of $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter.

CoreWeave stock soared on Wednesday, and its bonds rallied.

In March, CoreWeave closed an $8.5 billion financing under an investment-grade facility supported by its customer agreements with Meta $META Platforms, according to Bloomberg. The March facility is split into two pieces: a floating-rate portion priced at 2.25 percentage points above SOFR, the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, and a fixed-rate portion at roughly 5.9%.

#5534. Reliability Remains Healthcare's Greatest Opportunity, Qualtrics XM Institute Finds

Patients who encounter operational friction give recommendation scores up to 37 points lower

New State of Patient Experience 2026 report analyzes 43.1 million patient encounters

PROVO, Utah, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Likelihood to Recommend (LTR) scores rose year over year in emergency departments, medical practices, ambulatory surgery, and inpatient care, but improving averages tell only part of the story, according to a new report from the Qualtrics XM Institute.

The State of Patient Experience 2026 report, which draws on data from more than 43.1 million patient encounters from organizations that partner with Qualtrics, finds that experiences vary widely by admission type and by whether patients encountered operational friction, such as delayed appointments and poorly coordinated handoffs. The most pressing challenge for leaders is making consistently positive experiences the norm, regardless of when, where, or how patients receive care.

Key findings in State of Patient Experience 2026

Friction drags recommendation scores down. Problems with access, scheduling, communication, and handoffs can make care hard to navigate. Across three care settings, patients who reported operational friction gave LTR scores 30 to 37 points lower than those who did not: 51.8 vs. 88.7 in ambulatory surgery, 60.3 vs. 96.4 in medical practices, and 60.3 vs. 90.6 in inpatient care.

Experiences are inconsistent across admission types. Patients at the same hospital can rate their care very differently depending on whether their admission was planned, especially at lower-rated hospitals. The median gap in overall ratings between planned and unplanned admissions was 18.2 points at bottom-quartile hospitals, more than twice the 8.9-point gap at top-quartile hospitals.

Patients notice when care teams work together. Patients rarely see the teamwork behind their care, but they feel it. There are telltale signs, such as a nurse who already knows what the physician discussed, consistent answers from different caregivers, and a handoff that doesn't make them repeat their story. In fact, hospital units in which employees reported strong teamwork were 1.9 times as likely to earn top patient experience ratings.

Completed post-discharge calls are associated with higher scores. On average, scores from patients who received a completed post-discharge call ranked 17 percentile points higher on the Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (HCAHPS) overall hospital rating and 12 percentile points higher on LTR than scores from patients whose calls were attempted but not completed.

Emergency care ratings differ by race and ethnicity. In emergency departments, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, and Black/African American patients consistently rated care below the overall averages at the facilities where they received care. The largest gap in overall ratings exceeded 8 points, with differences extending to courtesy, respect, communication, and listening.

The State of Patient Experience 2026 outlines nine priorities for healthcare leaders to focus on in 2027, including reducing operational friction through proven care practices, using AI to predict and mitigate poor experiences, and looking beyond overall averages to determine which patient groups are having the least favorable experiences.

"State of Patient Experience 2026 highlights that the patient experience bar keeps rising. Patients experience whether their care team is a real team, whether they are talking to each other, and whether someone checks on them after discharge," said Thomas H. Lee, MD, Executive Director of the Qualtrics XM Institute. "Healthcare is the ultimate Experience Management 'stress test.' When people are most vulnerable, they look for access, empathy, coordination, and cutting-edge care, delivered safely. I challenge leaders to look past the averages: find the moments where care breaks down for your patients, fix the systems behind them, and build experiences every patient can count on."

The data comes from organizations that partner with Qualtrics, representing more than 2,500 hospitals and 490,000 medical office sites across all nine AHA hospital regions. The analysis builds on a dataset with 40+ years of healthcare experience data from more than 41,000 facilities.

#5533. Housing demand shows signs of stabilizing. Does your market?

Housing demand may be stabilizing nationally, but the housing market looks different from one community to the next. In Florida's Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area, new pending listings rose 20.2% year over year in October 2026, even as some neighboring cities experienced declines. The divergence shows why local housing market trends, including buyer activity, new listings and pricing conditions, matter more than regional averages alone when evaluating market momentum.  AI Summary

Lower mortgage rates are helping stabilize housing demand even as inventory has declined, according to Logan Mohtashami’s latest Housing Market Tracker.

But a national housing demand signal doesn’t mean every local market is following. And even within the same metro area, buyer activity can tell very different stories.

The Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Florida offers a useful example.

New pending listings across the metro area increased 20.2% year over year in October, according to HousingWire Data. A closer look at individual cities, however, reveals that the improvement was far from uniform.

In Ormond Beach, Fla., new pending listings increased 116.7% year over year in October, rising from 72 in 2025 to 156 in 2026.

Nearby Port Orange recorded an 80% increase, while Daytona Beach saw a 63.2% gain.

But Deltona, one of the cities that gives the metro area its name, experienced a 24.3% decline. New pending listings fell from 136 to 103. New Smyrna Beach also recorded a decline of 25.3%.

Different patterns of buyer activity. This chart compares weekly new pending listings in Ormond Beach and Deltona over the past six months. While both cities experience fluctuations in weekly activity, their October year-over-year trends tell different stories. Adjust the date range or select YoY to explore how each city’s activity compares with its historical performance.

For housing professionals, the distinction matters. A regional market can be gaining momentum while individual communities within it are moving in the opposite direction.

Fall typically brings a slowdown in housing activity, but the timing and magnitude can vary significantly by market.

That’s why a change in new pending listings needs seasonal context.

Consider the average weekly new pending listings in three Volusia County cities between September and October 2026:

Historical trends add another layer. Ormond Beach also experienced an increase in average weekly new pending listings between September and October in 2025, but the increase was smaller. Deltona experienced an increase during that period in 2025 before reversing direction this year.

The lesson isn’t that one city is stronger than another. It’s that seasonal changes can play out differently even in neighboring communities.

A decline in new pending listings may be consistent with a market’s typical seasonal pattern. A smaller-than-usual decline could signal improving momentum. And an increase in activity deserves a closer look to determine whether it represents a sustained shift or a short-term fluctuation.

The Florida example raises a useful question: Are changes in buyer activity consistent across the communities you serve, or is the broader market trend masking important differences?

Four metrics can help you recognize changes, understand what they might signal and put that information to work.

What to watch: Compare new pending listings with the same period last year and track changes over several consecutive weeks. Look for activity that differs from the market’s typical seasonal pattern.

What it could mean: Sustained increases may indicate strengthening buyer activity, while declines can signal weakening demand. A smaller-than-usual seasonal decline may also be an early sign of stabilization.

How to use it: Identify communities where buyer activity is changing. Agents can use that information to set expectations with buyers and sellers, while loan officers can help referral partners understand where transaction opportunities may be improving.

What to watch: Compare the number of new listings entering the market with new pending listings. Is the gap between them widening or narrowing?

What it could mean: When new pending activity increases relative to new listings, buyers may be absorbing a greater share of incoming supply. When new listings grow faster than new pending activity, more homes may be competing for buyers’ attention.

How to use it: Evaluate whether buyers are likely to encounter more competition or more choices. For agents, that can inform pricing and offer strategies. For lending teams, it can help identify markets where purchase activity may be gaining momentum relative to available opportunities.

What to watch: Track the share of active listings with price reductions and whether that share is rising or falling over several weeks.

What it could mean: A rising share may suggest sellers are having difficulty attracting buyers at their initial asking prices. A declining share could indicate better alignment between pricing and buyer expectations, although changes in listing mix and seasonality can also influence the metric.

How to use it: Bring evidence into pricing conversations rather than relying solely on recent comparable sales. Loan officers can use the same information to help referral partners understand negotiating conditions and where pricing expectations may be changing.

What to watch: Compare median days on market with recent weeks and the same period last year. Look for whether homes are spending more or less time on the market.

What it could mean: Shorter marketing times alongside stronger new pending activity may reinforce evidence of improving demand. Longer marketing times, particularly when new pending activity is declining, may indicate that buyers are becoming more selective or that listings are taking longer to find the right price.

How to use it: Set more realistic expectations for listing timelines, buyer urgency and transaction pipelines. Brokerage and lending leaders can also use changes in market pace to inform team planning and activity forecasts.

If new pending listings are increasing, new listings are flat and days on market are declining, the combination provides stronger evidence of improving buyer activity than new pending listings alone.

But if new pending listings are rising alongside increasing price reductions and longer marketing times, the market may be experiencing a more complicated adjustment.

Consider Port Orange, Fla., where the share of listings with price reductions has declined since late September, but weekly new pending listings have fluctuated without a sustained increase. Fewer price reductions may be an encouraging sign, but they don’t necessarily indicate stronger buyer activity.

Different signals, different stories. In Port Orange, the share of listings with price reductions has fallen while weekly new pending listings have remained uneven. Adjust the date range to explore how these trends have changed over time.

Then compare neighboring communities. As the Florida example demonstrates, the same combination of metrics can tell different stories within a single metro area.

You can track these metrics and customize charts by city or ZIP code in HousingWire Intelligence.

The objective isn’t to predict the next market shift. It’s to recognize what is changing, understand what the evidence suggests and bring a more informed perspective to conversations with clients, referral partners and your team.

Logan’s national analysis suggests housing demand is finding some stability as mortgage rates ease. But the Florida data shows why that broader trend is only the starting point.

The more useful question isn’t simply whether the housing market is improving. It’s whether your market is improving, how you know and what that means for your business.

National trends provide context. Local data helps you make better decisions.

Methodology: The analysis uses HousingWire Data and covers single-family residential listings in the Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Volusia County, Florida.

October year-over-year comparisons use five weekly reporting periods in both 2025 and 2026. September-to-October comparisons use average weekly new pending listings to account for the different number of reporting weeks in each month.

New pending listings measure properties newly entering pending status during the reporting period, rather than the total number of properties under contract or completed sales.

All figures reflect data available through Nov. 6, 2026.

#5532. Qvyon launches with $8M to improve safety for physical AI deployments

Physical AI validation infrastructure and software development company Qvyon Technologies Inc. launched today with $8 million in total funding to help companies validate autonomous vehicles and robots before deployment.

MaC Venture Capital led the funding, with participation from BDC Capital, BKR Capital and Spotlight VP.

Physical AI is artificial intelligence that moves from digital brains to the real world, allowing smart machines to perceive, reason about and act within physical environments. This can include factory floors, retail shopping aisles, the kitchen or the roadway.

Before companies can deploy smart machines, such as robots or self-driving cars, into the real world, they must understand how these systems will operate under both normal and abnormal conditions. Reproducing strange, unlikely and dangerous conditions in the field is difficult and risky. For example, a car might suddenly pull in front of a truck during a rainstorm or a sensor array on a robot might become blocked or damaged while working on a production line.

To address these examples, Qvyon released Mimic Core, a platform that takes real-world sensor recordings into simulated environments to produce varied test scenarios, allowing developers and engineers to access data and test physical AI models and robotics setups in virtual environments without repeatedly collecting field data.

A single recording can allow an engineer to create many test variations to tease out where systems make mistakes. This allows development teams to catch problems before putting robots to work in the real world.

“We spent years building AI for vehicles and saw how hard it was to prove those systems were ready for the road,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Frantz Saintellemy. “Companies need to test what happens in their own vehicles and factories by using their own recordings.”

Qvyon’s system ingests camera, lidar and radar data. It uses this to reconstruct environments in 3D and time-sequence snapshots, capturing scenes and how they change over time. It uses this to generate challenging conditions to test AI models against the hardware they will drive in simulation. The platform produces traceable datasets and validation evidence that engineers can use to evaluate smart machines’ performance before deployment.

Mimic Core works alongside the same virtual testing tools that companies already use and helps them better understand the scenarios and conditions robots and smart machines will face.

The company offers the product as software-as-a-service and as a self-hosted solution for companies that want to keep everything in-house. Qvyon stressed that when using its cloud product, customer data is kept separate and is never used to train AI models for other customers.

Mimic Core is available today via Qvyon Cloud with a 14-day guided evaluation, or for companies to run on their own systems.

The company said the funding will support Mimic Core and its rollout through the United States, Europe and Japan. Qvyon is also developing Mimic Validation OS, planned for the first half of 2027, to help companies measure and document test results, and Mimic Learn, planned for late 2027, to help improve AI using information from machines already in operation.

#5531. Kraft Heinz is projecting a return to sales growth in second-half 2027

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Kraft Heinz expects 2027 organic net sales to be relatively flat for the year and adjusted operating income to decline

Kraft Heinz $KHC expects to return to sales and profit growth in the second half of 2027, the company said on Thursday as it hosts its 2026 Investor Day.

For full-year 2027, the company expects organic net sales to be "relatively flat," with growth returning in the second half. It expects adjusted operating income to decline by a low single-digit percentage versus 2026, with a return to growth in the second half. Free cash flow conversion is expected to remain at least 100%.

Kraft Heinz said it will provide formal 2027 guidance on its fourth-quarter earnings call. Management is sharing the initial contours of its expectations at the investor event, which has a webcast starting at 10:30 a.m. ET.

The company laid out milestones through 2029. In 2026, it said it is narrowing market share losses, recovering its top line from 2025 levels and improving volume trends in all regions. It expects consistent top-line growth and margin expansion in 2028. By 2029, it expects to deliver double-digit total shareholder return, with a balanced contribution from earnings growth and capital returned to shareholders.

"With the right team, a business-unit-led operating model, and greater, consistent investment behind our brands, we are positioning Kraft Heinz to create long-term value for shareholders," Chief Executive Officer Steve Cahillane said in a statement. The company said its strategy centers on volume-led profitable growth.

Cahillane has led the turnaround since taking the helm in January, according to Bloomberg. Having shelved the proposed breakup, he directed $700 million toward marketing, pricing, additional staff and research and development. The company's breakdown of that spending is $325 million for marketing, $250 million for pricing, $75 million for new employees and $50 million for products and packaging.

Kraft Heinz projects that new launches will represent 5% of its retail net sales in the U.S. in 2027, versus 3% in 2026. The company said its worldwide market share rose 30 basis points this year relative to 2025, and that sales of its macaroni and cheese line are growing again, according to Bloomberg.

Cahillane told analysts last week that Kraft Heinz is likely to lift prices in 2027 as inflation persists, according to Bloomberg.

Kraft Heinz last week raised the low end of its 2026 organic net sales forecast when it reported third-quarter results. The company now projects a full-year organic net sales decline of 0.5% to 1.25%, improved from the earlier outlook of a 0.5% to 2% drop.

In the third quarter, net sales fell 2.0% to $6.1 billion and organic net sales fell 1.1%. North America net sales fell 3.4%, Europe and Pacific Developed Markets net sales fell 5.6%, and Emerging Markets net sales rose 13.8%.

#5529. Education, not operations, are holding back reverse for purchase deals

Reverse mortgage for purchase loans often close in seven to 25 days, panelists said at NRMLA Annual. Down payments typically run from 45% to 65%, and early counseling plus contract management can prevent delays.  AI Summary

Reverse mortgage for purchase loans work much like other types of home purchase financing. Even so, many real estate agents, financial advisers and loan officers don’t know how they work, according to experts who spoke this week at the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio.

Peter Morris, an Arizona-based senior vice president at Revolution Mortgage, said the ideal reverse for purchase prospects are seniors who want to upsize, downsize or relocate. He also frequently works with borrowers who don’t qualify for traditional 30-year loans or home equity products due to debt-to-income or credit constraints.

Morris said he’s seeing rising interest in these financing options among real estate partners. He recently hosted a continuing education course where “I had the most Realtors that I’ve ever had in a CE class.”

Senior homeowners with high levels of equity and a need to move are able to utilize the federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) program or proprietary programs to purchase their next primary residence. The typical down payment ranges from 45% to 65%, depending on the appraised value, interest rate and age of the borrower. For example, an 80-year-old buyer has a smaller down payment requirement than a 70-year-old buyer since they have a shorter life expectancy.

Morris relayed a story about an agent partner in North Carolina with five listings between $400,000 and $800,000. While an all-cash buyer with $400,000 — typically a highly coveted buyer — could afford only some of these listings, a reverse for purchase borrower with the same $400,000 might be able to afford each of them, he told the agent.

“You have to educate your Realtor and show them that they are losing out, and they have the potential of making a lot more money with such a simple product,” Morris said. “I can show you how you can do less transactions and make more money, because you can buy more of a house in a reverse purchase.”

Shain Urwin, national reverse mortgage director for C2 Financial Corp., and Agi Glukhovskiy, SVP of business support and operations for Rate, explained some of the differences between traditional and reverse for purchase deals.

Borrower counseling through an independent third party is required on all HECM for Purchase deals insured by the Federal Housing Administration and for most proprietary reverse mortgages. Reverse transactions also have unique forms, including a Good Faith Estimate (GFE) and a HUD-1 form, rather than the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms commonly associated with forward mortgages.

Glukhovskiy said the absence of conventional forward lending documents are actually an advantage for reverse deals since they won’t have a mandatory federal waiting period. Urwin noted that a handful of states, such as California and Idaho, have implemented their own waiting periods. Beyond that, however, the steps are largely the same as any traditional deal as the process moves from application to underwriting, appraisal, title and approval.

The panelists sought to dispel ideas that reverse purchases are slow to close. Glukhovskiy said her team has wrapped them up in seven to 10 days, and although the average is 20 to 25 days, the idea that the process takes 45 days is “absolutely nonsense,” she added. Neil Sweren, a Baltimore-based reverse division manager for Atlantic Coast Mortgage, recalled a recent deal that closed in seven calendar days.

Angel Booth, national sales manager for title and settlement services provider Premier Reverse Closings, clarified to HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily that the typical 10- to 15-day process cited by lenders is “absolutely attainable” once the loan is clear to close.

Glukovskiy said the keys to a quick closing are finishing counseling prior to the start of the home search process, collecting income documentation, and setting expectations with agents and lending operations staff. Loan officers should read the purchase contract and know every contingency date, Urwin said, as trouble begins when they overpromise. And Sweren pointed to timing: If a closing date gets pushed back and falls within six months of the borrower’s birthday, the amount of cash needed to close can change.

Simultaneous closings, where the borrower sells one home and buys another, can be difficult but not impossible to pull off. Glukovskiy recommended that sale proceeds should go straight to the title company handling the property being purchased, rather than going to the borrower.

Urwin told a cautionary tale about a borrower who took their sale proceeds and paid down a home equity line of credit on another property, leaving them ineligible to use the borrowed funds to buy their new house. “I learned from that very painfully, but those kinds of nuances matter when tracking those funds,” he said.

For loan officers who are new to reverse for purchase deals, panelists urged them to study up before they present the benefits to agents.

Continuing education courses are a prime way to teach agents, with Sweren saying they often come to his classes to help their own parents or grandparents. Many agents happen to be senior homeowners and may need assistance for themselves. Being the go-to loan officer when a listing includes a reverse mortgage should be part of everyone’s market strategy.

The panelists admitted that financial advisers may be a harder sell. Urwin noted that because these referral partners focus on cash and assets under management, they may not recommend a client put their cash into a home. But he relayed a success story where an adviser partner took out a reverse mortgage on his own home, then began sending referrals to Urwin when he had older clients who wanted to pay cash for a house.

The goal in these situations, Urwin said, should be to avoid an all-cash purchase. Clients should consider long-term tax strategies and the choice between leaving illiquid home equity or highly liquid cash to their heirs.

Sweren also mentioned the advantage of reverse mortgages in planning for rising healthcare costs, something he believes the industry “has not gotten past the tip of the iceberg” with. HECM lines of credit serve as “the most flexible borrowing instrument in the market by far,” he said, as borrowers can qualify for relatively large amounts, withdraw funds as needed, and have available proceeds grow over time based on the interest rate and annual mortgage insurance premium.

Sweren said reverse mortgage professionals should remember that “this is a very emotional transaction for seniors” as they may be leaving a home they’ve lived in for decades. They also may be widows or widowers who didn’t handle their family’s finances, meaning they’ll need additional support to get the deal over the line.

“Respecting that and understanding the emotional journey your client is on — and explaining that to the rest of the team that’s involved — is super helpful,” he added.

#5528. Canada's ambassador warned Trump's tariffs are raising the cost of investment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Mark Wiseman called for removal of Section 232 and 338 duties as U.S.-Canada talks resume after collapsing in August

Mark Wiseman, Canada's ambassador to the U.S., cautioned on Wednesday that the tariffs President Donald Trump has imposed make investing more expensive and give companies reason to hold back on growth, according to CNBC.

"Uncertainty increases your cost of capital," Wiseman told attendees of the B20 summit, an event the U.S. Chamber of Commerce organized in Washington for global business leaders, according to CNBC. "If you're going to build a new plant, add a new ship, spend money on R&D, the more certainty you have, the more likely you're going to do that."

Wiseman, a former BlackRock $BLK executive, became ambassador in February. He urged that the duties levied under Sections 232 and 338 of American trade law be lifted, arguing that settling the dispute would let businesses plan their investments over the long haul. "The sooner, the better," he said, according to CNBC. He said Canada wants to get back to "as close as we can to free trade."

Washington and Ottawa returned to the bargaining table after discussions broke down in August, according to CNBC. The talks center on lowering duties on steel and cars from Canada. Trump has levied duties as high as 50% on some Canadian products, and Canada has hit back with countermeasures aimed at U.S. exports worth billions of dollars. Trump has justified the tariffs as a way to shield American manufacturers and workers, and he has charged Canada with discriminatory trade practices.

According to CNBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada still treats the Trump administration as its main counterpart in trade talks.

U.S. exports to Canada totaled $265.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, and imports from Canada totaled $304.6 billion, according to Census Bureau data. That left a goods trade deficit of $38.7 billion.

Trump signed a proclamation on Oct. 23 changing the list of Canadian products covered by Section 338 tariffs, effective Oct. 30. The 50% duties apply whether or not a good originates under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement and stack on top of Section 232 tariffs. Gellert Global Group, a U.S. food importer, has filed a lawsuit in the U.S. Court of International Trade arguing the administration exceeded its authority under Section 338.

New York Fed economists found in a study of tariff pass-through into consumer prices that nearly 90% of a tariff is reflected in higher import prices. About 26% of any given tariff increase reaches consumer goods prices.

Germany's ambassador to the U.S., Jens Hanefeld, said at the same summit that tariffs were something firms could adjust to, but that an "ever-changing regulatory environment" proved harder to handle, since it pushed companies to devote more money to legal help in making sense of evolving trade rules, according to CNBC.

BARCELONA, Spain and LOS ANGELES, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MSI, a global leader in AI PCs, gaming, and high-performance computing, announced the renewal of its strategic partnership with Red Bull, a global pioneer and powerhouse in action sports and esports culture. #5526. Why the 2026 fake foreclosure crisis never happened

Foreclosure activity in 2026 rose off low levels but did not signal broad credit stress. With 9- to 18-month timelines and LTV at 44.2%, the data points to normalization, not a crisis.  AI Summary

The 2026 foreclosure crisis that some people predicted has failed to materialize, and now those people look silly. We should be thankful for the regulations and laws enacted that laid the foundation for such a sound housing credit market: The 2005 bankruptcy reform law and the 2010 Dodd-Frank laws that established qualified mortgage guidelines were historically positive for the U.S. economy.

Looking at the New York Fed’s Household Debt and Credit Report for Q3, we can clearly see that the anticipated foreclosure crisis hasn’t happened. All the headlines showing a high percentage of year-over-year growth in foreclosure data didn’t amount to anything near a crisis.

For those who expected a situation worse than what we experienced in 2008, it has been an embarrassing year. This highlights the dangers of listening to economic discussions from those without the necessary expertise. So let’s talk about where these doomers get it wrong.

The idea that the FHA foreclosure moratorium, which ended in October 2025, would lead to a surge in distressed listings has been a popular topic this year. It’s gotten a lot of headlines, but has fallen flat on its face, since that isn’t how the foreclosure-to-listing process works in America. At minimum, it takes 9-18 months from the start of the foreclosure process to finally add that supply to the marketplace.And foreclosure data has not, at any point since 2014, shown any material sign of credit stress building up in the pipeline. Always remember, 1%-4% of all mortgages are always going to be in delinquency; it’s when that data breaks above historical norms that it should get everyone’s attention.To illustrate what a true foreclosure crisis might look like, we can consider the historical context: since World War II, we have experienced 13 recessions with an average unemployment rate of 7.8%, but only one significant foreclosure crisis, which was the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession.

It took four years for the foreclosure credit market to build up before the 2008 recession hit. As we finish Q3 of 2026, we still haven’t returned to pre-COVID levels of foreclosure credit stress, as the data below has always shown for anyone who believes in reading.

The New York Fed foreclosure credit stress data line moves slowly, and unless this index is above 200, there isn’t much activity out of the norm. The many posts this year predicting a foreclosure crisis have proven to be exaggerated. The scale of the situation is small, and it’s clear that many commentators lack the experience to accurately discuss the current market conditions.Additionally, I want to highlight HousingWire’s new listing data. During the previous housing crisis, credit foreclosures directly impacted new listing data, pushing weekly listings to between 250,000 and 400,000 — for years. These listings represented distressed sellers who were forced to sell in an underwater market. All those increases from 2005-2008 in foreclosures eventually became distressed sales, and none of that is happening today. Let’s compare the new listings data for last week to the same week from 2009-2011:

The 2008 massive credit boom and bust took many years to create. We have not seen this kind of credit boom in housing from 2010-2026, so it’s impossible to have a credit bust like 2008 — or “worse than 2008,” as many untrained fake housing analysts have talked about for years. A lot of people can’t let go of the past, as they’re still dancing with the ghost of the 2008 housing crisis. They should relax, have a glass of wine, and reflect on their bad takes.In contrast, over the last 16 years, FICO scores in America have remained strong. Most homeowners have 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and qualification guidelines are much more stringent and effective now. Rising wages and homeowners staying in their properties longer have contributed to the overall financial health of American households.

Despite claims of an impending foreclosure crisis, the reality is quite different. In 2010, over 23% of homes in America were underwater, with loan-to-value ratios reaching nearly 86% in 2011. Currently, the loan-to-value figure is down to 44.2%, as the chart below shows.

It’s crucial to be cautious about who you listen to, as the narrative of a looming crisis has been overstated for many years. If someone tells you it’s housing 2008 or a foreclosure crisis is here, tell them to read a book instead of burning it, and read HousingWire.

#5525. Scout Motors has about 212,000 reservations as South Carolina plant nears completion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CEO Scott Keogh said reservations for the Terra truck and Traveler SUV could top 400,000 before customer production starts

Scout Motors, the Volkswagen-backed electric vehicle maker, has about 212,000 reservations for its Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

Scout said on Thursday that construction of its $2 billion plant in South Carolina is in its final phase, according to CNBC. Keogh said the plant is roughly 85% finished, and crews are still installing related infrastructure as well as a supplier park valued at $300 million.

Full production of the two vehicles is expected to begin in 2027, with customer deliveries starting in 2028, according to CNBC.

Scout is building validation vehicles at the plant, with stamping, welding and paint operations under way, according to The Drive. Those builds are set to carry on into 2027 while the company gets ready for pre-production, according to The Drive. Scout also said most of the plant's manufacturing equipment is in place, The Drive reported.

“What we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper,” Keogh said in a statement.

Keogh told CNBC that reservations could top 400,000 ahead of the start of customer production. He said the bigger challenge is getting early enthusiasm to become buyers, and he expects Scout to have 12 to 18 months of orders lined up before production starts.

"The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell," Keogh said.

Reservations are no guarantee of sales, according to CNBC, which cited the Ford $F F-150 Lightning and Tesla $TSLA Cybertruck as electric trucks whose early excitement never grew into large numbers of buyers.

Scout will offer all-electric versions and extended-range electric vehicles, known as EREVs, which carry a gas engine that acts as a backup generator, according to CNBC. Slower adoption of electric vehicles, along with rising expenses, pushed Scout to work the EREVs into its plans.

Keogh said about 87% of reservations are for EREV models and 75% are for SUVs. He said Scout plans to launch the EREVs ahead of the all-electric versions and to begin with mid-level models rather than the highest-priced ones.

Keogh said the goal is to reach 100,000 units quickly, the point at which he said the company can "start to punch through."

Reservations opened in October 2024, when Scout revealed the Traveler and Terra, according to CNBC.

HubSpot named co-founder Brian Halligan chief executive on Thursday, replacing Yamini Rangan, and announced that Chief Financial Officer Kate Bueker will retire in February 2027.

Rangan is stepping down as CEO and from the board effective Thursday and will stay with the company through Dec. 1 to help with the transition, the company said. Halligan has served on the board since 2005.

HubSpot reaffirmed the fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 guidance it gave on Nov. 4 in its third-quarter earnings release.

Halligan co-founded HubSpot in 2005 with Chief Technology Officer Dharmesh Shah and served as CEO for 16 years. He plans to reimagine the company across product, go-to-market and culture, the company said.

"This is a refounding, and I can't wait to start!" Halligan said in a statement.

"The Board is united in its support of his refounding of the company," Lorrie Norrington, chairperson of the HubSpot board, said in a statement.

During Rangan's tenure, which began in September 2021, HubSpot's customer count grew from 135,000 to more than 311,000, the company said. Revenue rose from $1.3 billion in 2021 to an expected $3.7 billion in 2026.

"I don't want to see HubSpot swallowed up by a private equity firm or shrink — I want to rebuild it and reimagine it," Halligan told Bloomberg. He suggested HubSpot might have prioritized near-term financial goals over developing its products, according to Bloomberg. "I don't know if you looked at the last earnings, but the numbers aren't great," Halligan said.

HubSpot stock is down 50% so far this year, as of Wednesday.

The leadership change follows a restructuring. HubSpot announced in October that it was eliminating about 660 positions, roughly 7% of its global workforce. Rangan said at the time that the goal was a flatter organization with fewer management layers.
