#5521. What pricing and execution inefficiency really costs mortgage lenders

MBA data shows the top 20% of lenders earned $4,551 per loan in Q2 2026 while the bottom 20% lost $2,551. The column argues PPE engines should be evaluated on accuracy, execution and scalability, not only implementation cost.   AI Summary

The gap between mortgage lenders that are making money and those that are losing it is striking: According to the Mortgage Bankers Association, the top 20% of lenders earned an average production profit of $4,551 per loan in the second quarter of 2026, while the bottom 20% lost an average of $2,551 per loan.

MBA Vice President of Industry Analysis Marina Walsh says revenue, rather than expenses, appears to be “the more prominent differentiator” in lender profitability, pointing to product mix, pricing discipline and secondary marketing strategy, among other factors.

For mortgage executives, the findings underscore the importance of evaluating technology investments not only as expenses, but also as potential contributors to revenue and profitability. That is particularly relevant to product, pricing and eligibility (PPE) engines, which play a central role in determining which loan products lenders can offer, how accurately they price them and how effectively they execute their secondary marketing strategies.

Yet when mortgage executives evaluate whether to replace a PPE engine, the conversation often turns quickly to the cost of making a change:

Those are reasonable questions. They are also relatively easy to place in a spreadsheet. Implementation labor, training, internal resources and transition requirements can usually be identified, estimated and assigned to a defined period.

The largest economic issue may not be the cost of changing a PPE engine. It may be the cost of continuing to operate with pricing inaccuracies, inefficient workflows, inconsistent execution, avoidable exceptions, high product-maintenance demands, limited operational scale, slow product launches and unrealized revenue opportunities.

Transition costs are typically finite. Performance costs can repeat with every transaction.

That distinction should change how executive teams evaluate PPE engine investments.

Mortgage technology evaluations often begin with product automation: how much time a system can remove from a process or how many manual steps can be eliminated.

Time savings matter, but they are only one component of financial impact and often not the most impactful one.

A more complete assessment of financial and operational impact considers four dimensions:

Focusing only on automation is insufficient because risk reduction and transaction execution can be larger drivers of total financial impact.

This is particularly important in a PPE engine decision. The economic value of the engine is not limited to the minutes it removes from a pricing task. It also includes the quality and consistency of the decision produced, the accuracy of eligibility determinations, the efficiency with which lenders can manage margins and translate pricing strategies into execution, the effort required to maintain products and rules, the speed and accuracy with which new products can be introduced and the organization’s ability to scale and respond to market volatility.

A lower visible technology cost does not necessarily mean a lower enterprise cost.

Executive teams should separate the business case into two categories.

This category includes implementation, training, integration work, data migration and temporary disruption. These costs should be measured carefully, but they generally have two defining characteristics: they are finite, and they are primarily incurred during the transition.

A prudent analysis should identify the internal resources required, external costs, expected timing and operational dependencies. Those numbers belong in the investment model.

They should not, however, become the entire investment model.

The second category includes errors, inconsistent pricing, reduced execution quality, workflow friction, exception management and lower productivity. It also includes opportunity costs, such as the inability to deploy products quickly, fine-tune margins, improve closing performance or respond effectively to market volatility.

These costs may be less visible because they are distributed across business units and individual transactions. Pricing leakage may appear in secondary marketing results. A process deficiency may appear as extra lock-desk work. Weak integration may appear as duplicated effort. Inaccurate eligibility may appear as an exception, a rework event or a lost opportunity.

Individually, each event may appear manageable. Across an enterprise loan population, recurring differences in precision and execution can become economically significant.

Pricing and eligibility accuracy are often discussed as matters of control, compliance or user experience. An inaccurate decision can create rework, exceptions and downstream adjustments, but its effect can also extend to the economics of the loan itself.

While lenders may not be able to calculate the exact cost of every error, recurring inaccuracies can add up quickly across thousands of transactions. Treating accuracy as only an operational benefit can therefore understate its financial importance.

A PPE engine should return accurate pricing quickly. Its broader value lies in helping an organization execute its pricing strategy consistently. This includes enabling teams to respond to market movement, manage margins efficiently, evaluate options and maintain consistency from pricing through delivery.

Execution is therefore a core consideration in a PPE investment decision. Organizations should evaluate whether the platform enables accurate, timely and consistent decisions that protect margins and support an effective response to market volatility. In that context, incremental differences in licensing costs may be less significant than the platform’s effect on financial performance.

This is a two-part series; in part two, understanding how PPE technology affects loan-level profitability is only the first step. In the next installment, we look at the broader opportunity costs of technology decisions and outline eight questions lenders can use to build a more complete business case.

Jordan Brown is the founding principal and CEO of MarketWise Advisors, LLC, a management consulting firm focused on the mortgage and financial technology industries.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5519. New York City Council is expected to ban stores from using personal data to set prices

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The bill would let the city fine retailers up to $1,000 per violation and take effect one year after enactment

The New York City Council is expected to vote on Thursday on a bill that would forbid businesses from relying on algorithms and personal data to quote shoppers varying prices for identical goods, according to The New York Times.

Council Speaker Julie Menin, the bill’s sponsor, said the votes needed to pass it are comfortably secured. The Council’s Consumer and Worker Protection Committee has its vote set for 11 a.m. ET, with the entire Council convening later in the day, according to amNewYork.

"When corporations use algorithms and personal data to charge different people different prices for the same products, it's unethical and worsens our affordability crisis," Menin said in a statement, according to The New York Times. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the move. "New Yorkers' personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks," he said.

The bill, Introduction 891-A, would empower the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to look into violations and fine offenders as much as $1,000 for every infraction, according to amNewYork. Every consumer or transaction involved could be tallied as its own violation. The bill would also bar companies from gathering, selling or passing along personal information for use in surveillance pricing.

Routine sales, coupons, rewards for loyal customers and breaks for specific categories of people, among them veterans and seniors, would stay legal, according to amNewYork. The bill carves out some activities already under government regulation, such as pricing for insurance and credit.

Qualifying small businesses would be told of an initial violation and given 30 days to demonstrate that they have fixed the problem, according to amNewYork. The bill was revised after a June 17 hearing at which retail, hotel and technology groups warned it could restrict rewards programs and discounts. The effective date moved from 120 days to one year after enactment. The bill does not include the private right of action that the department's commissioner, Sam Levine, had requested.

Josh Gold, a spokesman for Uber $UBER, said the ban would hurt small restaurants. Uber Eats lets restaurants send targeted discounts based on consumers' searches and abandoned shopping carts, and the city ban would not allow that practice, according to The New York Times. "If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains," Gold said.

The state Legislature passed a similar ban, the One Fair Price Act, in June. It remained unsigned by Gov. Kathy Hochul as of Wednesday, according to amNewYork. Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey and Seattle have approved similar measures, according to The New York Times.

Seattle's City Council approved a policy in September barring large grocery retailers from using artificial intelligence and personal data to set prices for individual shoppers. That policy still allows openly advertised loyalty discounts for broad groups, such as seniors or veterans, and standard coupons.

If the Council passes the New York bill and Mamdani signs it, the ban would go into force a year after it is enacted, according to amNewYork.

#5518. Why the next Fed decision should not impact your house purchase

This analysis explains why the Fed funds rate and 30-year mortgage rates do not move in lockstep. It quantifies payment and interest differences across small rate changes, and frames decisions around affordability, time in the home and refinance costs.   AI Summary

A quarter point can dominate the housing conversation. It should not automatically dominate a household’s decision to buy.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% on October 28. But the vote was hardly an all-clear for lower borrowing costs: two officials preferred a quarter-point increase. With inflation still elevated, another increase remains a possibility.

That uncertainty leaves prospective buyers asking whether they should wait. My view is that buying a reasonably priced home you can comfortably afford can still be a sound way to build wealth. A modest difference in the mortgage rate deserves a calculation before it becomes a reason to put that decision on hold.

First, the Fed does not set the rate on a 30-year mortgage. Mortgage pricing reflects longer-term borrowing costs, inflation expectations and conditions in mortgage markets. A quarter-point Fed increase does not automatically produce a quarter-point increase in a homebuyer’s quote. And once a fixed-rate mortgage closes, a later Fed increase does not change its interest rate.

Still, buyers can compare what different mortgage rates actually mean. Consider a $300,000 loan, repaid over 30 years:

These are illustrative rates, not lender quotes. Payments include principal and interest only; taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance and association fees are additional. Freddie Mac’s national 30-year average was 7.24% on October 29.

Moving from 7% to 7.5% adds about $102 a month, roughly 5.1% to the principal-and-interest payment. That is real money. A buyer whose budget cannot absorb it should reconsider the price or timing. But for a financially prepared household, it may be manageable enough that other parts of the purchase deserve more attention.

A lower purchase price, fewer repairs or better loan terms can also change the economics. Buyers should evaluate the whole transaction instead of treating the interest rate as the sole measure of a good deal.

Freddie Mac’s mortgage-rate series reached 18.63% in October 1981. By the first week of January 2021, the average had fallen to a record low of 2.65%. Those extremes show how much the financing environment can change. They do not make today’s housing inexpensive: home prices, incomes and other ownership costs matter, too.

The payment math also shows why small changes should be distinguished from major shifts. On the same $300,000, 30-year loan, moving from 3% to 7% raises principal and interest by about $731 a month. Moving from 7% to 7.5% adds about $102. Both increases matter, but they present very different budget decisions.

It is easy to multiply that extra monthly payment by 360 and stop there. The half-point difference in our example adds approximately $36,625 over 30 years if the borrower keeps the original loan and makes every scheduled payment.

That is a valid lifetime comparison. It may not describe the buyer’s actual experience.

The National Association of Realtors’ 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers reported that the typical seller had owned the home for 11 years. That is a median among recent sellers, not an average for every homeowner or a prediction for a new buyer. Separately, Atlanta Fed researchers have described the average life of a mortgage as around seven to 10 years. Owning a home and retaining its original mortgage are different timelines.

Suppose our borrower sells after five years. At 7.5% rather than 7%, the borrower would have made about $6,104 in additional payments and would owe about $1,458 more at payoff. The additional interest cost is therefore about $7,562. Shorter ownership reduces the period of exposure; it does not erase the cost or the difference in remaining debt.

Refinancing can shorten that original loan’s life, sometimes substantially. ICE’s December 2024 Mortgage Monitor reported that rate-and-term refinancers in September and October had held their previous mortgages for an average of just 15 months. That was an unusually short period during a particular refinancing window, not a normal schedule every buyer can expect.

The decision should turn on the savings and costs. If a refinance costs $5,000 and reduces the payment by $200 a month, the simple break-even period is 25 months. Borrowers should also compare the remaining balances and repayment terms; restarting a 30-year clock can reduce the payment while increasing total interest.

The purchase needs to work at the rate available today. A future refinance can improve the outcome, but it should not be the condition that makes the home affordable.

Homeownership’s appeal extends beyond a future rate reduction. On our $300,000 mortgage at 7%, scheduled payments reduce principal by approximately $17,605 over five years and $48,687 over 11 years, without assuming any appreciation. That principal repayment builds equity, although it comes from the owner’s own cash payments and is not investment profit.

Appreciation can add to that equity, while falling prices can reduce it. Maintenance, transaction costs and the opportunity cost of the down payment also affect the result. Renting can be sensible for someone who needs flexibility or faces a substantially cheaper rental alternative.

For buyers with stable income, adequate reserves and plans to stay long enough to spread out transaction costs, ownership still offers a practical path to accumulating an asset while meeting a basic need for housing.

The Fed’s next move deserves attention. But a household’s ability to afford the home, maintain it and hold it through changing markets deserves more. A quarter point or half point should be part of that judgment. It should not make the judgment for them.

Author calculations use standard monthly amortization with 360 payments, a $300,000 initial balance and no points, financed fees, prepayments or tax benefits. Comparisons hold principal and term constant. The five-year interest comparison includes the difference in loan balances at payoff. Figures are calculated before rounding; rounded displayed amounts may differ by a cent when subtracted.

Jesse Brewer is a local county commissioner in Boone County, Kentucky, real estate broker, investor, property manager and private money lender.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5516. Bitcoin Price Cooked? Gensler 2.0 Fears as Fed Blocks Crypto Bank

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin is struggling to find its footing after another brutal sell-off pushed its price below $73,000. The decline wiped out hundreds of millions of dollars in leveraged positions, leaving us questioning if the market has entered a deeper correction phase.

Bitcoin is now trading around $73,600 after briefly losing the $73,000 level. Ethereum slipped below $2,100, while XRP approached $1.05 and Solana struggled to hold $82. More than $723 million in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with nearly 79% coming from long bets.

The timing is particularly uncomfortable for Bitcoin bulls. October’s hotter-than-expected US inflation report has revived concerns about interest rates, while recent US election results have introduced another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Now, a banking dispute involving the Federal Reserve is adding fuel to the fire.

The sell-off has several forces working against it. First, October’s US Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4% month over month, exceeding economists’ expectations of 0.3%. Core inflation also climbed 0.3%, above the 0.2% forecast.

The interest-rate outlook has become even more concerning. According to CME’s latest rate probability data, the chance of the Federal Reserve keeping its target rate unchanged at 3.75%–4% has fallen to zero. This represents a sharp reversal from just one day earlier, when the probability of unchanged rates stood at 16%. It was 17.3% a week ago and 15.9% one month earlier.

Markets now assign an 86.3% probability to a 25-basis-point rate increase, taking the target range to 4%–4.25%. Another 13.7% probability is assigned to a larger 50-basis-point increase.

The liquidation data paints an equally uncomfortable picture. CoinGlass recorded $732 million in forced closures across crypto markets over 24 hours on November 11. Long positions accounted for $578 million, meaning traders betting on higher prices absorbed most of the damage.

Bitcoin also lost its 50-week moving average near $76,100, ending a seven-week streak above the technical level. The breakdown followed a week of heavy institutional selling, with US spot Bitcoin ETFs recording approximately $1.28 billion in net outflows.

The combination of ETF withdrawals, leveraged liquidations and inflation uncertainty has created a difficult environment for buyers. Social chatter has pushed back against describing the move as a full-blown crash, pointing to comparisons with the Nasdaq’s monthly decline. Nevertheless, losing important technical levels has given bears another reason to test market confidence.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin price problems are unfolding alongside renewed political anxiety. Recent US midterm election results have strengthened Democratic influence in Congress, raising questions about the future direction of crypto regulation.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 CFTC Chair says they will "future-proof" crypto regulations."We can't allow Gary Gensler 2.0 to come in and tear it all up." pic.twitter.com/ik6gt3Xtns

The regulatory uncertainty could complicate efforts to establish clearer rules for the industry. While tokenization and stablecoin initiatives may continue under existing frameworks, Democratic oversight could slow new legislation and challenge the durability of regulatory guidance.

Meanwhile, Old Glory Bank CEO Mike Ring has accused the Federal Reserve of blocking his institution’s crypto-integrated banking launch at the last minute.

DeFi. The next level of financial freedom. Fly above the Fed! The blockchain is the runway.Hear CEO Mike Ring explain why. pic.twitter.com/AGlN7sU0Ou

Ring’s complaint, summarized in his public comments, shows the central bank remains hostile toward crypto-friendly banking initiatives. He described the setback as evidence that the Fed hates crypto.

Old Glory Bank is reportedly pursuing an alternative launch strategy that avoids requiring the same Federal Reserve approval, potentially targeting the first quarter of 2027.

What do all these mean for crypto? The immediate challenge for Bitcoin price remains getting back above $75,000 and rebuilding confidence after the latest liquidation wave. A deeper decline would put additional pressure on already nervous traders.

Yet the longer-term Bitcoin thesis has not necessarily disappeared. Concerns about government spending, monetary debasement, and currency purchasing power continue to support the argument for holding scarce digital assets.

#5515. ServiceNow launches AI-powered engine to accelerate migrations from CRM rivals

ServiceNow Inc. is bidding to steal business from other customer relationship management vendors with an artificial intelligence-powered engine that it says can reduce enterprise CRM implementations from months to weeks.

The new Autonomous CRM Engine uses AI to analyze existing CRM environments, recommend business process improvements and automate deployment of redesigned workflows on ServiceNow’s platform.

The offering represents a competitive challenge to established CRM providers such as Salesforce Inc. and Microsoft Corp. by potentially lowering the switching costs that help vendors retain customers. The initial rollout targets only Salesforce installations, and others are planned.

The announcement comes amid growing concern about the costs and limitations of aging CRM systems. Gartner Inc. last year warned that legacy CRM platforms can create hidden maintenance expenses, integration dependencies and security risks that impede modernization. The researcher predicts that by 2028, most enterprises will identify outdated CRM systems as an obstacle to effectively using AI.

Gartner recommends that organizations evaluate technical debt, integration dependencies, data quality and the full cost of maintaining legacy CRM systems before deciding whether to modernize or replace them.

The discovery process is one of the most time-consuming aspects of CRM modernization, said Terence Chesire, group vice president of CRM and industry workflows at ServiceNow. Organizations typically must interview employees across departments and geographies to understand how sales and service processes operate.

“We’re able to collapse that into literally days where we show them how all their sales processes occur by product line,” he said.

Autonomous CRM Engine uses metadata application programming interfaces to examine business objects, configuration settings, custom scripts and workflows. It organizes that information into a graph database and applies AI to reconstruct how activities such as sales approvals, customer escalations and service requests actually function.

ServiceNow claims the analysis can expose discrepancies between documented procedures and everyday practices, including approval steps employees routinely bypass.

Beyond transferring existing processes to a new platform, ServiceNow uses the discovery information to recommend redesigned workflows based on industry practices. Business leaders can examine proposed changes in a visual workspace and modify processes to accommodate unique business characteristics. Once approved, changes can be deployed directly into ServiceNow’s CRM environment.

Chesire acknowledged that automation doesn’t eliminate difficult organizational decisions or integration challenges. “The parts that potentially get extended are all those linkages to other systems because we always land inside a heterogeneous environment,” he said.

ServiceNow addresses those dependencies through its Workflow Data Fabric, which provides access to external information without the need to move or copy it. Its integration capabilities also extend to older applications through robotic process automation.

Gartner cautions that CRM modernization projects must account for hidden application dependencies, regulatory data-retention requirements and business processes that may rely on retired systems. It also recommends establishing clear data ownership and governance policies before making changes.

The research firm suggests measuring modernization success through operational improvements rather than retired applications. It suggests performance targets such as annual operating cost reductions of at least 20%, retention of 95% of historical data in searchable archives and a 35% reduction in duplicate or inconsistent records.

Chesire acknowledged that ServiceNow hasn’t conducted comparative productivity studies against competing CRM platforms, although the company demonstrates its technology to prospects using their own business processes and data. The firm cited several customer examples to demonstrate the potential benefits of consolidating customer operations.

Germany soccer league Bundesliga-Gruppe GmbH consolidated fan services from seven digital channels onto ServiceNow in about a month and now resolves 89% of fan inquiries on first contact, according to ServiceNow. Bell Canada connected 26 applications and 8,800 data silos to one platform to support 12,000 field employees, while Everpure Inc. eliminated 13 legacy systems and now resolves 72% of customer issues before they’re reported.

Chesire said AI adoption is increasing pressure to modernize systems whose business logic is buried in custom code. ServiceNow plans to extend Autonomous CRM Engine’s capabilities to continuously monitor configurations and eventually improve CRM operations autonomously.

The engine is available now, with additional capabilities planned for 2027.

ServiceNow said its CRM and Industry Workflows business has surpassed $2 billion in annual contract value. Its CRM net new annual contract value tripled both sequentially and year-over-year in the third quarter.

#5514. Wendy's rejected a $1.4 billion takeover offer as its stock rose 37% in 11 trading days

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Trian-led investor group offered $7.35 a share in cash, and the company adopted a one-year poison pill

Wendy's $WEN rejected a $1.4 billion takeover offer from an investor group led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management on Nov. 5, according to CNBC. On Oct. 28, the group proposed paying $7.35 in cash for each share, a bid that would take the burger chain private.

Wendy's stock has gained 37% in the past 11 sessions and now sits near $8. It did not post a losing session in that stretch, according to MarketWatch. The gain has nearly cleared the stock's decline for this year, but the shares still trade far under the highs north of $20 they hit in the early part of the 2020s.

Besides Trian, the investor group includes BlueFive Capital, Sixth Street Partners and Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees, according to CNBC.

Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors in February to assess any bid from Trian after the firm made a regulatory filing, according to CNBC. The committee concluded that the offer "substantially undervalues" Wendy's while overlooking the benefits the chain could see from its turnaround strategy, according to CNBC.

"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," said Art Winkleblack, who chairs Wendy's board and sits on its independent committee, in a statement, according to CNBC. Trian declined to comment on the decision.

As protection against an unwanted hostile bid, Wendy's put a poison pill, formally a shareholder rights plan, in place on Nov. 4 that runs for one year, according to CNBC. The Trian-led group rebuffed a proposal from Wendy's to sign a standstill agreement freezing further stock buying, and that refusal contributed to the decision to adopt the pill.

Wendy's stock dipped by under 1% during early trading on Nov. 5. The stock, which has shed roughly 60% of its value across three years, got a lift from the takeover offer, according to CNBC.

Wendy's named Peltz chairman emeritus in 2024 after he spent 17 years on its board, according to CNBC. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley Peltz, remain on the board.

#5513. Mortgage lock in decay is measurable, the annual unlock rate is 5.8%

Mortgage lock in is suppressing turnover, with existing sales near 4.2 million versus a 5 million norm. The article lays out 4 life event driven channels that can unlock listings, with a cited 5.8% annual decay rate.  AI Summary

Mortgage lock-in is real and measurable. It is also decaying on its own, because death, divorce, diapers, and diplomas keep arriving on schedule. Here is how to work that schedule.

There is a number floating around this fall that explains the mood in most sales meetings. Research by Compass economist Jonah Coste calculates that mortgage rate lock-in is preventing about 870,000 home sales in 2026 that would otherwise take place, with existing home sales running near 4.2 million against a long-run norm of 5 million. With the 30-year rate at 7.35% as of the November 12, nobody in the room expects relief soon.

Read that same research one paragraph further though, and you find the sentence a real estate professional should tape to the dashboard. About 5.8% of locked-in homes get unlocked every year through what the economists call normal demographic and economic activity. That is their phrase for it. This business has always had a shorter one. Death, divorce, diapers and diplomas. The four D’s.

Those four events are the reason lock-in decays whether rates fall or not. They are not a forecast. They are a tide chart.

A charter captain does not cancel the season because the weather turned. He fishes the tide, because the tide table was printed a year ago, and the tide shows up on time no matter what the sky is doing. The rate is the weather. The four D’s are the tide. An agent who only works when the weather is pleasant will spend most of this cycle tied to the dock. The one who learns to read the table will come back with a full boat while everyone else is refreshing the forecast.

Here is the table, one ‘D’ at a time: where the list lives, and what to bring when you show up.

Every estate holding real property ends in a sale or a transfer, and the people managing it are almost always doing it for the first time.

The List: Probate court filings, which are public, county-level and frequently online.

The Better List: The attorneys who file them. Estate attorneys, elder law attorneys, trust administrators. Add the liquidation companies and the move managers who empty the house before anyone thinks to call an agent.

What to bring: A valuation as of the date of death, at no charge, on any file where the attorney needs one. Every estate requires that figure for tax basis and most agents have never thought to offer it. Be the one who does. Do not contact a family off an obituary, ever. The professionals around the family are the door. Walk through it with service in your hands rather than a business card.

A divorce splits a household in half, and the house seldom fits either half. What makes these listings difficult is not pricing or marketing. It is that both spouses must agree on you.

The List: Family law attorneys, mediators, and the planners who specialize in divorce finances. They know about the house roughly six months before the MLS does.

What to bring. Neutrality in writing. A single page the attorney can give both parties explaining how the sale works, how proceeds are typically held, and what the timeline looks like. Offer to meet each spouse on their own. An attorney’s biggest worry is an agent who picks a side. Remove that worry and you become the standing referral for the whole practice.

No rate on earth holds a family in a two-bedroom once the second child arrives. The lock-in researchers can model payment shock with precision. They cannot model a crib in the dining room.

The List: Your own past clients first: every buyer you placed in a small home or condo three to five years back. Then the places young parents already spend their Saturdays, pediatric offices, daycare centers, parent groups, library story time.

What to bring. Your presence rather than your postcard. Sponsor the daycare fundraiser. Show up for the T-ball opener. One Fair Housing note that carries real consequences: advertise the house and the service, never who ought to live there, and have your broker review any audience targeting before it runs.

The August a family’s last child leaves is the August a four-bedroom colonial becomes three empty rooms and a tax bill. Parents feel it at once. They do something about it the next spring.

The List: Graduating senior names are still printed locally every June. Match those surnames to homes bought 18 to 25 years ago in the assessor’s records. What you are holding is a roster of parents about to stand in an empty bedroom wondering what comes next.

What to bring. An empty-nest conversation. Reserve the library meeting room, invite a financial planner, and talk about what happens to a house that got too big. No slides, no listing presentation, no pressure of any kind. Treat people like people in September and they call you in April.

“I’m not reaching out because you have to sell. I’m reaching out so that when life changes, and it changes for all of us, you already know somebody. No presentation and no ask. Only a name worth holding onto.”

Then stop talking. That is a conversation rather than a sales call, and it works across all four D’s because it is honest about who you are and what you want. Serve first, and the listing takes care of itself.

The agents waiting on a rate cut are watching the weather. The agents working the four D’s are fishing the tide, and the tide, unlike the weather, has never once missed an appointment.

#5511. Why Bitcoin, Nasdaq, AI Stocks, and Chips Move Together? The Liquidity Machine Explained

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin can fall alongside Nvidia, and Nasdaq can rally while Ethereum follows. Semiconductor stocks can plunge as investors reassess AI spending, dragging crypto sentiment down with them. These markets appear to have little in common. Bitcoin was designed outside traditional banking, while chipmakers supply the infrastructure powering artificial intelligence.

Yet they increasingly respond to the same financial force: liquidity.

The Federal Reserve, US Treasury, Wall Street, and institutional investors form a financial network connecting these seemingly unrelated markets. Understanding that network explains why everything from Bitcoin and Ethereum to Nvidia, TSMC, and AI infrastructure can move together.

The Federal Reserve sits near the center of this relationship. Its interest rate decisions influence borrowing costs, bond yields, financing conditions, and investor appetite for risk.

When interest rates fall, investors generally become more comfortable holding riskier assets. Cheaper financing can support technology valuations, speculative investments, and crypto demand. When rates rise, the opposite can happen. Investors reassess expensive valuations, reduce leverage, and move toward safer assets.

Quantitative tightening adds another layer, and here’s why: the Fed reduces its balance sheet, and Treasury securities return to private investors. This can reduce available reserves and put pressure on short-term funding markets.

The US Treasury also influences liquidity through government borrowing and its Treasury General Account. Large changes in government cash balances can affect money circulating through the banking system.

Banks, money-market funds, hedge funds and primary dealers connect these policies to financial markets. Repo financing, Treasury yields and institutional funding costs help determine how much capital investors can deploy.

The Federal Reserve’s August 2026 research examined these connections directly. It found that Treasury issuance and dealer holdings can put upward pressure on repo rates.

“The overnight Treasury repo market is one of the most important funding markets in the world. It sees more than $8 trillion in daily trading volume and plays a vital role in broader Treasury market liquidity and price discovery.3 Repo rates also determine the secured overnight financing rate (SOFR)—now the primary reference rate for trillions of dollars of financial contracts—thereby affecting broader financial conditions.” – Fed’s Research

This is why Bitcoin does not need a Federal Reserve policy change to affect its network. A change in financing conditions can influence investors holding Bitcoin, Nasdaq stocks, and other risky assets simultaneously.

Artificial intelligence has created one of the largest investment cycles in modern technology. But the boom extends far beyond software companies. Nvidia supplies GPUs powering AI infrastructure. AMD competes in accelerated computing, while Broadcom supplies networking and custom silicon.

TSMC manufactures advanced chips used across the industry. ASML supplies the lithography equipment needed to produce increasingly sophisticated semiconductors. Samsung and Intel also compete across memory, manufacturing and chip technology. These companies sit at the beginning of an enormous infrastructure spending cycle.

Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle are investing heavily in data centers, cloud computing, power infrastructure and AI capacity. This spending requires capital from multiple sources. Companies issue bonds, borrow from banks, tap private credit and use operating cash flows to finance expansion.

Reuters reported on November 6 that US investment-grade corporate bond issuance reached $1.88 trillion through November 4. Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle raised more than $370.7 billion as they financed AI and data-center investment.

Goldman Sachs expects bonds to fund 35% of hyperscalers’ capital expenditure in 2027. The consequences extend across financial markets. Investors buying AI-related stocks, semiconductor shares and corporate bonds must constantly reassess financing costs and expected returns.

Equity capital will continue to play a supporting role in funding the AI investment boom in 2027.Hyperscalers and other AI infrastructure companies accounted for roughly $65 billion in follow-on issuance (post-IPO equity offerings) this year, around 45% of the US total.In… https://t.co/O9UBnu9S1Z pic.twitter.com/jsBX59xJnw

When investors question AI valuations or the profitability of massive data-center investments, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and their customers can face selling pressure.

That same risk-off sentiment can reach Bitcoin, Ethereum and speculative altcoins. Hedge funds and institutional investors may reduce exposure across several asset classes simultaneously.

The connection is not that Bitcoin depends on Nvidia’s earnings. Both markets are exposed to changes in capital availability, leverage, and investor confidence.

Institutional adoption has fundamentally changed how crypto like Bitcoin markets interact with traditional finance like Nasdaq. BlackRock, Fidelity, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and other financial institutions now participate in digital asset markets through investment products, custody, trading, and infrastructure.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have created another channel between traditional portfolios and crypto prices. When institutional investors adjust their allocations, those flows can influence Bitcoin demand.

Meanwhile, stablecoins connect crypto directly to traditional money markets. Tether and Circle issue dollar-backed stablecoins supported by reserve assets, including US Treasury securities. Their growing importance creates another link between government debt markets and crypto liquidity.

BREAKING: The total circulating supply of onchain tokenized equities surged by +$932 million last week, the biggest weekly jump on record.This puts total supply above $4.7 billion, also a fresh record high.Amid the US Midterm elections and the resulting volatility, tokenized… pic.twitter.com/nkAMG23PJv

Tokenized stocks and Treasury products push this integration further. The SEC issued guidance on tokenized securities in January 2026, clarifying how existing securities laws apply to blockchain-based ownership structures. In September, it also introduced temporary conditional exemptions facilitating certain tokenized stock trading venues.

The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation (DTCC) is another important player in modernizing securities infrastructure through tokenization. Coinbase, Binance, and other crypto exchanges provide additional trading infrastructure connecting digital assets with global capital.

The irony is difficult to ignore. Bitcoin was created after the 2008 financial crisis as an alternative to central banks and traditional monetary systems. Yet its growing institutional ownership has exposed its market price to many of the same forces driving Wall Street.

The important gap is between Bitcoin’s technology and its financial market behavior. Bitcoin’s decentralized network still operates independently of the Federal Reserve. Its supply schedule does not change when Nvidia rallies or Treasury yields increase.

However, its market price is increasingly influenced by institutional positioning, leverage, ETF flows, and global risk appetite.

CME Group research found Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq-100 increased from virtually zero during 2014–2019 to 0.42 during 2020–2022. Its correlation remained around 0.30 between 2023 and April 2025. CME research also found crypto assets sometimes reached correlations of 0.35–0.60 with the Nasdaq during 2025 and early 2026.

This does not mean Bitcoin has become another technology stock. Correlation measures price behavior, not the underlying purpose or value of an asset.

But it raises an important question about Bitcoin’s original mission:

If Bitcoin rises when Wall Street has abundant liquidity and falls when institutional investors reduce risk, how independent is its market value from traditional finance?

#5510. Quantum software startup Q-Ctrl raised $290 million at more than $1 billion valuation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Salesforce Ventures led the Series C round for the quantum software company, which makes GPS-free navigation tools

Q-Ctrl, a quantum software company, raised $290 million in a Series C round led by Salesforce $CRM Ventures, the venture arm of Salesforce, the company said on Thursday. The round values Q-Ctrl at more than $1 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Q-Ctrl said it will expand its software work and scale globally to meet customer demand across sectors from finance to energy. It also plans to continue autonomy and aerospace programs.

The company's main product, Ironstone Opal, is a quantum navigation system that works when GPS is unavailable or denied. Q-Ctrl said the system is being deployed on commercial aircraft with Airbus and in autonomous platforms with Lockheed Martin.

Q-Ctrl counts DARPA, a U.S. military agency, the navies of Australia and Britain, and Airbus among its contract customers, Chief Executive Michael J. Biercuk told Bloomberg. The technology can fix its location with an error of no more than 10 meters (about 33 feet), according to Bloomberg. Jamming and spoofing have degraded satellite navigation signals amid the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Q-Ctrl's software can also make quantum computers more stable by cutting their error rates, according to Bloomberg. "Think of our software as the equivalent of noise-canceling headphones," Biercuk told Bloomberg.

"The hard problem in quantum is not building the machine, it is getting useful output from it," Robert Keith, a partner at Salesforce Ventures, said in a statement. Keith said Q-Ctrl's control software is the reason Salesforce Ventures led the round.

"Q-CTRL is one of the few quantum companies with real customers and real revenue," Per Roman, founding partner of Bullhound Capital and a Q-Ctrl board member, said in a statement.

#5509. HARVARD DIVISION OF CONTINUING EDUCATION LAUNCHES HARVARD DIGITAL DISCOVERY FOR HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS WORLDWIDE

New online program helps students explore academic interests, build essential skills, and prepare for college through flexible Harvard learning experiences.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Harvard University Division of Continuing Education (DCE) has launched Harvard Digital Discovery, an online program that gives high school students worldwide a flexible way to explore college-level subjects and build skills for college and beyond.

Designed for students still exploring what they want to study, Harvard Digital Discovery offers flexible, self-paced Harvard-developed courses including artificial intelligence, law, psychology, business, economics, and more. Students can explore a range of fields without committing to one or joining a traditional summer residential program.

"High school is a time of tremendous curiosity and possibility, but students are increasingly expected to make important decisions about their futures before they've had the opportunity to explore their interests," said Nancy Coleman, Ed.D., Dean of Harvard Extension School and Continuing Studies. "Harvard Digital Discovery gives students the freedom to discover what excites them, learn from pre-eminent Harvard faculty, build confidence in their abilities, and develop skills that will serve them throughout their education."

The program offers workshops on critical thinking, communication, time management, and resilience; academic webinars; and college preparation resources for students and families. Students who complete courses can earn digital badges recognizing their achievements.

"Bringing Harvard's tremendous intellectual breadth together with world class digital classes and college skill readiness is an amazing opportunity for young learners everywhere," said Vice Provost for Advances in Learning, Dustin Tingley, Ph.D.

The subscription-based program offers asynchronous courses students can take year-round, from anywhere in the world.

Developed by DCE and Harvard's Office of the Vice Provost for Advances in Learning (VPAL), Harvard Digital Discovery joins DCE's Pre-College Program and Secondary School Program. Together, these programs offer high school students academic exploration, immersive learning, and college-level study.

"We are delighted to bring this important learning experience to students around the world, extending Harvard's tradition of educational excellence and expanding access to meaningful opportunities for academic discovery," said Coleman.

About Harvard's Division of Continuing Education

The Harvard Division of Continuing Education is dedicated to bringing rigorous academics and innovative teaching capabilities to those seeking to improve their lives through education. We make Harvard education accessible to learners in all phases of life from high school to career through retirement. DCE also includes the Harvard Extension School, one of the 12 degree granting colleges of Harvard University.

About Harvard's Office of the Vice Provost for Advances in Learning

The Office of the Vice Provost for Advances in Learning creates and catalyzes deeply engaging and scalable learning experiences that make a difference at Harvard and beyond through on campus workshops bringing together educators, scalable technology investments, and deeply engaging digital learning offerings.

#5508. MSC Cruises is fighting a $1.8B U.S. trade secrets lawsuit in a U.K. court

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The cruise line wants a London judge to hear confidentiality claims from startup Dreamology Labs, which sued in Florida

MSC Cruises petitioned a High Court judge in London to rule that the trade secrets claims in a $1.8 billion U.S. lawsuit belong before British courts, according to Bloomberg.

Dreamology Labs, an immersive entertainment company, and founder Alessandra Maderni claim in the Florida suit that MSC Cruises copied their concepts without authorization during partnership talks. The suit also accuses MSC executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago of coercing her and committing sexual misconduct, according to Bloomberg. MSC did not ask the London court to block those claims.

MSC argues that London is the proper venue since the confidentiality agreements between the two sides fall under English law, and that Miami was the wrong place to bring the claims, according to Bloomberg. The company has yet to file its defense in the Florida court.

"We strongly dispute the allegations of the U.S. legal proceedings and the defenses made before the High Court in London," MSC said in an emailed statement, according to Bloomberg. "We will defend these claims vigorously through the appropriate legal process, including by holding Ms. Maderni and Dreamology Labs responsible for their false and defamatory statements." The company called the sexual misconduct allegations "false and without merit."

Maderni said in a statement sent to Bloomberg that MSC's response in the U.K. "has only made me more determined to pursue accountability for both the commercial and sexual exploitation alleged."

Dreamology's lawyers say in the Florida complaint that Vago and Maderni were introduced in 2019. Vago later reached out to her himself, a meeting was arranged, and the two sides executed a nondisclosure agreement before they began swapping proprietary ideas, according to the complaint.

Maderni’s lawyers allege that Vago asked her up to his Miami hotel suite in early 2022, while the two were discussing “multi-million dollar collaborations,” and gave her a kiss on the cheek. They allege he summoned her to his room again the next day and started a sexual encounter with her. When she protested, he promised to back her but canceled meetings and pulled out of a potential deal, the lawyers allege. In filings drawn up ahead of a Nov. 3 hearing in a London court, they said “a coercive dynamic developed in which Mr. Vago would connect sexual advances with promises of business dealings.”

Dreamology says MSC reproduced ideas it had been given, such as giant fish sculptures, ship structures draped in the tentacles of sea monsters and games aimed at younger passengers, in designs and activities on its ships. It says that conduct led to financial losses and also deprived the company of openings to expand, secure funding and form partnerships.

MSC Cruises ranks as the largest closely held cruise operator globally, according to Bloomberg.

#5507. Clipto enables ChatGPT and Claude to search and analyze years of people’s meetings and video calls

Artificial intelligence assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have become essential tools for millions of workers worldwide, helping them compose emails in seconds, generate complex code and draft reports by looking at whatever data that person has access to.

But there’s one thing that’s missing from those chatbots’ knowledge. Ask them what was discussed in the previous week’s team meeting or on yesterday’s call with a client, and it will be stumped.

It’s this shortcoming that a startup called Clipto Inc. is trying to solve with the launch of a new AI chatbot memory platform called Clipto Studio, which enables AI assistants to listen in on calls, presentations and meetings and search through them or analyze them upon request.

Clipto argues that this is going to be an important capability as AI becomes more pervasive in daily work. Though AI chatbots can sift through email inboxes and corporate databases in seconds, that’s not where many companies’ most valuable knowledge is actually stored. Rather, Clipto says the most important business insights are trapped in raw video and audio files.

Most of the big decisions are made during Zoom calls, customer interviews and team meetings, but the details of those discussions are stored in heavy, unstructured data formats that are incredibly expensive for AI to process. But AI can potentially provide much more meaningful help to workers if it has a way to access this knowledge.

That’s where Clipto Studio comes in. It’s a native skill set that integrates directly with ChatGPT, Claude and other AI assistants using the Model Context Protocol, powered by proprietary models that run locally on user’s Mac and Windows computers.

The software works by pre-indexing speech, individual speaker’s voices, facial expressions and other on-screen visuals before transforming the raw footage into a structured and easily searchable dataset that’s optimized for AI chatbots. Then, when the user asks a question about one of their recent conversations, or even one from two years ago, it can quickly find the answers it needs by searching through the metadata of those recordings.

Clipto founder and Chief Executive Henry Kang said AI knows basically everything that has been posted online, but has barely scratched the surface of the terabytes of audio and video data that’s sitting in people’s hard drives.

“The next generation of AI will need to understand the conversations, experiences and knowledge that never makes it into a text-based document,” he said. “That’s the future we’re building, giving AI the memory it needs to move beyond answering questions from the internet and start getting real world done with what we ourselves have seen and heard.”

Clipto Studio can be thought of as a kind of instant-replay service. For instance, a management consultant could ask ChatGPT to pinpoint the exact time when a project’s scope changed by looking at more than six month’s worth of calls and meetings, and it will surface the exact moment when that occurred. Alternatively, a researcher might prompt Claude to identify the most common problems with a particular product or service by looking at thousands of customer calls, and pull out direct quotes that illustrate the depth of those issues.

There are other use cases too. For instance, users could ask Clipto Studio to look at dozens of hours of event presentations they’ve attended and create a highlight reel that surfaces the most interesting or relevant moments from them.

Clipto Studio’s official launch is a big moment for the startup, which recently signaled its ambitions with the hiring of former Google LLC research scientist Dr. Mei Han as its new chief scientist. Han, who holds a doctorate in robotics from Carnegie Mellon University, has been tasked with leading the development of Clipto’s lightweight multimodal AI architecture.

Han said she believes in Clipto’s mission because it’s trying to help AI perceive the world in the same way as humans do, by seeing and listening to what’s going on around them.

“The challenge isn’t just recognizing speech or identifying what’s on screen,” she said. “It’s connecting that information across thousands of recordings so AI can understand the context and use it. We’re building the technology to make video and audio as accessible and as useful to AI as text, opening up an entirely new generation of applications.”

#5506. LinkSquares Named 2026 "Contract Management Solution of the Year" by LegalTech Breakthrough

BOSTON, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LinkSquares, the leading Agentic contract lifecycle management (CLM) platform, today announced it is the winner of "Contract Management Solution of the Year" in the 7th annual LegalTech Breakthrough Awards program conducted by LegalTech Breakthrough, a leading independent market intelligence organization that evaluates and recognizes standout legal technology companies, products and services around the globe.

LinkSquares' award-winning platform, powered by our advanced LinkAI engine, combines predictive, generative, and agentic AI to redefine contract lifecycle management (CLM). Predictive AI helps legal teams stay ahead of renewals and mitigate risks before they arise. Generative AI accelerates drafting and review with instant agreement summaries and intelligent clause recommendations. Agentic AI automates metadata extraction and validation with exceptional accuracy, empowering organizations to reduce risk, drive revenue growth, and unlock deeper insights from their contracts.

In 2026, LinkSquares rebuilt its platform around an agentic architecture, resulting in a model where autonomous AI agents can understand contracts as structured data, reason across that data, and take action based on what they find. LinkSquares AI architecture empowers users to deliver accurate results quickly. Able to simplify complex searches and generate tailored clauses, while delivering autonomous insights, the multi-agent approach ensures speed, accuracy, and smarter decision-making and legal clarity across every business function.

"LinkSquares is absolutely revolutionizing contract management. In-house Legal is not a low-stakes game for the organization it serves or the legal teams managing the workload. Contract management has long relied on manual effort that slows legal down, with teams challenged to find, track, and act on contract data fast enough to stay compliant and make informed decisions," said Bryan Vaughn, Managing Director, LegalTech Breakthrough. "LinkAI, the intelligence engine behind LinkSquares, powers advanced contract analytics, automated reviews, and smarter workflows, letting teams spot risk faster, accelerate deals, and extract clear insights from every agreement. We are proud to single out LinkSquares and its Agentic AI advances with 'Contract Management Solution of the Year.'"

"Traditional contract management tools and generic LLMs aren't built for legal work at scale, and most legal AI platforms have simply bolted AI capabilities onto legacy systems. We built LinkSquares' agentic platform from the ground up on agentic AI infrastructure, trained specifically for legal documents," said Andrew Leverone, Chief Product Officer at LinkSquares. "On behalf of LinkSquares, I'm thrilled to accept this award from LegalTech Breakthrough. We'll continue to enhance our technology to automate the entire contract lifecycle, from creation and negotiation through execution, obligation tracking, and renewal, helping clients extract key data, flag risk, and surface insights."

The legal technology sector is rapidly redefining how legal work gets done, transforming one of the world's most complex and vital industries. From AI legal assistants and agentic research to contract intelligence, eDiscovery, court and compliance technology, and connected legal operations platforms, legal technology is delivering greater speed, transparency and access to justice for law firms, legal departments, courts and the people they serve.

The mission of the annual LegalTech Breakthrough Awards program is to recognize the innovators transforming the global legal landscape with breakthrough technology. The program conducts a comprehensive analysis of the companies redefining how legal services are researched, drafted, managed and delivered. From AI-driven research and drafting platforms and contract lifecycle management to eDiscovery, case and practice management, regulatory compliance, legal spend analytics and access-to-justice solutions, these innovations are enabling legal organizations to work more efficiently, serve clients better and shape the future of the legal profession.

Built on more than a decade of experience partnering with general counsel and legal operations leaders, LinkSquares' all-agentic AI platform sets a new standard for how AI operates across the contract lifecycle. #5505. AI Infrastructure Numbers Keep Climbing While the Week's Headlines Turn to the Boardroom

NEW YORK, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Market Updates News Commentary - Much of this week's coverage of the AI chip trade has focused on a boardroom rather than a balance sheet. The reports filed by the companies that design, manufacture, buy and rent out AI computing capacity tell their own story, one built on revenue, backlogs and spending plans that are on the record. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM), Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN), and CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV).

What the Board Said, and What the Business Reported

At NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA), the board said on Nov. 8 that it is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, to be overseen by a committee of independent directors assisted by outside independent counsel. The board said it has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, and that it will provide further updates as appropriate.

The business underneath those headlines is a matter of record. For its fiscal second quarter ended July 26, 2026, Nvidia reported revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, including Data Center revenue of $89.0 billion, up 117%. The company guided third quarter revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and said its Vera Rubin platform is now in full production. Beneath the hardware sits CUDA, the parallel computing platform Nvidia launched in 2006. In March, marking 20 years of the platform, the company said CUDA now serves as the foundation for 6 million developers worldwide.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM) reported on Nov. 10 that consolidated revenue for October 2026 was approximately NT$586.89 billion, an increase of 14.7% from September and 59.7% from October 2025. Revenue for January through October totaled NT$4,485.62 billion, up 43.3% from the same period of 2025.

That followed a third quarter in which TSMC's revenue rose 50.9% year over year to NT$1,494.24 billion, or US$46.72 billion, with 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies accounting for 79% of wafer revenue. The company guided fourth quarter revenue to US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion and said it expects continued strong demand for its leading-edge technologies, including a steep ramp of its 2-nanometer process.

Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN) reported on Oct. 29 that AWS segment sales increased 39% year over year to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, which the company described as the unit's fastest growth in nearly five years, bringing AWS to a $184 billion annualized revenue run rate. Amazon said it continues to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion, and that the year-over-year increase in its purchases of property and equipment primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence.

CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV) reported on Nov. 10 third quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, compared with $1.37 billion a year earlier, and a revenue backlog of approximately $132.5 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026. The company said it has brought online multi-rack NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 deployments. CoreWeave raised its full year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion and now expects full year capital expenditures of $37 billion to $39 billion, raising the low end of its prior range, which it attributed to expecting to deploy infrastructure and deliver it to customers sooner than planned.

The next scheduled report comes from Nvidia itself. The company has said it will host a conference call on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 5 p.m. ET to discuss results for its fiscal third quarter, which ended Oct. 25, 2026, with CFO commentary provided in writing ahead of the call. Until then, the clearest view of AI infrastructure demand remains the one in the filings above, reported by the companies themselves.

#5504. Google agreed to add employee privacy safeguards to clear Spirit Airlines data deal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The revised agreement resolves union objections over AI training use of employee files and still needs bankruptcy court approval

Spirit filed the revised agreement Monday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in New York, according to The Wall Street Journal. It settles complaints raised by the unions for Spirit's pilots and flight attendants, which had cautioned that workers' personal records would be used to train commercial AI tools. The deal still requires bankruptcy court approval.

Under the new terms, the sale leaves out a range of worker records, including medical files, drug and alcohol test results, investigations tied to labor matters, records of grievances and arbitration, performance reviews and payroll, among other employment-related materials, according to The Wall Street Journal. An independent verifier will examine how the data is put to use and confirm that confidentiality and security obligations are being met.

A Spirit spokesperson said the carrier welcomed settling the unions' disputes about the "sale of deidentified data" while it works to get the most value it can for creditors, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Google won the August bankruptcy auction for Spirit's digital archives, according to The Wall Street Journal. The archives contain decades of payroll, travel and recruiting files, along with about 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts and millions of other digital items. Google has said the purchase excludes personal information, and that it intends to apply the data toward improving its products and AI models.

Google agreed to pay $10 million for Spirit's internal business data after winning the auction. AI hiring platform Mercor was the runner-up with a $7.5 million offer. Google said a third party would scrub personally identifiable information from the data before handoff.

Spirit ceased operations earlier this year after a government rescue package collapsed, leaving roughly 17,000 employees and contractors without work.
